nl_description:
Scoping the inpatient warehouse rebuild for a 900-bed tertiary centre. Volumes first, because they drive the partitioning: eleven years of history, about 1.4 million admission episodes, and the nurse-observation feed alone lands roughly 34 million rows a year.

Patients are identified internally by a UUID and externally by MRN; we hold date of birth, sex and blood group and nothing else demographic. An admission episode pins a patient to a specific bed, and beds sit in wards -- each ward has a named specialty and a fixed bed complement, and some beds are flagged isolation-capable. Every episode has an attending clinician (registered practitioners, each with a registration number, a grade and a specialty of their own), an admitted timestamp, a discharge timestamp, a derived length of stay in days, an admission source and a discharge disposition. Internal moves between beds are recorded as their own event with a from-bed, a to-bed, a timestamp and a reason -- we lose that history today and it is the main reason for the rebuild.

Coding is many-to-many. An episode carries several ICD-10 codes; each code, with its description and chapter, recurs across thousands of episodes; one of an episode's codes is flagged primary and the rest are sequenced.

Observations are heart rate, systolic BP, temperature in Celsius, SpO2 as a percentage and the computed NEWS2 aggregate, stamped to the second against the episode. Prescribing is one order per drug per episode -- dose in mg, doses per day, start and stop timestamps, and the prescriber -- and the drug catalogue itself carries an ATC code and a controlled-substance flag.

Distributions we have already measured: length of stay is log-normal, log-mean 1.1, log-variance 0.8. Heart rate is roughly normal at 82 with an SD of 14, temperature normal at 36.9 with SD 0.6. Admission source splits 61% emergency department, 24% elective, 9% inter-hospital transfer, 6% other. Drug usage is brutally long-tailed -- rank frequency fits a Zipf with exponent near 1.6.

Checks to enforce: SpO2 between 50 and 100, NEWS2 between 0 and 20, length of stay never negative. A controlled drug may only be prescribed by a clinician at consultant grade. Any observation with systolic below 90 or saturation below 92 must carry a NEWS2 of 5 or more.

I run a small allergy clinic on my own, two mornings and three afternoons a week, and the whole thing is currently held together by a filing cabinet and a spreadsheet my old receptionist built. I have got maybe eleven hundred people on the books and I see a dozen or so a day, so this is not a big system, but I would like it to stop being a spreadsheet.

The people who come in -- I say patients, the letters from the hospital say clients, it is the same thing -- I need their name, when they were born, a phone number, and who sent them, because nearly everyone arrives on a referral from their GP and I write down which surgery. I also want the date I first saw them, because for the insurers that matters.

Then the appointments. Date and time obviously, and whether it was a first consultation or a follow-up, because those are different lengths and different money. A first one takes about forty minutes and a follow-up twenty; across everything it averages out to something like twenty-eight minutes with maybe eight minutes of slop either side. A first visit is 120 and a follow-up is 70, and nothing in this place ever costs less than 70 or more than 120. My receptionist worked out that of every hundred booked slots, 87 turn up, 8 simply do not bother, and the other 5 ring beforehand and cancel, which at least lets me fill it.

The clinical bit is the skin prick testing. In one appointment we might test a dozen allergens, and for each one there is the allergen itself and the size of the weal in millimetres. Anything over three millimetres I call a positive. Most of the readings are basically nothing at all with a long tail up to the big reactors -- if you averaged every reading I have ever taken you would get about two and a half millimetres, and obviously it cannot go below zero. One more thing: whichever of the two nurses does the pricking initials the sheet, and I would like to keep that, it has saved me twice.

What I do not need is any of the hospital's coding nonsense. I do not bill insurers directly, the patients claim it back themselves, so there is no invoicing in this at all -- the fee on the appointment is the whole of the money side, and the card machine handles the rest. And before you ask: no, I do not want a portal, I do not want an app, and the last person who built me something put the date of birth in American order and I did not notice for a year. Whatever this ends up being, it needs to survive me typing into it at half past six on a Friday with the lights off.

I look after reporting for a dental group -- fourteen practices at the moment, three more in the pipeline. Roughly 400,000 registered patients across the group and we book something like 2.6 million treatment lines a year, so it is not enormous, but it is well beyond what the current spreadsheets cope with.

Each practice has a name, a town and a number of chairs. Chair counts run from three to nine and it is honestly pretty flat across that range -- there is no typical size. Dentists sit at a practice, have a GDC number, and some are flagged as specialists. For patients we hold the name, date of birth, the date they registered with us and which practice is their home one -- though they can be seen anywhere in the group, and that is exactly the bit that breaks the old reports.

An appointment ties a patient to a dentist at a practice at a time. Slots are 15, 30 or 60 minutes -- about half are 30, a bit over a quarter are 15 and the remaining fifth are the hour-longs. There is a status on the appointment, something like booked, attended, cancelled, failed-to-attend; I would have to check the exact list with the software people. A specialist's list is always booked in hour slots, no exceptions.

Under an appointment we record the individual items of work. Each one points at a treatment code from a central list -- the code carries a description, an NHS band and a standard fee -- plus the tooth it was done on and what we actually charged. Tooth numbering runs 1 to 48 because the children's teeth live in the same scheme. Any band 3 item is charged at least 282.80.

Fees are very skewed with a long right tail; the log of the charged fee sits around 3.9 with a log-variance of about 0.7. Patient mix is 55% NHS, 31% private and 14% on our own payment plan.

Oh -- we also flag when an appointment ends in a referral out to an implant specialist we do not employ. I am not sure that belongs in the same place, but it is on the form so it needs to land somewhere.

Dispensing warehouse spec. 480 community pharmacies, 61 million dispensing events last year, about 5 million new fact rows a month, so date partitioning throughout.

Stores carry a four-character store code, a region, an opening date and a 24-hour flag. Pharmacists have a home store and a council registration number, and exactly one per store is flagged superintendent. Customers are UUID-keyed with NHS number, date of birth, a prescription-charge exemption flag and, where they are exempt, the exemption code. The product catalogue holds a product name, an ATC code, the controlled-drug schedule, a unit cost and a cold-chain flag.

A prescription is received at a store for a customer from an external prescriber code, with an issue date, a received timestamp and a source, and explodes into one or more dispensing rows: drug, dispensing pharmacist, quantity, days supply, charge taken, dispense timestamp. Stock is per store per drug -- on-hand units, reorder point, last-counted timestamp -- and that pair is the natural key, no surrogate.

Measured: dispensing by product is near-Zipf, exponent 1.35. Quantity is Poisson-like around 28. Charge amount is log-normal, log-mean 2.2, log-variance 0.9. Source is 78% EPS, 15% paper, 7% repeat dispensing.

Enforce: on-hand units never negative; days supply between 1 and 90; Schedule 2 controlled drugs dispensed only by the superintendent pharmacist; cold-chain lines carry a reorder point of at least 12 units, since those deliveries are twice weekly.

This is for replacing the reporting layer on the LIMS at a regional pathology network. Scale, since you asked: we take work from just over 900 client sites -- GP surgeries, community clinics and three acute trusts -- and we report something like 19 million individual test results a year.

Work arrives as a specimen. A specimen belongs to a patient, and on the patient we hold a lab number, date of birth and sex. It was requested by a named doctor, with their specialty, who works at one of the client sites, and it has a specimen type, a collection time and a receipt time. Sites have a type and sit on a courier route; there has been talk of tracking the individual courier run that brought the bag in, but for now the route on the site is all we get. We also mark a specimen rejected, with a reason, when it turns up haemolysed or unlabelled -- and if it is rejected there has to be a reason recorded, because the current system lets that through empty and it is a standing audit finding.

Priority is routine or urgent, plus the STAT ones the wards ring through: about 82% routine, 15% urgent, 3% STAT. A STAT specimen has to be reported within four hours.

Tests are identified by a test code with a name, an owning department, a unit and a turnaround target in hours. Doctors mostly order panels rather than individual tests, and a panel is just a named bundle of test codes with a display order -- the same test code shows up in several panels, so that pairing is its own thing. On average a specimen ends up carrying 7.4 tests and the count behaves like a Poisson.

Each result records the numeric value, a high/low/normal flag, when it was reported, the elapsed turnaround in hours and which analyser produced it. Analysers have a model, a department and an install date. The analytics team fitted turnaround to an exponential with a mean of about six hours.

Reference ranges are held per test code, split by sex and by an age band with a lower and an upper limit on the value. Ages in that table run 0 to 120.

Imaging data mart. About 310,000 studies a year across two sites -- roughly 240 million images, though we hold counts, not pixels.

Grain is the study: accession number, patient, the scanner it ran on, modality, body part, a start timestamp, a duration in minutes, whether contrast was given, and the recorded dose in mGy. Duration means scan time, not room time; the two get conflated in the current reports and we are standardising on scan time. Below a study, one row per series with a series number, an image count and a slice thickness in mm.

Patients carry an MRN, date of birth, sex and weight in kg, since weight drives protocol selection. Scanners have a modality, a manufacturer, a room and, for the MR units, field strength in tesla. Yes, modality lands on both the scanner and the study -- keep both; the study-level value is what the reports read and it does occasionally get overridden.

One report per study: the radiologist, a dictation timestamp, the narrative text, a critical-finding flag and a status. Radiologists have a subspecialty and a consultant flag, and a critical finding must be signed off by a consultant. Somebody has asked for the referring clinician on the study too -- that lives in the RIS and we are deliberately not pulling it across this phase.

Shape: modality mix is 54% plain film, 21% CT, 14% MR, 9% ultrasound, 2% nuclear medicine. Study duration is log-normal, log-mean 2.6, log-variance 0.45. Series image counts are heavy tailed, close to Zipf with exponent 1.9. Patient weight is normal, mean 78.5 kg, SD 17.

Constraints: a plain film never logs more than 20 mGy and never negative -- CT runs far higher, so that ceiling is modality-specific, not global. Slice thickness 0.5 to 10 mm. A series has at least one image.

OK so, background: we are a telehealth outfit, four years in, and last year we did just under 900,000 consultations. The database we are on was built by a contractor in a hurry and I want to start again properly before we sign the next enterprise deal.

We have members. The doctors insist on calling them patients, and honestly the app says 'patient' in two screens and 'member' everywhere else, which tells you how carefully any of this was thought through. Either way -- somebody signs up with a name, an email, their date of birth, the country they are in, and they sit on one of our plans. There is a free tier, a paid personal one, and the employer-sponsored one we bill differently. We keep the sign-up date too.

The doctors are on a panel rather than employed by us. We need to know where each one is licensed, when they joined the panel, and which languages they speak -- right now that last one is a comma-separated string in a single box, which I am told is grim, but it is what we have.

Then the consultation, which is the thing everyone wants to report on. Somebody hits the button, that is a request time, and at some point they get connected, so there is a connect time and a wait in between. Most people are through in a couple of minutes but a few sit there for ages -- the average wait comes out around four minutes and the tail is long. The call itself is nine and a half minutes almost every time, plus or minus about three. It is video, phone or chat: video is about 62%, phone 29%, chat is the rest. Free-tier members only ever get chat, that one is a hard rule and it is the whole reason people upgrade.

At the end there is an outcome -- advice only, prescription, referral, or send them to A&E -- and the member rates the call one to five stars. People are generous: two thirds give five, about a fifth give four, and the bottom three ratings together are a bit over a tenth of everything.

When the doctor does prescribe, we log what the drug was, how much of it and when it was issued, one line per drug. That gets handed to a partner pharmacy, but their system is not my problem.

Two things I want to be clear about because the last contractor got them wrong. First, a consultation is always exactly one member and exactly one doctor. We tried group sessions for physio, it went badly, and nobody is bringing it back. Second, doctors are not employees and I do not want payroll, rotas, or availability calendars in here -- the scheduling system does that and it can keep doing it. What I want is to be able to answer, in one query, how long people wait by plan and by country, and which doctors are getting the bad ratings. Right now that takes a data person two days and a lot of swearing, and the number is different every time depending on who runs it.

I am the practice lead at a small psychological therapies service -- nine therapists and around 600 people on the caseload at any one time, so we are talking thousands of rows, not millions. We are finally moving off paper diaries and a shared spreadsheet.

The people we see: on the clinical side we hold initials rather than full names, a date of birth, where the referral came from, and the dates we opened and closed the file.

Therapists have a modality -- CBT, EMDR, psychodynamic -- and an accreditation body. Everyone except the two most senior has a supervisor, and the supervisors are therapists here too, so I think that just points back at itself rather than being a separate thing.

Work is organised into episodes of care: one person, one therapist, an open date and a close date, a number of sessions planned, and a discharge reason at the end. A block is usually eight sessions, sometimes six, sometimes twelve. The risk rating sits on the episode rather than on the person, because it genuinely does change between episodes and we got caught out by that in the old spreadsheet.

Then the sessions themselves. People write session, appointment or just meeting depending on who is filling the form in; they are all the same thing. Each one has a date, a length, whether the person turned up, and whether it was in the room or over video. The standard hour is really fifty minutes -- about three quarters are that, then a chunk of thirty-minute check-ins, and the trauma work runs to eighty. Roughly four in five are attended, about 13% get cancelled and the remaining 8% are did-not-attends. If an episode is flagged high risk then the sessions have to be face to face, never remote.

We take outcome measures at sessions -- PHQ-9 mostly, GAD-7 on the anxiety pathway. Each one is the instrument name, a total score and the date it was taken. PHQ-9 totals run 0 to 27; people arrive scoring around fifteen, give or take five or so, and the scores drift down over a block, though I could not put a number on the drift.

Right, so it is me and one other vet, plus Sandra on the desk. We have got about eighteen hundred animals on the books, maybe a bit fewer if you take out the ones we have not laid eyes on in three years.

Everything hangs off the owner, really -- name, mobile number, address, and the date they first registered with us. I say owner, Sandra says client, and the invoices say customer. Same person, three words for it, that is going to have to be sorted out at some point.

Each owner brings in one or more animals, sometimes a whole houseful. For the animal we want the name, what it is, the breed if we know it, roughly when it was born, its weight, whether it has been done, and the microchip number. Weight is the awkward one -- the average across the whole book is about sixteen kilos, but that is a nonsense number: most of them are under ten, and then there is a handful of sixty-plus dogs dragging it upwards. Nothing under a hundred grams and nothing over ninety kilos, that much I can promise you.

What they are: about half dogs, call it 52%, then 38% cats, rabbits are 6%, and the rest is guinea pigs, a few birds and one very old tortoise.

Then the visits. The date, what they came in for, which of us saw them -- we just initial it, there are only two of us -- and the money. A consultation is 42 flat, or 78 if it is out of hours; nine times out of ten it is the 42. We sell food and flea treatment over the counter as well and that goes onto the same bill, we just total it separately from the consult, so if they have bought anything at all then the bill comes to more than the consult fee on its own. And we note when the animal is next due for whatever it is -- boosters, a weight check, that sort of thing.

One thing I should say is that I do not want a stock system. I know that is the obvious next question. We buy the wormers from the wholesaler on a Tuesday, Sandra puts them in the cupboard and when the cupboard looks empty she buys more, and that has worked for nineteen years. The money on the visit is enough. Same with lab work -- the bloods go off to an external lab and the results come back on paper and go in the folder, and I am not putting that in a computer for anyone.

What I actually want out of this is to be able to see, at the start of the week, which animals are overdue for something, and to be able to find an owner from a mobile number when they ring up and start talking without saying who they are, which happens roughly hourly. Anything beyond that is a bonus.

Requirements for the clinical and operational data store that replaces our three siloed extracts. Volume, for sizing: 1.9 million emergency calls a year, 2.4 million dispatch legs against them, and roughly 1.4 million patient encounters.

A call is the entry point -- receipt timestamp, caller number, the location as reported plus the geocoded latitude and longitude, a chief-complaint code, the triage category the call taker assigned, and the control-room staff member who took it. Control-room staff have a name, a centre and a role.

Dispatch is a separate grain, because one call can generate several: one row per vehicle assigned, carrying the call, the vehicle, the shift it was working, and the four timestamps we are measured on -- assigned, mobile, on scene, cleared -- plus the derived response time in seconds, the on-scene minutes and a dispatch outcome. Vehicles belong to a station and have a call sign, a type and an in-service date; stations have a division and a location. Shifts are per vehicle with a start, an end and a shift type. Crew are rostered onto shifts many-to-many, with a role recorded on each rostering, and a crew member has a home station, a qualification and a professional registration number.

Where a patient is actually treated we open an encounter against the dispatch: age, sex, presenting problem, GCS, systolic BP, heart rate, whether they were transported and the receiving hospital. Hospitals carry trauma-centre and PCI capability flags and a location. Interventions performed during an encounter come from a coded list -- each code has a description and a paramedic-only flag -- and one encounter can have several of them, each with a timestamp and the crew member who performed it.

Fitted distributions from the current extracts: response time in seconds is log-normal, log-mean 6.2, log-variance 0.35. On-scene time is roughly normal at 27 minutes with an SD of 9. Triage category splits 6% category 1, 31% category 2, 38% category 3, 19% category 4 and 6% category 5. Patient age is normal-ish, mean 58 with an SD of 22.

Hard rules: GCS is 3 to 15; response time is never negative; a category 1 call must be responded to within 420 seconds; and a paramedic-only intervention must be performed by a crew member holding the paramedic qualification.

domain: Retail Bank Accounts and Branch Network
nl_description:
I look after operations for a mid-sized bank -- we came out of a building society merger about a decade ago, and a fair bit of our record keeping is still held together with string, which is really why we are talking to you.

The centre of it all is the customer. For each one we hold their name, their date of birth, the address we post statements to, and the date they first joined us. We never delete a customer when they close everything down, we just stop them being active, because the auditors want the history.

Then there are the accounts. Current accounts, instant-access savings, and a small number of fixed-term savings bonds. About two thirds of what we hold open is a current account, roughly three in ten is instant access, and the rest -- maybe 4 percent -- is the fixed bonds. Every account belongs to a branch, because our staff bonuses still depend on which branch owns the relationship, and each account has a sort code and account number, the balance, the date it was opened, whether it is still open, and the rate it pays. An account can be a joint account -- we have quite a lot of couples on our books -- so one account may have two or even three people named on it, and equally one person often has several accounts with us. That relationship is the thing our current system handles worst of all.

Balances are all over the place. A typical current account sits somewhere around 2,400 pounds, but there is a very long tail of people holding far more than that. By rule an account is never allowed to go below minus 500 -- that is the arranged overdraft floor we set for everybody, no exceptions.

Every movement of money has to be kept: the date and time it happened, the amount, whether it was money in or money out, a short description of what it was, and the running balance afterwards. The median payment going out is about 38 pounds, though we process the occasional six-figure transfer and that skews everything. Across the whole book we are looking at something like three million of these a month, sitting on 610,000 open accounts.

We have 84 branches, each with a name, the town it is in, and its own sort code. Oh, and one more thing I keep forgetting -- every branch has a manager, and the manager is one of our own staff. So we need basic staff records too: name, job title, which branch they work out of and the date they started. Around 1,900 people all in.

On rates: the instant-access savings pay 3.1 percent and always have, the current accounts pay nothing at all, and the fixed bonds are on 4.6. And for those bonds the money in has to be at least 1,000 pounds and no more than 85,000, which is where the deposit protection stops.

Mortgage origination store for a UK lender, Postgres 16, sized for 1.2 million applications over five years of history against roughly 900,000 properties.

An application is raised by exactly one applicant and is always against one property; joint applications are out of scope for this release, so hold the cardinality at one applicant per application. Applicant rows are identity only -- name, date of birth -- because the bureau score is a point-in-time pull, so we snapshot credit_score onto the application itself rather than the applicant. Applications also carry the channel and the submission timestamp, plus a nullable FK to the broker who introduced the case; direct business leaves it null. Brokers have an FCA reference, a firm name and a panel-tier code.

Property holds the address, postcode, a short property-type code, year built and tenure. A property can be valued more than once -- desktop first, then a physical inspection when the desktop comes back outside tolerance -- so valuations are their own table with the valuation date, the valuer's estimate and the method.

Declared income is one row per source per applicant (employment, self-employment, rental, pension) with the gross annual amount and a verified flag, because affordability is computed over the set. Products are a reference table: product code, initial rate, fixed period in months, and the reversion rate.

When underwriting completes we write a decision row against the application -- the decision, its timestamp, the underwriter's name, free-text notes, and a materialised submission-to-decision lag in days. If the decision is an accept we also write an offer naming the product we priced it on, the advance amount, the LTV, the term in months, the rate actually given and the offer expiry. Payslips and bank statements hang off the application with a document type and an upload timestamp.

Shape from the current warehouse: credit_score is 300-999, mean 780, sd 90. Advance amount is log-normal with a median near 210,000. LTV clusters around 75 with a standard deviation of about 10 and must sit in (0, 95]. Decisions run 62 percent accept, 23 decline, 15 refer. The decision lag is exponential with a mean of 9 days.

Pricing is a tiered lookup on the snapshotted score and the LTV: above 900 with LTV at or below 60 prices at 3.99; above 900 with LTV over 60 prices at 4.29; anything scoring 700 or below prices at 5.75. Separately, the five-year fixes -- the products with a 60-month fixed period -- are only available up to 85 LTV.

I'm the product analyst on our cards book and we are rebuilding the reporting layer from scratch, so here is roughly what has to be in it.

We issue to individuals. I call them cardholders, the ops team still says customers and means exactly the same people. We hold the usual on them: name, date of birth, the address on file, when they were onboarded, and an internal risk band that the scoring job writes back overnight. The band runs A through E and the book skews good -- A is about 18 percent of it, B is 31, C is 27, D is 16 and E is the remaining 8.

A cardholder can have more than one card account. The account is where the credit limit, the APR, the statement day of the month and the current balance live. Cards then sit under the account, physical and virtual, and there can be several of them -- a primary plus an authorised user, replacements after fraud -- each with its own last four digits, expiry date, network and status. Roughly 14 million cards live against about 9.5 million accounts.

Every authorisation that settles becomes a transaction against the card it was made on: the timestamp, the amount, the currency, the merchant, the MCC, and whether it was card-present. Volume is the real problem here -- we are a bit over 900 million settled transactions a year. Spend is extremely concentrated by merchant: a handful of merchants take a wildly disproportionate share and it tails off very fast after them, a textbook power law. The amounts themselves are small and skewed, median somewhere around 24 dollars with the odd very large one. On the merchants we only need the legal name, a category code and the country they are acquired in.

Monthly we cut a statement per account: the period start and end, the opening and closing balance, the minimum payment due and the due date. We also track rewards redemptions -- which account, when, how many points were spent, what they were redeemed for and the cash value we booked.

Limits are set straight off the risk band. Band A accounts get 15,000, band C gets 5,000, and anyone sitting in band E is capped at 1,000. A minimum payment is never less than 25 dollars, and no account anywhere can carry a limit above 50,000 -- that one is a board-approved ceiling and it does not flex.

Motor claims mart for a personal-lines insurer. 6.8 million in-force policies and around 41 million claim-related rows across eight years of history, so partitioning and column ordering both matter.

Policyholder is the paying customer: integer surrogate key, name, date of birth, postcode, date of first policy. A policy is annual, keyed on policy_id, and carries inception and expiry dates, the annual premium as DECIMAL(10,2), a voluntary excess, a cover type of TPO / TPFT / COMPREHENSIVE, and the single vehicle it covers -- one vehicle per policy in this book, no multi-car. We also keep a denormalised annual claim count on the policy row for pricing pulls. Vehicles hold registration, make, model, year of manufacture, engine capacity in cc and a market value.

Named drivers are the genuine many-to-many: a driver appears on several policies (a spouse on both household cars) and a policy names one to four of them, so there is a junction keyed on (policy_id, driver_id) carrying the relationship to the policyholder and a main-driver flag. Driver rows themselves hold licence number, date of birth and years of driving experience.

A claim references both the policy and the driver who was at the wheel, and holds the incident date, the notification date, a notification lag in days that we materialise on write, the claim type, a reserve amount, the settled amount and a status. Payments against a claim are separate rows -- amount, paid date, payee type -- because there are normally several. Where a third party is involved we record their name, their insurer and whether they were legally represented. Repairs go to a panel garage, so a claim optionally names one; garages have a name, a town and an hourly labour rate.

Distribution facts from the last full year. Annual premium is log-normal, median near 640. Cover type splits 71 percent comprehensive, 21 TPFT, 8 TPO. The annual claim count per policy is Poisson with lambda 0.14. Settled amount on a claim is log-normal with a median around 1,850. Driver experience is close to uniform between 1 and 45 years. The notification lag is exponential with a mean of 4 days.

Rules to enforce: voluntary excess is between 0 and 1,000; engine capacity between 600 and 6,500 cc; anything notified more than 30 days after the incident is forced to status REFERRED_SIU; and on a third-party-only policy there is no own-damage cover at all, so the settled amount on those claims is capped at zero.

We are a small outfit -- we only write about 900 new policies a year -- so nobody here has ever needed a proper system, and honestly the spreadsheet has got away from us now.

What happens is that somebody applies for cover through one of our agents. The proposal (we call them proposals, the agents call them applications, the compliance folder says submissions, it is all the same piece of paper) comes in with the person's details, how much cover they are asking for, the term, and the date we received it. Then we go through underwriting. There is a medical questionnaire, sometimes a nurse's report, and a doctor's letter if we have asked for one. Somebody here reads all of that and prices it, and the answer is either standard rates, or we load it by some percentage, or once in a while we just decline.

The people we are covering. We keep the life assured's name, when they were born, whether they smoke, their height and their weight, and what they do for a living. Smoking matters more for pricing than anything else on that list. We do not see many smokers, maybe one in six. Heights come out about average for the population -- five foot nine, give or take three inches -- although I have never been sure whether we ought to be keeping that in feet or in centimetres, and over the years we have done both, which is part of the mess.

Cover amounts vary enormously. Most of what we write is modest, a couple of hundred thousand, but we have done a handful in the millions, so it is very skewed and there is no typical case really. The term is nearly always 25 years -- about six in ten of them -- and the rest splits evenly between 15 and 30.

The medical evidence is the fiddly part. One proposal can have several pieces of it, and for each piece we need to know what kind it was, when it arrived and a short summary of what it said. And the agents -- they are self-employed, there are eleven of them, we pay them a commission rate, and we absolutely have to know which agent brought each proposal in, because that is how they get paid.

Once a proposal is accepted it becomes a policy, with a start date, the monthly premium, and the sum assured, which is the cover amount again under a different name. Policies lapse when people stop paying, and about a fifth of them do.

Two things the regulator cares about. We do not cover anybody under 18 or over 74 at entry, and we will not write more than 3 million on a single life. And where we have loaded somebody for smoking, the loading is never less than 100 percent -- they pay at least double.

Spec for the settlement engine's operational store. Three tables, deliberately -- everything else lives upstream in the ledger and we are not duplicating it.

A participant bank is identified by its BIC, eleven characters, but give it an integer surrogate key as well because it sits on the hot path of every join. Beyond that: legal name, country ISO code, and the central-bank account number we settle against.

A payment instruction is the row that matters. UUID primary key, the debtor participant, the creditor participant, amount as DECIMAL(18,2), a three-letter currency, a value date, a scheme code out of SEPA_CT / SEPA_INST / CHAPS / FPS, a status, and the timestamp we accepted it. We also stamp the inter-arrival gap in milliseconds on the row, because latency analytics used to need a self-join to compute it and that did not scale. We ingest around 38 million instructions a day and retain thirteen months, so it is partitioned by value date.

Instructions are grouped into settlement batches for net settlement. A batch has an id, the cycle number it belongs to (we run six cycles a day), its scheme, the cut-off timestamp, the count of instructions it contains and the net settlement amount. Every instruction carries an FK to its batch, nullable until it has been assigned to one.

Observed shape, from last quarter. Scheme mix is 46 percent SEPA_CT, 34 SEPA_INST, 14 FPS and 6 CHAPS. Instruction amounts are log-normal with a median of 118 euros. The inter-arrival gap within a cycle is exponential, mean 2.3 milliseconds. Instruction count per batch averages about 6.3 million.

Hard rules: an amount is strictly positive and no single instruction may exceed 999,999,999.99; SEPA_INST instructions are capped at 100,000 by scheme rule; and the cycle number is 1 through 6.

Product owner here. We run a retail investing app -- about 480,000 funded accounts, doing something like 12 million orders a quarter -- so nothing exotic by volume, but the data model we inherited is a mess and we are re-specifying it properly this time.

Clients sign up, we KYC them, and we hold the name, email, date of birth, country of residence, the date they were verified and their tax residency. A client normally has one account, but a stocks-and-shares ISA and a general investment account are separate accounts, so allow several per client: each has an account type, a base currency, the cash balance and the date it was opened.

Instruments are the securities we let people trade -- ticker, name, ISIN, asset class (share, ETF, trust) and the exchange that lists it. Exchanges have a code, a name, a country and their trading hours in local time.

An order is placed on an account for one instrument, with a side, an order type of market or limit, the quantity, the limit price where there is one, when it was placed, the status, and the notional value which we compute and stamp on the row. Commission we charge once per order rather than per fill, so that sits on the order too. Orders fill in pieces, and each fill is its own row: the executed quantity, the execution price, the venue and the fill timestamp.

We snapshot positions per account and instrument -- the quantity held and the average cost, one row per account and instrument pair. Cash in and out is its own ledger: the movement type (deposit, withdrawal, dividend, fee), the amount, the currency and the timestamp.

Watchlists are technically a nice-to-have but people love them. A client makes a named list and puts instruments on it; an instrument can be on many thousands of lists and a list holds many instruments, and we want to know when each one was added. Corporate actions get mentioned a lot by the ops team -- splits, dividends, that sort of thing, recorded against an instrument with an ex-date. We do not do much with them yet.

Shape of it: order flow is brutally concentrated, a few dozen tickers take almost everything and it drops off very steeply after those. Order sizes are small and skewed, median around 6 shares. Commission averages 1.10 with hardly any variation, call it 15p either side. Orders end up filled about 82 percent of the time, cancelled 13, rejected 5.

Two things that are rules rather than tendencies. A limit order always has a positive limit price on it. And commission is zero on any ISA account -- that was a promotion we launched and never turned off. Also nothing below 1 pound notional or above 250,000 gets through the gate.

Front-office store for the treasury FX desk. Low volume, high value: we book maybe 300 tickets a day and the whole table is a few hundred thousand rows, so no partitioning and no sharding -- correctness beats throughput here.

A deal has an integer ticket id, the pair traded, a direction, the notional in USD, the all-in rate, a trade date, a value date, a materialised tenor in days, a product of SPOT / FORWARD / SWAP, the counterparty, and the trader who booked it. Currency pairs are a small reference table: base and quote ISO codes, the pip decimal places, and a flag for whether the pair is in today's tradeable set. Counterparties carry a legal entity name, an LEI, a jurisdiction, an internal credit rating and a notional limit. Traders have a name, a desk, and their booking authority limit in USD.

Note the desk also books internal transfers against our own book. Treat those as a counterparty like any other; we are not modelling them separately, whatever ops say.

Shape: notionals are log-normal with a median around 2.4 million USD. Product mix runs 58 percent spot, 33 forward, 9 swap. The all-in rate across the pairs we actually trade averages 1.19 with a standard deviation of 0.07 -- yes, that is a mixture across pairs rather than one clean distribution, but it is what we have.

Controls that have to be enforced in the data rather than in the UI: notional is positive and no single ticket exceeds 250 million; the tenor in days is never negative, which is how we express that a value date cannot precede its trade date; a spot ticket has a tenor of at most 2 days; and any ticket over 50 million has to have been booked by a trader whose authority limit is at least 50 million.

Right, so we buy debt. Portfolios come to us from banks and utilities, we buy them at a discount, and then we chase them. There are maybe 2.3 million of these accounts on our books at the moment, which is exactly why the spreadsheets have stopped working.

Every one of them is a person who owes money. We call them debtors, the letters call them customers, the client's own file will say account holder -- same thing, three names, and that inconsistency is half our problem. What we need on them: the name, the last known address, a phone number if we have got a working one, the date of birth where we know it, and the balance outstanding. Also whether we have flagged them as vulnerable, because that changes everything we are and are not allowed to do.

The balances are mostly small. Loads and loads of little ones and a handful of big ones that pay for the whole operation -- the average sits somewhere around 900 pounds but that average is honestly close to meaningless given how spread out it is.

Then there is the chasing. Every time we contact somebody, or try to, that is a record: when it was, how we did it -- letter, phone, SMS, email, doorstep -- which of our agents did it, and what came of it. Phone is still about half of everything we do, letters a quarter, and SMS and email make up most of what is left, with doorstep just a sliver of it now.

When somebody agrees to pay in instalments we set up an arrangement: how much, how often, when it starts, and whether they are keeping to it. About 60 percent break them, which is depressingly consistent year on year.

Oh, and the portfolios themselves matter for reporting: who we bought each batch from, when, what we paid for it, and its face value. Every account came in on one of them.

Rules from the FCA side, and these are not negotiable. We never set up an arrangement below 5 pounds. The interest we add to an account is capped at 8 percent. And where somebody is flagged vulnerable we do not add interest at all and we never, ever go doorstep.

I do the reporting for our outwards reinsurance and I am trying to write down what a proper database for it would actually look like, because right now it is four spreadsheets and a shared drive and I am the only one who understands any of it.

We are the cedant. We buy protection on our own book, treaty by treaty. A treaty has a reference, the class of business it covers, the underwriting year, the inception and expiry dates of the period it runs for, whether it is proportional or excess-of-loss, the retention we keep ourselves, the limit sitting above that, and the estimated premium income we declared at inception. We only have about 40 live treaties -- it is a small programme -- but there are ten years of them, so call it 400 rows in total.

Now the awkward part, and it is precisely the bit the spreadsheets cannot do. A treaty is not placed with one reinsurer. It is placed across several of them -- we say reinsurers, the brokers say the market, the slips say participants, and they all mean the same firms -- and each one takes a percentage line. One reinsurer sits on many of our treaties, and each treaty has anywhere from three to twenty of them on it. Per placement we need the signed line, the written line, and the date they signed.

On the reinsurers themselves: legal name, domicile, and their financial strength rating. That rating drives an approved-for-placement flag we keep against them -- anything rated below A- is not approved, and an unapproved reinsurer cannot hold a line at all, it has to be zero. We also will not give any single reinsurer more than 25 percent of one treaty.

Premium and claims move against a treaty by quarter. Each statement has the quarter it covers, the ceded premium, the brokerage we paid away, the commission we got back, and the paid and outstanding losses. Recoveries we claim off a treaty are separate again: the underlying loss reference, the date, the amount claimed and the amount we actually recovered.

Brokers place all of this for us and we do need to know which broker placed each treaty, although we hold almost nothing else about them beyond the name.

The mix: about two thirds of what we buy is excess-of-loss and the rest is proportional. Signed lines are typically fairly small, averaging around 8 percent, with one or two big lines on each treaty carrying most of it. Ceded premium per statement runs in the low hundreds of thousands and is very variable. And on the excess-of-loss side we never write a retention below 250,000 -- there is no point, the attritional stuff stays with us.

Handover notes for the marketplace core, written up before the shard migration so the next person has something to read.

Two populations at the top and they are deliberately separate accounts. A seller carries a display name, the country code it trades from, the date it onboarded, a rolling average of the stars buyers have left it, and a suspension flag. A buyer is little more than an email, a signup timestamp and a country. Listings hang off a seller and off one node of the category tree, which is self-referencing -- each category row names its parent. On the listing itself: the ask price as DECIMAL, an integer quantity available, a status, the moment it went live, and a denormalised view counter that Redis owns and we flush hourly. Buyers watch listings; many buyers per listing, many listings per buyer, and the only payload on that pairing is when it was added.

Orders are buyer-level with a placed_at timestamp, a total and a status. Each line under an order points at exactly one listing and freezes quantity and unit price at checkout. Shipments are per line rather than per order, because sellers dispatch independently -- carrier code, dispatch time, delivery time. Reviews are also per line: the buyer who left it, a star rating and free text. Sellers are paid fortnightly, one row per seller per period, holding gross, our commission and a hold flag.

Distributions, measured: view counts are Zipf with exponent about 1.35, so a few thousand listings absorb most of the traffic and the tail never breaks single digits. Order totals are log-normal, log-mean 3.4, log-variance 0.9. Line quantity is Poisson, lambda 1.4. Stars land at 60 percent five, 22 percent four, 8 percent three, 4 percent two, 6 percent one. Seller rating averages cluster around 4.5 with a standard deviation near 0.4.

Invariants worth enforcing: stars are 1 to 5; quantity available never goes negative; ask price is at least 1.00 and hard-capped at 250,000, and outside the collectibles category the cap is 15,000; and any payout above 2,000 is held when the seller's average rating is under 4.0.

Volume, current: about 40 million live listings, 120 million orders a year, and shipments running slightly ahead of that.

So we've got three shops now. The original one on Bridge Street, then Cross Lane, then the little kiosk by the station which honestly barely counts but it's on the same card scheme. I want to know for each of them what it's called, where it is and roughly when we opened it, because I keep having to look that up.

The scheme itself is dead simple. Someone signs up, we take their name and a mobile number and the date they joined, and from then on every time they come in and buy a drink they get a stamp. Ten boxes on the card, when it's full the next one's free. It lives in the app now rather than being a bit of card, so I need to know at any moment how many stamps a given regular is sitting on -- and they're spread all over the place, some are on nought because they've just claimed, some are on nine and pestering us, and it's pretty flat across the range in between. Most of them have a shop they treat as theirs and it'd be nice to have that written down against them.

The bit I actually care about is the visits. Every time one of our members buys something I want the date and time, which shop, what they spent, what they had, and how many stamps it earned them. On the what-they-had -- I don't need the whole order, just the main drink. Roughly a third of everything we sell is a latte. Flat whites are about a fifth, americanos a bit under that at eighteen percent, cappuccinos maybe fifteen, tea's small at eight or so, and then five percent is odds and ends -- hot chocolate, the babyccinos, that sort of thing. Spend per visit is normally about four pounds eighty and it's rarely more than a pound or so either side of that.

Stamps: one per drink, but if someone's buying a round we cap it at three in one go. And if they spend over a tenner in one transaction they get two stamps minimum -- we started that in January and it's stuck. Claiming a free one costs exactly ten stamps, and I want the claim written down against the visit it happened on, with the date and what they actually took, coffee or cake or whatever they picked.

Scale-wise it's tiny, which is why the spreadsheet lasted this long. About eight hundred people signed up, we see maybe two hundred visits a day across all three, and the free ones are a handful a week.

Whoever's on shift does the stamping but I don't need to keep track of that.

Proposed schema for the merchandising and stock side, replacing the nightly AS/400 extract.

Style level and variant level have to be modelled separately -- that is the whole point of the exercise. A style belongs to a brand (brands have a name and a country of origin), and carries the style code the buyers use, a display name, a department -- womenswear, menswear, kids, outerwear, accessories -- a season code, and the list price. The thing that actually has a barcode is the variant: one row per size and colour combination under a style, with its own SKU and barcode. Stock is held per store per variant, that pair is the key, and each row carries what is on hand and what is reserved against click-and-collect. Stores get a name, a city and a floor area in square metres.

Tills write one sale header per basket -- store, timestamp, basket total, payment method -- and one line per variant scanned, with quantity, the unit price that actually rang, and the discount percentage applied. Returns come back against a specific sale line and carry a timestamp, a reason code and the refund amount.

Numbers from the current warehouse. Size mix on variants sold: XS 7 percent, S 20, M 31, L 26, XL 12, XXL 4. Basket totals are log-normal, log-mean 4.0 and log-variance 0.6. Units per line is Poisson with lambda 1.2. We also keep a year-to-date unit count on the style, and it is brutally Zipfian -- exponent around 1.5 -- a couple of hundred styles out of the eleven thousand we list do most of the volume and the tail moves a handful of units a season. Return reasons split wrong size 46 percent, changed mind 24, faulty 12, not as pictured 11, arrived late 7.

Constraints for the DDL: on-hand can never be negative; the line discount sits between 0 and 70 percent; and anything sold at more than 50 percent off is final sale, so a return raised against such a line must refund zero.

Sizing: 340 stores, about 11 thousand styles, 95 thousand variants, roughly 9 million sale lines a year.

Notes from the platform scoping session -- what the till and supply side actually has to hold. I've written it as prose because the modelling call is not mine to make.

Stores first. We run three formats and about 62 percent of the estate is convenience, roughly 30 percent supermarket and the remaining 8 percent superstore. Each store has a name, a city, the date it opened and its floor area.

Products sit in a department, and some departments are chilled, which changes how deliveries into store get handled, so that flag belongs on the department rather than being repeated. Each product comes from exactly one supplier, and on the product we hold the name, the unit it is sold by (each, kilo, litre), the shelf price and whether it is age restricted. Suppliers have a name, a nominal lead time in days, and we mark the ones who make our own-brand lines: own-brand partners are contractually inside three days, everyone else is allowed up to 21.

Promotions run more or less weekly -- a name, a start date, an end date and a mechanic, which is multibuy or price cut or meal deal. A promotion covers many products and a product can be in more than one at a time, and the promotional price is a property of that pairing, not of either side on its own.

The transactional core is the basket: which store, which till, the timestamp it went through, the total, the number of items on it, and the loyalty card if one was swiped. We hold no name against a card, only when it was registered, the postcode district and a declared household size, because that is all legal will let us keep. Basket lines point at a product and carry a quantity -- fractional for loose goods, so don't make it an integer -- the line amount, and whether the operator did the age check.

Two more things around the edges: deliveries arriving into a store from a supplier, with the arrival timestamp and a pallet count, and the waste log, which is store, product, date, units binned and a reason. Someone also asked for shelf-edge label printing but that is not this project.

Distributions we already know: basket totals are log-normal with log-mean 3.1 and log-variance 0.8; items per basket is Poisson around 14. Weekly units per product is a very long tail -- Zipf, exponent about 1.4 -- a couple of thousand lines out of the forty thousand we list drive most of the volume and thousands of others sell in ones and twos.

Non-negotiable: an age check has to be recorded on any line for an age-restricted product, and a basket has at least one item on it.

Volume: 1,100 stores, about 9 million baskets a week and something like 130 million basket lines a week behind them.

Product notes on the data behind the box, from the kick-off doc.

The people first. We have called them subscribers, customers and members in three different parts of the app and I have stopped fighting it -- it is one group of people, one list. What we hold on them: an email, the day they joined, which plan they are on, whether they are live or paused or gone, and their referral code. Plans, there are three of them, at twelve, twenty-eight and forty-five pounds a month, and the top one ships two boxes a month rather than one, so the boxes-per-month figure belongs to the plan.

Every month has an edition -- a theme, the month it goes out and what the box cost us to put together. The things inside a box belong to the edition rather than to any individual parcel, which took us a while to work out: a product name, the brand it came from and what it retails for on its own. A typical one is four pounds, most sit between two and eight, and occasionally we talk a brand into putting in something worth thirty -- so the tail is long on the expensive side.

Then the parcels themselves, one per person per edition, with the day it went out, which carrier took it, what the postage cost and where it got to. Postage runs about 4.20 a parcel, plus or minus 80p.

Retention is the number the board asks about. Most people do not last. The average person is with us about seven months, but a big chunk cancel after a single box and a few have been here since the start, so it is the usual exponential-looking decay curve. I would rather have the months-active number sat on the person's record than derive it every time someone opens the dashboard.

Feedback comes in against a parcel -- a one-to-five rating and usually a comment, with the time it was submitted. We get 41 percent fives, 34 percent fours, 15 percent threes, 6 percent twos and 4 percent ones.

Two rules that actually bite. Ratings are one to five. And if someone is paused nothing ships -- the parcel gets marked cancelled before the carrier collects it, we do not just delete the row.

Size: a bit over 90,000 active subscribers and about 1.4 million parcels sent since we started.

We're a producing house with two spaces. The main auditorium seats 480 and the studio upstairs is 90, and I know the studio is unreserved half the time but for this let's pretend every seat is a seat. Each one has a row letter, a number within the row, the price band it falls in, and whether it's one of the wheelchair spaces, because the box office gets asked that constantly and currently the answer lives on a laminated plan.

A production runs for a few weeks -- it has a title, what sort of thing it is, a first night and a last night. Inside the run there are the individual performances, each one in one of the two spaces at a particular date and time, and we do need the matinees flagged because they price differently.

The people who book give us a name, an email and a postcode, and we note whether they're one of our members -- there are about 900 of those and they get priority booking, which is the main reason anyone joins.

A booking is one person buying for one performance, and it comes in through the website, over the phone, at the window, or as a group sale. The website is about 58 percent of it now, phone 22, the window 18, and group sales are the last 2 percent. We keep when the booking was made and how many days ahead of the performance that was, and that number is a horrible skew -- most of it arrives in the last fortnight, the average works out around eleven days, but every so often somebody books six months out. Under the booking sit the actual tickets, each one against a specific seat, with what was paid for it, whether a concession was applied and which one, and whether it was a comp.

Prices: the average ticket goes for about twenty-four pounds fifty, and the spread is maybe seven pounds either side. Nothing is ever over sixty-five. Comps are free, so nothing at all, not a nominal penny. And we only count something as a group sale if it's over two hundred pounds all in.

It really isn't a lot of data. Two hundred and fifty-odd performances a year, a few thousand tickets a month, and the mailing list is under a thousand people.

POS backend for eleven sites. Terse, because you've seen the last one.

A site has a name, a city and a nominal seat count. Tables within a site carry the code the floor staff shout at each other, a seat count of their own, and a flag for the two private rooms. The menu is per site, because London prices diverge from everywhere else, and each item has a course, a price, an alcohol flag and a target prep time in minutes -- the kitchen average is 12 with a standard deviation of about 4.

Recipes need modelling properly this time: an item is made of many ingredients, an ingredient goes into many items, and the quantity is a property of the pairing rather than of either end. Ingredients carry a unit of measure and an allergen code.

A tab is opened against a table and holds an open timestamp, a close timestamp, a cover count, a subtotal, the tip, the service charge percentage, and a channel -- 71 percent dine-in, 19 percent takeaway, 10 percent through a delivery app. Lines on the tab reference a menu item with a quantity, the unit price that rang, and a void flag, because voids have to survive for the audit rather than being deleted.

From last year's extract: covers per tab is Poisson, lambda 2.6; subtotals are log-normal with log-mean 3.6 and log-variance 0.5.

Business rules that need to be in the schema, not the app. A party on a normal table is 1 to 8 covers, but a private room booking is 10 to 22. Desserts are all priced between 4 and 9. Anything with alcohol in it rings up at 5.50 or more. And the service charge is exactly 12.5 percent whenever the cover count is 6 or above.

Volume is about 4 million tab lines a year across the estate.

Half-finished spec for replacing the delivery whiteboard, which is, still, literally a whiteboard.

Six showrooms, three of which have a warehouse attached. Everything we sell comes from a supplier -- mostly Poland and Italy -- and the supplier's quoted lead time in weeks is the number the sales floor promises against, so it lives on the supplier. An item has a name, the range it belongs to, its retail price, a weight, whether it's flat pack and whether it's a two-person carry. Weights are all over the place -- a lamp is two kilos and a corner sofa is ninety -- so it's a heavy log-normal, log-mean around 2.6 and log-variance 1.1. Flat pack is capped at 40 kilos, that's a warehouse rule and it's never been broken.

Customers give us a name, a phone number, an email and a postcode. An order is placed by one customer at one showroom on a date, and carries a total, the deposit we took and a status. Orders average around 900 pounds with a long right tail -- log-normal again, log-variance about 0.6. Lines on the order are an item and a quantity, usually one, Poisson with lambda 1.3, plus the unit price at the time of sale.

Deliveries are the awkward part and the reason for the whiteboard. We build slots: a date, a start and end time for the window, the van's registration, how many crew are on it and the maximum drops we'll allow. Crews are two people 78 percent of the time and three the rest. A delivery then puts one order into one slot at a position in the run, and we record when it actually landed, whether the customer refused it on the doorstep, and whether they asked for assembly. No van does more than twelve drops in a day, so the position in the run is 1 to 12. And any order over three thousand pounds gets assembly thrown in free, so those always come through flagged as assembly requested.

When something goes wrong we raise a complaint against the delivery -- the date it was raised, a category, how it was resolved and any goodwill payment. Damaged goods is 41 percent of them, late 27, wrong item 14, missing parts 12, and 6 percent is everything else.

Deposits obviously can't be negative. We're doing about 40,000 orders a year and have roughly 300,000 deliveries on record.

Single-site community pharmacy, dispensing side only. The front-shop till is a different system and out of scope here.

Four things to hold. Drugs: a name, the form (tablet, capsule, liquid, cream), the strength in milligrams, whether it is a controlled drug, and the pack price we pay. Strengths span orders of magnitude, 5mg through to 1000mg, so model it log-normal with log-mean 3.0 and log-variance 1.4. Patients: NHS number, year of birth, and whether they are charge exempt -- we deliberately hold no name in that table.

Every dispensing event is a row: the patient, the drug, the date it went out, the quantity of units, the days supply it covers, what we charged, and whether it came off a repeat. Days supply is overwhelmingly 28 at 62 percent, with 12 percent at 7 days, 9 percent at 14, 11 percent at 56 and 6 percent at 84. Quantity of units is Poisson-ish around 30.

Two regulatory rules to encode. A controlled drug may not be dispensed for more than 30 days supply. And the prescription charge is 9.90 flat per item while exempt patients pay nothing, so the charge sits between 0 and 9.90 and must be exactly zero whenever the patient is exempt.

Separately the CD cabinet and the fridge get counted every week: the drug, the date, the units on the shelf and the discrepancy against what the system thinks. A shelf count is never negative.

It is small. About 1,800 patients on file and 2,500 items dispensed a month, so under half a million rows in total after eight years of trading.

I'll describe this the way I'd describe it to my mum, and you can turn it into whatever it needs to be.

It's a place where people sell their old stuff to other people. Everyone is the same kind of account -- I sell you my drill on Tuesday and bid on your bike on Friday -- so I really do not want two separate lists of people. Someone has the handle they picked, when they joined, the town they're in, and a feedback score out of five which is just the average of what people have said about dealing with them.

A listing is one thing someone has put up for auction. There's a title, roughly what kind of thing it is, the price they want to start at, and how long they want it to run. We let them pick anywhere from three to ten days and it comes out pretty evenly spread across the options, no real favourite. We also keep a count of how many people are watching it, how many times it's been looked at, the day it finished and whether it actually went. The looking is wildly uneven -- maybe one listing in ten thousand gets tens of thousands of views because it hit the front page or somebody shared it, and the enormous majority sit at single digits forever, which is exactly the long tail everyone tells me to expect. Starting prices are lopsided the same way: the middle of the pack is about two pounds, loads of things go up at 99p, and then there's the odd thousand-pound thing that drags the average miles above what anyone actually starts at.

Bids: who bid, on what, when, how much, and whether it was one of the automatic ones where the system keeps bidding for you up to a limit you set. Stuff that sells typically gets three or four bids -- some get thirty, plenty get one -- and I'd like that count sat on the listing so the page doesn't have to add it up every time somebody loads it.

Once a deal is done either side can leave feedback, which is stars out of five, a note, and the day it was left, and it hangs off the listing it was about. Nearly everyone leaves five: three quarters of it is five stars, fifteen percent four, five percent three, and the ones and twos are about three and two percent between them.

Two things I know we need to actually stop people doing. The run length has to be inside that three to ten days. And anyone whose feedback score is under two can't bid more than a hundred pounds -- that came out of a fraud thing last year and it isn't negotiable.

Oh, and the pricey stuff, anything starting over five hundred quid, we always run for the full ten days.

It's big now, which is the whole problem: something like twelve million listings live at any one time and we took a quarter of a billion bids last year.

Notes for the new parcel platform, replacing the two systems we run today.

Depots are either regional hubs or spoke branches -- each one has a three-letter code and sits in exactly one region, and a spoke never spans regions. Around 12,000 named contract accounts book against us; the contract records a committed monthly parcel volume per account. A booking (we call it a shipment) is one account sending from one origin depot to one destination postcode at one service level, timestamped at booking, carrying a declared value in money. We sell four service levels, each with its own code, a promised transit day count and a hard per-parcel weight cap. A shipment holds one or more parcels; a parcel is barcoded and carries a dead weight in kg plus length, width and height in cm from which we derive a volumetric weight.

Operationally: a route belongs to a depot and has a code, a day of week and a planned stop count. A route run pins one route to one driver and one vehicle on a given date, with departure and return timestamps. Drivers are assigned to a home depot and hold a licence class. Vehicles record registration, type and payload capacity, which runs from 750 kg panel vans up to 7.5 tonne rigids. Every parcel accumulates typed, timestamped scan events at a depot, and zero or more delivery attempts, each against a route run, numbered, timestamped, with an outcome.

Measured behaviour, from the current warehouse: dead weight is log-normal, log-mean 0.6, log-variance 0.8. Destination postcode frequency is Zipf with exponent 1.35 -- a few hundred postcodes carry most of the traffic. Planned stops per route are Gaussian, mean 92, sd 24. Attempt outcomes split 88% delivered, 7% carded, 2% refused, 2% missorted, 1% damaged.

Rules to enforce: nothing over 31.5 kg enters the network and nothing under 10 g. Route plans are never written below 40 or above 160 stops. Declared value is capped at 2,500 on the express service (promised transit of one day) -- other services have no cap. Next-day bookings are only accepted at hub depots. After a third failed attempt the parcel's next attempt outcome is recorded as returned to sender. Sizing: roughly 40 million parcels a quarter, so scan events run into the hundreds of millions.

Right, so what we do is take chilled and frozen food off the suppliers and get it out to the shops. I'll try to explain it the way it actually works rather than the way the last lot wrote it down.

The suppliers are mostly UK but we've a fair few Dutch and Spanish ones too, so we do need to know which country each one is in -- it matters for the paperwork. Every line we sell comes from one supplier and one only. For each line we hold the name, how many days of life it has when it arrives, what a case of it weighs, and which temperature band it belongs in. Six in ten of our lines are chilled, three in ten frozen, and the rest are ambient bits that ride along on the same lorries.

We've four depots -- distribution centres if you want the official word, but nobody says that -- each in its own town. Every shop is served out of one depot, never two, and we keep the shop's name and town.

A run goes from a depot to a shop. We note the lorry's registration, whether it's a chilled run or a frozen run, when it left, when it got there, and how long it took door to door. Most runs are done inside a couple of hours but the odd one drags on for half a day if there's trouble on the motorway -- long tail, that, average is about an hour and three quarters. On each run there's a list of what's on it: which line, how many cases, and the set point the cabinet is meant to be held at. A line is usually a dozen or so cases, fourteen on average.

The probes are the bit the auditors care about. Each one is stuck somewhere in the trailer -- front, middle, back of the box -- and it writes the temperature every few minutes against the run. Most of what comes back sits right around three degrees, within a degree either way. On a chilled run the probe should never read below zero or above five, that's the line the auditor draws. Anything frozen has to be set at minus eighteen or colder, no argument.

Shelf life is anywhere from three days to three weeks and it's pretty evenly spread across that. Nobody sends a zero-case line, obviously.

Volume-wise we're putting through something like four hundred thousand delivery lines a year and the probes throw off a couple of million readings on top of that.

We're re-platforming the WMS for our two national fulfilment sites and I've been asked to write down what the data side has to hold. I'm an analyst, not a DBA, so treat the types as advisory.

Each site has a code and a floor area in square metres. Inside a site you have zones -- ambient, chilled and frozen -- and each zone has its own code and belongs to exactly one site. Zones contain bins; a bin has a location code, a capacity in units, and a flag for whether it's a pick face or a reserve location.

The stock table is the one people always get wrong. It is not one row per SKU. It is one row per bin and SKU together, because the same SKU legitimately sits in several bins at once and a bin can hold more than one SKU -- the row carries the quantity on hand and the date it was last cycle-counted, and the bin plus the SKU is what identifies it. A SKU itself has a code, a description, a per-each weight in kg, a unit cost, and an ABC class from the annual review: 15% of our SKUs come out A, 30% B, 55% C. On-hand quantities per bin are heavily right-skewed -- log-normal, log-mean about 3.4, log-variance 1.1.

Inbound: a receipt is one delivery against a purchase order reference, at a site, with a timestamp. Its lines say which SKU, how many were received, and which bin they got put away into.

Outbound: an order arrives against a site with a placed timestamp, a ship-by date and a priority. Order lines are SKU and quantity ordered -- typically one or two units, average 2.6. SKU demand is the classic long tail; when we fitted it the Zipf exponent came out about 1.2, and the top handful of codes really do account for most of the picks.

We release work in waves. A wave is raised for one zone at one site at a released timestamp and carries a line count -- normally around 220 lines, standard deviation about 60. Frozen is the exception: a wave in a frozen zone is capped at 40 lines, because there is a limit to how long anyone should be stood in there. Each pick task in a wave points at one order line and the bin it was picked from, and records the picker's badge, the quantity actually picked, when it was picked, and whether it went short. If a picker records nothing picked at all, the task is flagged short. And we never let an A-class SKU sit below 20 eaches in any bin it's held in -- that's a replenishment trigger, not a nice-to-have. Obviously on-hand can't go negative.

Returns do come back through the buildings but they live in a different system entirely and are out of scope here.

Scale: about 60 million pick tasks a year across the two sites, roughly 9 million orders.

Terminal operating system, data layer. Two terminals under one operator; each has a quay length in metres and a set of berths, and a berth has a code and a maximum permissible draft -- ours run from 8.5 m on the feeder berth to 17.5 m on the deep-water pair.

Vessels belong to a shipping line (line code plus name) and are keyed on IMO number, with a name, TEU capacity and length overall. Capacity is log-normal across our call mix, log-mean 8.6 and log-variance 0.45. We handle nothing shorter than 90 m LOA and nothing longer than 400 m. A vessel call is one voyage number of one vessel at one berth, with ETA, actual arrival and actual departure. Anything over 340 m LOA can only be worked at a berth whose permissible draft is 16 m or more.

Boxes are keyed internally but carry the container number; we store nominal size in feet, a reefer flag and tare weight. Size mix is 34% twenty-foot, 61% forty-foot, 5% forty-five. A container visit is one box arriving on a discharge call, sitting in one yard slot, with a discharge timestamp, a gate-out timestamp (that is when the road haulier takes it), and a dwell in hours. Import dwell is exponentially distributed with a mean around 48 hours. Reefers are a different matter -- plugged boxes must be off the terminal inside 24 hours.

The yard is blocks, each block belonging to a terminal with a code and a slot count; a slot is identified within its block by row and tier. Cranes belong to a terminal, have a code and a rated moves-per-hour that is Gaussian around 30 with sd 4. Every crane move records the crane, the call it was worked against, the box, the move type and a timestamp -- 42% discharge, 40% load, 13% reshuffle, 5% hatch cover. Customs holds sit against a box with a reason code, a placed timestamp and a release timestamp.

Rail sidings are coming in phase two; ignore them for now. Throughput is 3.1 million TEU a year, about 9 million crane moves.

We're a forwarder -- we don't own a single aircraft or ship, we buy space and sell it on. What I want out of a new system is one place where a job lives from the day we open it to the day the last invoice goes out, because at the moment it's half in the accounts package and half in people's heads.

A job -- some of the older hands call it a file, and the operations lot say consignment, it's all the same thing -- belongs to one client. Clients are companies and we need to know where they are, country-wise, because that drives who can sign what. Each job has a mode: roughly half of what we do is air, a bit over a third is sea and the rest goes by road. It has a place it comes from and a place it goes to -- we write them as port or airport names, which I know is a bit rough -- and the date we opened it. And it has a chargeable weight, which is the number everything else hangs off. The average job is about 500 kilos chargeable but the spread is enormous, we've had 20-tonne machinery moves and we've had a 30-kilo box of samples. We won't take anything under 30 kilos chargeable any more, mind -- it isn't worth the paperwork.

A job moves in legs. Each leg is with one carrier -- airlines, shipping lines, hauliers, all in the same list with which mode they are -- and legs are ordered, so leg one, leg two and so on, with the date it went and the date it landed, and how many days it took. A leg usually clears in a week or so but plenty run much longer. If we're booking with a shipping line we never quote a leg at less than ten days, that's a hard rule from the commercial director after we got burned.

Charges are where the money is. Each charge sits on a job, has a type -- freight, fuel, handling, duty, our own fee -- an amount and the currency it was billed in. Duty is always billed in sterling, no exceptions. Most charge lines are a couple of hundred pounds but every so often you get one in the tens of thousands. Nothing is ever billed negative; if we've overcharged we raise a credit through the accounts package, not here.

Documents hang off the job too -- the bill of lading or air waybill, the packing list, the certificate of origin, whatever the corridor wants -- with what kind it is and when it was issued.

Oh, and the cargo insurance is placed through an underwriter, but that's their paperwork, not ours, so leave it out.

We're opening somewhere north of two hundred thousand jobs a year now and each one throws off roughly a dozen charge lines.

Schema brief for the rail freight planning store. Eight entities, and I want the consist modelled properly this time.

Yards: code, region, siding count. Locomotives: class designation, tractive effort in kN, fuel type (diesel or electric). Wagons: running number, wagon type, tare weight and maximum payload, both in tonnes -- payload runs from 20 t on the oldest vans to 102 t on the new bulk hoppers. The fleet is 34% hopper, 30% box van, 22% flat and 14% tank.

A service is the timetabled product: a service code, an origin yard, a destination yard, a scheduled departure time and a distance in km, which is uniform between 40 and 620 across the book. A run is one dated operation of a service behind one locomotive, with actual departure and arrival timestamps, a delay in whole minutes and the consist length. Delay is exponentially distributed with a mean of about 12 minutes and is never negative -- early arrivals are recorded as zero. Consist length is Poisson with lambda 42.

The consist itself is a many-to-many: a wagon appears in many runs over its life and a run has many wagons, so it is its own relation keyed on the run and the wagon together, carrying the wagon's position in the train. Any run booked over 400 km must be assigned a locomotive rated at 300 kN or better.

Consignments are the customer-facing side: a customer (name, sector), a commodity code, a tonnage, an origin and destination yard, and the wagon and run it travelled on. Tonnage is Gaussian, mean 58, sd 12, and we accept nothing below 1 t or above 100 t. A consignment loaded into a tank wagon is always liquid bulk -- the commodity code follows from the wagon type there.

Sizing: about 180,000 runs a year, a couple of million consignments over the seven-year retention window, and around 7.5 million consist rows.

So this is for the courier side of the app and honestly the spec is a bit thin because the ops team keeps changing its mind. I'll give you what I'm confident about.
