We've got about 220 riders on the books. Everyone calls them different things -- riders, couriers, delivery partners -- it's the same person, one record each. We hold their name, when they joined, what they ride (bike, moped or car), and a rating. The rating is out of five and some of the ops people put halves in, so it's not a whole number. Most riders sit at 4.6 or so, very few below 4, standard deviation is something like a third of a point. Nobody can be rated below one.

A rider signs up for shifts. A shift is a date, a start and end time, and a zone -- we run three, central, north and out-of-town. Bikes are not allowed on the out-of-town zone, it's too far. We also keep a count of drops on the shift; a busy shift is a dozen, which is about the average.

Drops belong to a shift. Each one has the address, the merchant it came from, when it was dropped, a status, and the tip. Merchants have a name and sit in one of our zones. Statuses: 94% of drops go through fine, about 4% get cancelled and the remaining 2% we mark failed. If a drop is cancelled there's no tip on it, obviously -- and no tip is ever negative. Tips average around two pounds but loads of them are nothing at all, it's very skewed.

We've been talking about tracking the insulated bags each rider carries so we know who's got what, but nothing's decided, so don't build it.

This is a small dataset -- we only hold the live quarter, so about four thousand drops sitting in there at any time and a few hundred shifts a week.

Customs brokerage back end. Importers are keyed on our own surrogate but carry the EORI number, legal name and country code. Each importer may hold one deferment account with an account number, a credit limit and a running balance; an importer whose deferment limit is under 50,000 is put on prepay, which is a declaration-level status.

A declaration belongs to one importer and records the MRN, the mode of transport as the UN code (48% road = 3, 34% sea = 1, 16% air = 4, 2% rail = 2), a lodgement timestamp, the total customs value with its currency code, a status, and the number of item lines it carries -- line counts are Poisson with lambda 6. Customs value is log-normal, log-mean 8.9, log-variance 1.6, and cannot be negative.

Declaration lines hold the commodity code, a free-text goods description, net mass in kg, the line value, the duty rate applied as a percentage and the resulting duty amount. Applied duty rates are roughly uniform between 0 and 12% but the schema must tolerate anything from 0 to 25%. Where a line's value is 135 or below, no duty is charged -- the duty amount is zero.

Tariff measures are a reference table: commodity code, the duty rate, a preference code and a valid-from date, one row per measure version.

Queries raised by customs sit against a declaration with a reason code, a raised timestamp, a resolved timestamp and the hours it stayed open, which is exponential with a mean of about 22 hours.

Volumes: roughly 900,000 declarations and 5.5 million lines a year.

Returns desk tooling. Small piece of work, but the spreadsheet has finally fallen over so we need it in a database.

When a customer wants to send something back they raise a return with us. We take the order reference as a string -- the order itself lives in the webshop platform and we are not duplicating it here, so a reference is all we get -- plus the email they contacted us on, the date it was raised, a reason code and a status we move through as it progresses. Reasons break down about like this: 31% too small, 22% not as described, 20% changed their mind, 18% arrived damaged and 9% turned up too late to be useful.

One return can cover several items, and each item line names the SKU as a code, how many units (nearly always one, occasionally two or three -- averages about 1.3, never zero), the grade we settle on -- people say condition and grade interchangeably, it's one field -- and the refund we agreed. Refunds average about 34.50 with most within twenty pounds either side, and we never refund a negative amount. Change-of-mind returns are the one case where finance caps us: no more than 250 back on those, whatever the item was worth.

Then the warehouse inspects each item -- one inspection per item line, with the date, who did it, an outcome and a flag for whether it went back into sellable stock. Just under six in ten come out fit to restock, about a fifth go to refurb, a sixth get scrapped and the last few percent go back to the vendor. Anything graded A goes straight back on the shelf; anything scrapped obviously does not.

We see maybe 40 returns a week, so a couple of thousand rows a year -- this is not a big table by anyone's standard.

My son said I should write this down properly before I ring anyone, so here goes. We hold spare parts for industrial laundry machines and we send them out to the engineers who fix them. Been doing it since 1988 out of the same unit.

The parts. Everything has a part number stamped on it or printed on the bag, and a name, though half the names in the book are wrong and the lads just call them bits. Each one lives somewhere on the racking and we write the shelf spot down or we'd never find anything. We know what we charge for each and how many we've got, and there's a level written on the bin card where you're supposed to reorder. Most of them are a few pounds -- seals, clips, that sort of thing -- but the big drum assemblies run into the thousands, so it's a very lopsided list. And here's the thing nobody outside believes: it's the same forty or fifty numbers that account for nearly all the movement. The rest sit on that racking for years. Obviously we can't have a minus figure in the stock count, and nothing is ever priced below nothing.

Then the orders. An engineer rings up or emails, and we take his name -- we don't hold anything else about them, they work for the customers not for us -- the date, and how urgent it is. About a quarter come in urgent and one in twenty is a proper breakdown, machine's dead, factory's stopped. The rest are just normal restock. A breakdown has to go out the same day, that's nothing, zero days. Normal ones we allow three days. We write down the day it actually went out too.

On the order there's a list of what he wants: which part, how many -- usually one or two, sometimes a handful -- and what we charged for that line. The one rule we keep to is that we won't send more than two of anything over a thousand pounds on the same order, not without someone senior saying so, because if it's wrong we've a fortune sat in a van.

We get most of the parts from two places up north but that's just phone calls and invoices, there's nothing to keep about them.

It's not big. Three thousand and something part numbers, and maybe sixty orders a week.

Enrolment platform for a federated university -- the record system behind roughly 41 million historical enrolment rows and about 210,000 active students, so partitioning is a live concern.

Faculties own departments; a department has a short code, a name, and the faculty it sits under. Departments own both degree programmes and the course catalogue. A programme carries a degree level and a required credit total: undergraduate programmes require 360 credits and postgraduate ones 180. Instructors belong to one department and carry a rank and a hire date. Students matriculate against exactly one programme and keep a matriculation number, an entry year and a running cumulative GPA on a 0.0 to 4.3 scale; across the student body that GPA sits at 3.05 with a standard deviation of 0.52.

Courses have a catalogue code, a title, an integer credit-hour value and a numeric level code from 100 up to 700. Prerequisite structure is course-to-course and many-to-many: a course may list several prerequisites, each with a minimum grade-point threshold the student must already have achieved, and the same course can appear as a prerequisite for many others.

Each term -- term code, start and end dates, add/drop deadline -- a course runs zero or more sections. A section belongs to one term, one course and one instructor of record, and carries a section number, a seat capacity, a live enrolled count and a delivery mode: in person about 62% of the time, hybrid 23%, fully online the rest. Capacity is lognormal in shape, median near 40 with a thin tail of 500-seat lecture theatres. Demand across the catalogue is brutally long-tailed -- a Zipf law with exponent near 1.6 fits section enrolled counts well. Graduate sections, meaning any section whose course level is 500 or above, are capped at 25 seats.

Sections meet in weekly slots: day of week, start and end clock times, and a room. Rooms are identified by building code and room number and have a seat count between 12 and 480, except the Old Quad buildings (code 'OQ'), which never exceed 60 seats.

An enrolment is one student on one section and records the date it was made, a status, and final grade points on the same 0.0 to 4.3 scale. When a section fills, students queue on a waitlist with an integer position and the timestamp they joined.

I look after the office side of a two-form-entry primary school, so this is really about knowing where every child is and who to ring when something happens. Nothing here is big data -- 420 children on roll, about 700 parents and carers on the contact list, 45 staff including the lunchtime supervisors, and a register that adds a few thousand lines a term.

Every child has the obvious stuff. A first name and a surname, a birthday (which matters more than you would think, we sort by it for admissions), the date they joined us, and whether they are entitled to free school meals -- that one drives funding so it has to be right. They sit in one class, and our classes are named after trees rather than year numbers, which confuses every supply teacher who walks in, so we keep the year group on the class as well as on the child, plus which room the class is in and how many children are currently in it. Two classes in each of the seven year groups from Reception up to Year 6. Reception is always a bit smaller than the rest and the others are pretty much level -- out of the whole school Reception is maybe thirteen percent and each of the six other year groups is around fourteen and a half. Classes are meant to be thirty and mostly land within two or three either side. The legal cap is thirty-two, and for Reception we hold it to twenty-six because of the adult ratios.

Each class has a class teacher, who is one of the staff. Staff records are thin -- name, job title, when they started, and whether they are teaching staff or not.

The register is the big one. Twice a day, every child, a mark. Present is about ninety-four percent of all marks, authorised absence three and a half, late just under two, and unauthorised absence the little bit left over. When a child is late we are supposed to write down how many minutes, and late children are typically about eight minutes late, though some of the office team just tick it and move on, which I keep asking them not to do. Obviously the minutes can never be a negative number, and if the mark says late then there had better be a number bigger than zero sitting next to it.

For the grown-ups we hold a name, how they are related to the child, a mobile number, an email if they will give us one, and an address. An adult can have more than one child here and a child can have more than one adult listed, and we flag which adult is the first person to ring.

Oh, and trips -- I nearly forgot. Someone books a trip for a class: the name of the trip, the date, and what we are charging per child. That runs from four pounds for the museum walk up to about forty-five for the residential deposit, and it is never a negative number.

Backing store for a consumer online-course marketplace. Volume to design against: 6.4 million learners, 9.1 million enrolments and about 74 million lesson-progress rows. Learner and certificate identifiers are UUIDs; everything else is a surrogate bigint.

Learners have an email, an ISO country code, a signup timestamp and an account tier. Instructors are separate entities with a display name, a long-form bio, a revenue share percentage and a join date -- anyone who joined before 2019-01-01 is grandfathered onto a 70% share.

A course belongs to exactly one instructor and carries a title, a category, a list price of at most 199.99, a published timestamp and a free flag. If a course is flagged free then every enrolment against it records a price paid of zero. Courses decompose into ordered modules and modules into ordered lessons. A lesson has a content kind and, where it is video, a duration in seconds that is lognormal with a median around nine minutes. Some lessons carry a quiz, which has a pass mark percentage between 50 and 100 and a question count.

Enrolment is learner-to-course with an enrolment timestamp, the price actually paid and a completion percentage between 0 and 100. Completion is the ugly number: mean around 12% with an exponentially decaying shape. Paid prices cluster near $18 with a long right tail, lognormal again. Progress is tracked per enrolment per lesson -- that pair is the key -- and stores watched seconds and a completion timestamp.

Quiz attempts are per learner per quiz with an attempt number, a start timestamp and a score percentage that comes out roughly normal, mean 71 with a standard deviation of 16. Certificates are issued against an enrolment and carry an issue timestamp and a printable serial code.

Reviews are one per learner per course: an integer 1-5 star rating, a free-text body and a submission timestamp. The rating histogram is the usual J shape -- 55% fives, 27% fours, 10% threes, and 4% each at two stars and one.

Coupons belong to a course and carry a code, an integer discount percentage, an expiry timestamp and a redemption cap. Any coupon on a course listed under $20 is capped at 25% off.

We are a small language school above a bakery. Three rooms, four tutors, and me. I want to stop running the whole thing off one spreadsheet that only I understand.

The people who come to us -- I will call them students, though the website says learners and the invoices say client, and it is all the same person. I need a name, a phone number, what their first language is, because that changes how you group a class, the level they are at, and when they first signed up. Levels are the usual A1 to C2 ladder, except our own website says beginner and improver, which map onto the bottom two rungs, and I would rather we settled on one set of words. Out of every ten people who walk through the door, three are complete beginners, another two and a bit are only just past that, two are properly intermediate, and it thins out fast above there -- upper intermediate is maybe one in seven and the very top level is about one in twenty-five.

We sell blocks, not individual lessons. A block is one language at one level, taught by one tutor, starting on a date, running for so many weeks, with a price and a number of seats. Most blocks are the ten-week one, about a quarter are the six-week version, and the rest are four-week intensives. The price depends on the length and lands somewhere between a hundred and twenty and four hundred pounds, spread fairly evenly across that range. We never run a class with fewer than four booked or more than twelve in the room.

People book onto a block, and plenty of them do two or three different blocks over a year, so one person turns up against several blocks and a block obviously has several people on it. For each of those I want the date they booked, what they actually paid, because sometimes it is less than the list price and sometimes they pay in two goes, and how many sessions they turned up to. A ten-week block is ten sessions and people typically make about eight of them. The four-week intensive runs twice a week, so eight sessions is the ceiling on that one.

For the tutors I barely need anything. A name, which languages they can teach, and what we pay them an hour, which is between twenty-two and thirty-four depending on how long they have been with us.

Two hundred and sixty people on the books at the moment. Maybe nine hundred all told since we opened.

I am the data analyst at a national exam board and I am specifying the awarding database that sits behind the summer session. Volume for context: around 640,000 candidates and just under 1.9 million marked scripts in a single session.

Candidates are entered through a centre. Each candidate has a candidate number, a name, a date of birth, and a flag for whether they have access arrangements. The centre has its own code, a name, a region and a type -- about 61% of our entries come from state schools, 19% from FE colleges, 14% from independent schools, and the remaining 6% are private candidates who enter through an examination centre rather than a school.

What a candidate actually sits is a paper, and papers belong to a specification. A specification has a code, a subject, a qualification level and a total UMS value: A level specifications are marked out of 300 UMS. A paper has a number within its specification, a session code, a maximum raw mark and a percentage weighting toward the overall grade.

The script is the row that matters. One candidate, one paper, a raw mark, the converted UMS mark, the examiner who marked it, the date it was marked, and a flag for whether it went through second marking. Raw marks come out roughly normal, mean about 52.4 with a standard deviation near 17.1, and a raw mark is never negative. Every script marked by an assistant examiner is second marked -- that is a hard rule from the standards team.

Examiners have a name, a seniority, a subject, and an allocation count. A normal allocation is around 340 scripts and we cap anybody at 600, but senior examiners are held to 200 because they also moderate.

Grade boundaries are set per paper after marking closes: a grade letter and the minimum UMS needed for it.

Finally, remarks. A candidate can ask for a script to be looked at again. We record the request date, the fee -- a flat 42 pounds -- the outcome, and the change in mark, which averages a little under one mark upward with a tight spread of a couple of marks either side.

Product owner in the accommodation office. We are replacing a 2009 Access database and I need the data model straight before anyone writes a screen.

The estate is eleven halls of residence, eleven thousand beds give or take, each one on a named campus, each with a postcode and a bed count, and each with a warden who lives on site and gets rung at three in the morning. We hold the warden's name and a contact number and honestly not much else, but it has to be its own thing because wardens move between halls and one warden can cover more than one over a career.

Inside a hall you have flats. A flat sits on a floor, has a code, and has some number of bedrooms sharing a kitchen -- typically five or six of them. Some flats are the accessible ones and those are always on the ground floor, which we number zero. Nothing anywhere in the estate goes above the fourteenth floor.

A room is a bed, basically. One occupant, a room code, a type, a weekly rent, and a floor area we are now obliged to publish. Roughly four in ten rooms are en suite these days, about the same again are plain standard rooms with a shared bathroom, and the remaining thirteen percent are studios. Rent runs from about a hundred and ten a week for a standard room in the older halls up to two hundred and fifteen for a studio, and it is fairly flat across that range. No studio is ever under a hundred and eighty.

Then the residents. Tenants. Students. Whichever word you like, it is one record per person, with a student number, a name, a year of study and whether they are international, because internationals and postgrads take the longer contract. First years are guaranteed a place so they are the bulk of it, about six in ten, and the other three years split what is left roughly evenly. The tenancy links a person to a room for a start and an end date, with a length in weeks -- the standard is forty-four weeks and that is around seven in ten of them, the fifty-one-week contract is about a fifth, and there is a handful of thirty-eight-week deals left over from an old scheme. There is a deposit on it too, two hundred and fifty normally, four hundred if the room is a studio, and a status field because people withdraw. Call it nine thousand seven hundred tenancies a year.

Maintenance I should mention, since the helpdesk feeds us jobs: against a room, with the date reported, a category, a priority and the date it was closed. There are something like three hundred thousand of those in the archive and nobody has ever deleted one.

Circulation database for a university library system: eight branches, 2.4 million items and roughly 38 million loan rows accumulated since 1998, so the loan table wants range partitioning on the checkout timestamp.

Bibliographic records hold an ISBN, a title, a publication year -- anything from 1470 to the current year, we have incunabula -- a Dewey class, a language code, and a denormalised circulation count refreshed nightly. Circulation per bib record is textbook Zipf with an exponent near 1.35, so any capacity planning that assumes even demand across the catalogue is wrong. Items are the physical copies: one bib record, a barcode, a home branch, a shelf location, a status, and an acquisition cost that is roughly normal around 38.50 with a standard deviation of 14. Branches carry a code, a name and a seat count.

Borrowers have a card barcode, a category, a faculty, a registration date and a running outstanding-fines balance which is never negative. The category mix is 58% undergraduate, 21% postgraduate, 13% staff, 5% alumni and 3% external members.

A loan joins one item to one borrower with a checkout timestamp, a due date, a return timestamp and a renewal count of at most six. We stamp the entitled loan period onto the row at checkout, because entitlement is a function of borrower category -- undergraduates get 14 days and staff get 84 -- and we stamp the realised days out once the item comes back. Days out is exponentially distributed with a mean of about nine days.

Fines hang off a loan with an amount, the date they accrued and a waived flag. They run at 20p a day and are capped at 15 pounds, and in log space the amount sits around 0.9 with variance 0.8.

Holds are placed against a bib record rather than a specific item, with a queue position, the timestamp it was placed and an expiry date.

Financial aid team here, and honestly the current setup is three spreadsheets and a shared mailbox, so treat this as a green field.

The unit of work is an application. Someone -- we call them applicants, the decision letters say candidates, the students' union calls them students, all the same human being -- applies to a scheme. About forty-six thousand applicants a cycle and roughly a hundred and eighty thousand applications sitting in the system across eleven years of running it.

On the person we hold a student number, a name, the household income figure off the assessment (whatever they have declared, we do not audit it), their entry tariff points, their domicile for fee status, and a flag for care leavers. Median household income on the forms is about twenty-seven thousand and there is a long right tail running up past a hundred and something thousand, so it is nothing like symmetric. Entry tariff points average around thirty-four out of forty-five with a spread of five or so. Income obviously cannot be negative.

A scheme has a name, where the money comes from, an annual budget, the biggest single award it is allowed to make, and whether it is means tested. That maximum is never below two hundred and fifty and never above nine thousand.

The application itself is who, which scheme, when it came in, the decision, how much was awarded if anything, and the name of whoever assessed it -- just the name, we do not need a whole staff record for that. Roughly a third get awarded, about half are rejected outright, one in eleven is withdrawn by the applicant, and a few percent are still pending at any given moment. The typical award is around twelve hundred pounds and the shape is a sharp decay, masses of small awards and very few big ones. Nothing over nine thousand has ever gone out of the door. Means-tested awards top out at four thousand. And care leavers are never rejected outright, that is policy -- they get something or the application gets referred.

Awards are paid in instalments against terms, so there is a payment row with the date, the amount and which term it was for. Some schemes are one-off and some pay per term and the spreadsheet does not currently distinguish, which is half the reason we are doing this at all.

I am director of development here -- fundraising, alumni relations, the events, all of it. What I have inherited was built for printing mailing labels, so let me just describe what we actually do and you can tell me what it needs to look like.

Our people are graduates of this place. We say alumni, the vice-chancellor says members, the old database calls them constituents, which nobody outside this office understands. Three hundred and forty thousand of them on file, going back to 1946, and something like one and a half million gift records behind that. For each person we need a name, the name they actually like being called, the year they finished, an email if we have a live one, and two flags that matter more than anything else in the system -- whether they have died, and whether they have asked us never to contact them again. We also keep a running lifetime giving total on the record, because it is the first thing anybody asks me.

A lot of them have more than one degree from us. Did their undergraduate here, came back for a masters. So the degrees have to sit separately from the person: the degree code, the subject, the year it was awarded and the class of honours.

Addresses are a mess and always will be. One person can have several on file and only one of them is the current one, and we need the country on it because that drives which tax scheme applies. Same shape for jobs -- the employer, the job title, the sector and when they started. We keep the history, because "she has just moved to a hedge fund" is exactly the sort of thing that changes an ask.

Fundraising is organised into campaigns. A campaign has a name, a target amount, a launch date, a close date and a cause area -- scholarships, buildings, research, that sort of split. Underneath a campaign we run appeals, which is the actual sending: which channel it went out on, when, how many people it went to, and how many replied.

Gifts come in against an appeal, from a person, into a fund. Funds have to be separate because the finance office insists on it -- a fund has a name, whether it is restricted or unrestricted, and the year it was opened. A gift into a restricted fund has to be at least a thousand pounds; that is the minimum to open a named restriction and finance will not budge. Most gifts are tiny, the median is around forty pounds, and then we get the occasional seven-figure one, so the spread is enormous. Nearly half arrive by direct debit, a third on a card, about one in nine still by cheque, then bank transfers at about nine percent, and a very small number as gifts of shares. Anything recurring is direct debit, always -- we do not offer recurring on any other method. And we do not record anything under a pound.

Pledges are a different animal from gifts. Someone signs up to give a total amount against a campaign over some number of instalments. A third pay in one go, most spread it over a year, some over three years and a few over five. We will not take a pledge under a hundred pounds.

Events: the reunions, the black-tie dinner, the regional drinks. A name, a date, a venue, how many we can fit in, and a ticket price which runs from free up to two hundred and fifty a head for the dinner. People say whether they are coming, some of them actually turn up, and they bring guests -- a bit under one guest each on average, and we cap it at two, or three if there is a good reason. One person goes to many events and one event has many people, obviously.

Last thing, and it always gets forgotten: some of them volunteer for us. Mentoring, chairing a regional branch, interviewing applicants. A role with a name and a start and end date against the person.

Small driving school. Four tables at most, but I want the constraints living in the model rather than scattered through the booking app.

Pupils: name, provisional licence number, date of birth, the date they registered, and a denormalised running count of hours logged. That count averages about 45 by the time they sit the practical, standard deviation around 12.

Instructors: name, ADI badge number, the car's registration, what transmission it is, and an hourly rate somewhere between 32 and 44. Three of the nine cars are automatic only, and any lesson taught in one of those is logged with an automatic lesson type, because the rate card depends on it.

A lesson is one pupil, one instructor, a date, a start time, a duration in hours, the amount charged, and a lesson type. Types are the usual set -- standard, motorway, mock test, pass plus -- and I will admit the list has grown organically and nobody has ever written it down properly. Slot length: just over half are two hours, about a fifth are 90 minutes, the rest are single hours. Nothing shorter than an hour and nothing longer than three.

Test bookings: the pupil, the test centre, the date, whether it is theory or practical, the outcome, the attempt number, and the minor fault count for practicals. Pass rate is 48%, fails 49%, and about 3% get recorded as not taken -- weather, no-shows, examiner strikes. Minor faults average about 5.3 and more than 15 minors is an automatic fail regardless of anything else, though the column itself we allow up to 40 because of data entry from the paper sheets.

Scale is trivial: 260 active pupils, nine instructors, about 6,000 lessons a year.

Handing this over: the playback warehouse for our VOD subscription, as we actually run it.

The volume decides most of the design. 78 million live billing accounts, up to six viewing profiles under each one, and the play-event stream lands roughly 1.4 billion rows a month -- that table gets a UUID and date partitioning, everything else is INTEGER surrogates, and plans key on their short code because those codes show up in a dozen upstream systems.

Billing sits at the account: which plan code it is on, when it signed up, ISO country, the contact email. The plan reference itself is narrow -- a display name, the monthly price, and the ceiling on simultaneous streams -- but it does a lot of work, because most entitlement questions resolve to it. Profiles are what people actually use; each has a display name and a maturity ceiling expressed as an integer age. We also register devices against the account and keep the device class and the registration timestamp, since the stream ceiling is enforced against that list.

Playback always resolves to an episode, never to a title, so movies get one synthetic episode row. Episodes hang off a title with a season number, an episode number, runtime in minutes and an air date. The title is where the interesting columns live: name, movie or series, release year, content rating, and a denormalised total view count we refresh nightly. Genre and watchlist are both genuinely many-to-many -- genre against title, watchlist from a profile to a title with the date it was added -- so both are association tables keyed on the pair.

A play event carries the profile, the episode, the start timestamp, seconds watched, the device class it came from, and which rung of the bitrate ladder it settled on. Separately, invoices are one row per account per billing period with the amount, the currency and whether it cleared.

Fits we already trust: title view counts are a textbook Zipf with exponent 1.15; seconds watched is lognormal, mu 6.9 and sigma-squared 0.8 in log space; episode runtime is near-normal at mean 44 minutes, sd 13; device class comes out 41 percent TV, 27 mobile, 19 web, 13 tablet.

Four things the loader has to hold. Monthly price is between 6.99 and 24.99. Runtime is at least 1 minute and never over 240. A kids profile -- maturity ceiling under 16 -- must never appear on a play event above bitrate rung 3. And any account whose country is IN gets invoiced in INR.

We're rebuilding the reporting side of the music app and I want the data model straight before the engineers start arguing about it.

The centre of everything is the stream: someone hit play on a track and we logged it. That is about 640 million rows a day right now, which is why nobody wants to touch it. Each one knows who listened, which track, when, how many milliseconds actually played, and where the play came from -- a playlist, an album page, search, radio, an artist page. We also flag whether the play was monetised, because royalties only count a play once at least thirty seconds have gone through, and that flag is what finance reads.

Listeners are what marketing calls users and what billing calls customers. Same people. We hold an email, the signup date, their country and whether they are on free or premium. Free listeners are capped at 128 kbps and premium goes higher, and the stream row records the bitrate actually served, which is how we prove the cap works -- on a free listener's stream expect it between 64 and 128.

The catalogue is artists, their albums, and the tracks on those albums. We do not model record labels properly; there is a label name sitting on the album and that is as far as it goes, which annoys licensing but has never actually broken anything. A track row carries the title, duration in seconds, an explicit flag and a running stream count. Duration averages 214 seconds with a standard deviation of about 62. The stream counts are the ugly part: our data-science people fitted a Zipf with exponent 1.2 and it holds up well. Artist monthly-listener figures are lognormal-ish, log mean around 8.5 with variance 2.1 -- the median artist is a few thousand and the top end is absurd.

Playlists belong to a listener, have a name and are public or not, and a track can obviously sit in any number of playlists, so we keep the position of each track inside each playlist along with when it was added. Positions start at 1.

Other things to police: a clip under ten seconds is not a track, and we bounce uploads longer than thirty minutes. And play source breaks down roughly 38 percent playlist, 21 album, 16 search, 15 radio, 10 artist page.

So we run a podcast hosting outfit -- small, family-ish operation, three of us plus a contractor. Right now there are 340-something shows on the platform and I think about twenty-six thousand episodes all told, which sounds like a lot until you realise a big chunk of that is one true-crime show that has been going since 2016.

What I care about keeping straight is the shows and everything hanging off them. A show has a title, a category -- comedy, true crime, business, that sort of thing -- the date it launched, and a host. Some shows have two hosts and honestly we just type both names into the one field. Not elegant, but nobody has ever needed to search on it, so please do not build me a whole separate thing for hosts.

Episodes are where the detail is. Each one belongs to a show, has its own title, the date it went out, how long it runs and the download count our stats provider hands us. Length varies a lot but the average is about thirty-eight minutes, give or take a quarter of an hour either side. Nothing under three minutes goes out as a real episode -- those are trailers and we do not publish them here -- and the longest thing we have ever hosted was just shy of four hours. Downloads are wildly uneven: most episodes land somewhere around a thousand or two, and then every so often one gets picked up somewhere and does forty thousand.

The money side is the sponsor reads. An episode can carry more than one -- we have done three on a couple of the big ones -- and for each read we note which sponsor it was, where in the episode it sits (pre-roll, mid-roll, post-roll) and what we billed for it. The rates run from two hundred and fifty dollars up to four thousand depending on the show, and pre-roll is the premium slot, so a pre-roll read never goes out under a thousand.

Oh, and reviews. Listeners leave a star rating out of five plus a bit of text, and that is against the show rather than any particular episode. They skew high, as these things do -- about six in ten are five stars, roughly two in ten are four, and then there is a stubborn little clump of one-stars from people who are angry about something unrelated.

Product owner here, writing up the model for the paywall analytics rebuild. We are a metropolitan daily: 4.2 million registered readers, around 90 million article views a month, roughly 380 journalists on staff.

Readers register with an email and we keep the registration date, the city they gave us, and a status that says whether they are an active subscriber, lapsed, or have never paid. A subscription is its own record because people churn and come back -- it points at the reader and at the product they bought, and has a start date, an end date once it is over, the amount we bill monthly, and an active flag. Products are the four or five things we actually sell: a code, a display name, the list monthly price, and how many premium articles that product allows per month. Prices sit between 4.99 and 34.99. The one called Digital Plus is 14.99 a month and every subscription on it bills exactly that -- no grandfathered pricing on that product.

Editorial side. Journalists have a name, the desk they sit on and a hire date. Sections -- metro, business, sport, culture, opinion -- have a code, a display name, and one journalist who edits them. An article belongs to a section and carries a headline, a publish timestamp, a word count, a premium flag and a running page-view total. Bylines are shared often enough that the article-to-journalist link is many-to-many, with the byline order recorded on it. Word counts average about 780 with a standard deviation of 340; the shortest thing we publish is a 120-word brief and features top out around 6,000. We never put anything under 400 words behind the paywall.

On traffic, a view row records the article, the reader, when it happened, how many seconds they were on the page and where they arrived from. Time on page is exponentially distributed with a rate of 0.02 per second, so about fifty seconds on average. Referrers break down 44 percent search, 21 social, 19 direct, 12 our own newsletters and 4 aggregators. Page-view totals per article are lognormal, log mean 7.0 and variance 2.2. A paywall hit is logged separately whenever a metered reader gets stopped, with the reader, the article, the timestamp and whether they converted on the spot -- and once someone converts there, that reader's status is active.

The newsletters are a smaller concern: each has a name, a send day and a running subscriber count, and a reader can sign up to any number of them, so that pairing is its own record with the signup date. Comments sit on articles, written by readers, with the body, the posted timestamp and a flagged marker for the moderators.

Telemetry schema for the shooter, post-mortem edition -- what we should have built the first time round.

Player identity is a UUID handed to us by the account service; locally we keep the platform, a region code, the creation timestamp and the current account level. Level is close to exponential with rate 0.045, so a mean somewhere around twenty-two and a thin tail of grinders. About 11 million players touch the game daily and the participation table takes roughly 2.3 billion rows a month, which is the constraint that shapes everything below.

A match is also a UUID, with the mode, the map code, the server region, a start timestamp and a duration in seconds. Duration is near-normal: mean 1080, sd 240. Ranked and casual behave differently -- a ranked match is never shorter than eight minutes and never runs past an hour, whereas a casual lobby can collapse in ninety seconds. Participation is the many-to-many between match and player, keyed on that pair, and carries the team slot, kills, deaths, damage dealt and final placement. Kills per participant are Poisson with lambda 4.6. Placement runs 1 through 100 because that is the lobby size.

Store side: an item has a name, a rarity and a gem price, and rarity comes out 58 percent common, 27 rare, 11 epic, 4 legendary. A purchase records the player, the item, the timestamp, the gems actually charged and the currency source. Legendaries are priced at 2,400 gems and up, so a purchase of one never lands below that.

Client health is deliberately separate: sessions per player with start and end timestamps, the client version and a crash flag, and then a crash report against the session with the stack hash, the OS build and when it arrived.

Anti-cheat signals also land in this cluster but they belong to another team's pipeline -- leave them out of scope here.

Notes from the platform standup -- someone asked me to write down what we actually store for the feed, so here goes, and be warned it is not tidy.

Members, users, accounts: three names for one thing, pick one and stick with it. Whatever you call them, they have a handle, a join date, a bit of profile text, and a follower count we keep denormalised because computing it live was killing us. There is a verified marker too. We only ever verify someone once they are past ten thousand followers -- that is a hard rule from trust and safety, no exceptions have ever been granted.

Following is directional, and it is the obvious pair-of-ids arrangement plus the date it happened. The follower curve is basically a power law: a handful of accounts are in the millions and the median person has a couple of dozen. Our analyst fits a Zipf around 1.1 and nobody has argued with him yet.

Posts belong to whoever wrote them and have the text, a timestamp and a like count. Replies are just posts that point at another post, which the mobile team hates but it is what we have. We store the character count on the row because the limits differ -- a reply is capped at 280 characters, a top-level post can go to two thousand -- and having the count sitting there saves the feed ranker a computation. Like counts are lognormal, log mean about 1.9 with variance 1.8. None of these counts ever go negative, obviously.

Reactions are a separate thing from the like count, before anyone asks. Each one is a member reacting to a post at a particular time with a type. It is mostly the plain like -- call it seventy-one percent -- then laugh at eleven, heart at nine, angry five, sad four. We are pushing about three hundred million reactions a month across roughly 900,000 active people.

Hashtags: we pull them out of the post text at write time and keep a running use count per tag, and a post can obviously carry several of them, so there is a link between the two sides.

People can report posts as well, but that goes into a completely separate tool that Trust runs, so do not build it here.

Right, I will try to explain this the way I would explain it to my sister.

We make a picture-sharing app. People sign up with a username, we know roughly where they are from the phone, and we note the day they joined. There is something in the region of seven hundred thousand people signed up and I would guess forty million pictures sitting on the servers now, which the hosting bill certainly reflects. Most of them are American -- close to three in ten -- India is the next biggest at about a fifth, then Brazil around a ninth, Indonesia a bit less than that, and the rest is scattered everywhere else.

When you put a picture up you can write a caption, and we keep the time it went up, how big the file is, and whether it is public or just for you. Sizes are mostly two or three megabytes but there is always someone uploading a monster off a proper camera, so we stop them at twenty-five meg. We also count views, and that is very lopsided: the ordinary picture gets a couple of dozen looks and then once in a while one travels round the world. If a picture is set to private it is not in the public feed at all, so its view count just sits at zero.

Then there are albums. We called them galleries for the first two years and half the team still does, so if you see 'gallery' in the old code that is the same thing, not a second feature. An album belongs to whoever made it, has a name and a created date, and you pick one of the pictures in it to be the cover. The important bit people get wrong: a picture can be in several albums at once. My holiday photo is in 'Italy' and in 'Best of last year' and that is not two copies, it is the same photo.

There is a comments feature as well but it is barely used and I do not want it in this piece of work.

We stream ticketed live gigs. I have been asked to spec out the warehouse side and I think it is fairly clean, so this should be short.

Last year we ran 2,800 events for about 1.1 million registered viewers, and there were roughly 6 million stream sessions across them.

An act is the performer: a name, a home country, a genre code. An event belongs to exactly one act and has a title, a scheduled start, how long it is meant to run, whether it is ticketed or free, and the list ticket price. Run times average 95 minutes with a standard deviation of about 25, and list prices are spread pretty flatly from eight dollars up to forty-five.

Viewers register with an email, a country code and a date. When a viewer buys into a paid event we write a ticket: the event, the viewer, the purchase time, the price they actually paid, and the promo code if they used one. Comped tickets come through at zero and nothing is ever above forty-five. Promo codes are their own small reference -- the code, the discount percentage, and the window it is valid in. Discounts run between 5 and 100 percent, and we do hand out a few full-comp hundred-percent codes for press, which land the ticket at exactly zero.

The watching itself: a session records the event, the viewer, when they joined and left, minutes watched, the peak bitrate they were served and the device type. Minutes watched decays exponentially at a rate of about 0.025 per minute, so forty minutes on average -- most people dip in and out. Bitrate lives between 400 and 8000 kbps, but free events are capped: a session on a non-ticketed event never goes above 2500. Devices come out 46 percent mobile, 24 TV, 22 web, 8 tablet.

Chat is on per event -- who said what and when, plus a flag the moderators set when something has been pulled.

I run the reading app -- webcomics and translated manga, mostly. It is small: a hundred and ninety series, somewhere around eleven thousand chapters, and just under eight thousand people paying us.

A series has its title, whoever made it, the language it is in, and where it is at -- ongoing, finished, or on hiatus. Most of what we carry is Japanese, about four in ten; Korean is another quarter or so, then English at a bit over a fifth, and a little Chinese. The creator is just a name to us. There are translation teams involved on a lot of these and they matter enormously to the readers, but all of that is handled over email and never touches the app.

Chapters sit under a series, numbered, with the date they went up and the page count. Twenty-odd pages is normal -- twenty-two is about the average and they do not wander more than six either side of that. Anything under four pages we would send back, and the biggest we have ever taken was eighty. Some chapters are free and some sit behind coins. The coin price is three most of the time, five for the ones the publishers make a fuss about, and if a chapter is free then obviously its price is nothing at all.

Readers -- subscribers, members, whatever you want to call them, it is the same person -- have a display name, the date they joined, whatever coins they have left, and which plan they are on. Balances cannot go below zero, and they are all over the place: most people are sitting on a handful of coins, and a few have thousands because they bought a big pack in a sale.

When someone opens a paid chapter we take the coins and record it, so we know who unlocked what, when, and what it cost them. Opening a free chapter gets recorded the same way but charges nothing. Reads spike very hard the day a new chapter lands and then fall off a cliff, in case that matters for whatever you are sizing.

Schema for the moderation console -- this is the internal tool, not the content firehose, so the volumes are tiny and I would rather have it normalised than fast: 240 moderators, about 60 live policies, 1,800 appeals filed since launch, and a couple of thousand audited decisions in the sampling table.

Moderators have an employee code, a hire date, a seniority level from 1 to 5 and a locale. Queues have a name, the kind of content they hold and an SLA in minutes; the SLAs are spread fairly evenly from fifteen minutes on the imminent-harm queue up to a full day for the low-severity backlog. A moderator is certified on some set of queues and a queue has many certified moderators, so that pairing gets its own row carrying the certification date.

Policies carry a code, a title, a severity tier and a retired flag. Tiers run 1 to 4, and the live book is roughly 20 percent tier 1, 34 tier 2, 28 tier 3 and 18 tier 4.

A content item is a UUID with its content kind, a submission timestamp, a hashed author identifier -- we never join back to the user service from in here -- the queue it landed in, and a report count. Reports per item are Poisson with lambda about 1.7, and each report knows the item, when it came in, what kind of reporter filed it, and the policy cited.

A decision is one moderator on one item: a timestamp, an outcome, handling seconds, the policy applied and an escalation flag. Outcomes split 49 percent keep, 34 remove, 9 age-gate, 8 escalate. Handling time is lognormal with log mean 3.6 and variance 0.7 -- median a bit over half a minute -- never under 2 seconds, and we cut anything past an hour as a stuck session. Anything decided on a tier-4 policy is escalated, no exceptions.

Appeals point at a decision with a filing time, an outcome and a resolution time. Audit samples point at a decision too, naming the auditor, who is another moderator, when it was audited, whether they agreed and a free-text note. Enforcement is kept separate from the decision so we can re-issue it: an action code, a duration in days and when it was applied. Suspensions run one to thirty days; a keep decision can still get a bookkeeping enforcement row, and in that case the duration is zero.

Schema notes for the reservations and operations side of a mid-size network carrier. Airports are keyed on their IATA code and carry a name, a city, a country and a UTC offset as a float, because half a dozen of our stations sit on half-hour zones. Each aircraft type record holds the manufacturer, the certified seat count and the still-air range in km; individual airframes hang off that by tail number with a delivery date. A route is an origin/destination pair of airports plus a great-circle distance, and a flight is one dated operation of a route by one airframe -- scheduled and actual off-block timestamps, planned block time in minutes, an operational status code and the observed load factor. Load factor is a fraction and must stay between 0 and 1; across the network it is roughly Gaussian, mean 0.83, sd 0.09. Route popularity is brutally skewed: flight volume per route follows a Zipf law with an exponent around 1.2. Fare classes are their own small dimension -- a one- or two-letter booking code, the cabin it sits in, a refundable flag and a change fee. Passengers carry a name, a date of birth, a frequent flyer number and a tier; the tier mix is about 71 percent base, 17 silver, 8 gold, 4 platinum. A booking is identified by its six-character PNR and records when it was made, the sales channel, the lead passenger and the total fare. The coupon table is the many-to-many core: one row per PNR, flight and passenger, keyed on all three, holding the fare class flown, the fare actually paid, a checked-in flag and the number of free checked bags on that coupon. Economy coupons price between 39 and 900. Platinum passengers get three free bags on every coupon. Any flight whose route exceeds 6000 km is planned with at least 480 minutes of block time. Bags are tracked individually by tag against a PNR and a flight; weight is normal around 18.6 kg with sd 5.4 and we refuse anything over 32 kg. Delay events are logged per flight with a duration in minutes -- exponentially distributed, mean about 27 -- and an IATA reason code. Volumes: 1.3 million flights and just over 40 million coupons a year, so the coupon and baggage tables want partitioning by flight date.

We run 60-odd hotels and I am trying to spec out the reservation database properly before we hand anything to a vendor, so bear with the level of detail here.

Every property has a name, a city, a star rating and a total room count. We are mostly mid-market -- call it 12 percent three star, 58 percent four and 30 percent five. Within a property we sell room types rather than named rooms: a short code, how many people it sleeps and a base rate. The physical rooms exist too, each with a floor and a room number, and each one belongs to exactly one room type.

Reservations are the busy bit. A reservation is for one property, one room type and one guest -- the commercial team says customer and ops says guest, it is the same person, and all we hold on them is a name and an email -- with a check-in date, a check-out date, the night count, adults, children, a rate plan, a status, the total amount and when it was booked. Length of stay averages 2.4 nights and behaves like a count. The total amount is heavily right-skewed so log-normal is the sensible assumption. Party mix is about 30 percent single adult, 52 percent two adults, 8 percent three and 10 percent four. We do not take a booking longer than 21 nights in this system, and obviously not shorter than one.

Rate plans belong to a property and have a name, a cancellation window in hours and a refundable flag. The non-refundable plans have a zero-hour window; the flexible ones give the guest somewhere between 24 and 72 hours. Anything booked on a non-refundable plan is prepaid, always, and we want that recorded on the reservation. And if the room type only sleeps two we cannot put more than two adults on the reservation.

We also keep seasons per property -- a name, a date range and the multiplier we apply to the base rate over that range.

Charges get posted to the reservation as they happen (room, breakfast, bar, parking, that sort of thing) with a charge type, an amount and a timestamp. Housekeeping raise a task per room per day, with a date, a status, who it went to and how long it took -- about 28 minutes on average, sd 9.

After check-out we email for a score out of five. It is a 1 to 5 thing and it clusters high: 2 percent ones, 3 percent twos, 9 percent threes, 27 percent fours, 59 percent fives, plus an optional free-text comment and the time it came in. Volume-wise we are looking at roughly 400,000 reservations a year across the estate.

Right, so we have got the place in Lisbon and a smaller one in Porto now, and everything is still on paper and a shared spreadsheet, which is honestly a nightmare on changeover days. What I need is something that knows which beds are free. Both buildings go in, each with its own name and the city it is in, and that is all I want held about the buildings themselves.

Each building is split into dorms -- we call them rooms half the time, same thing -- and a dorm is anywhere from four to twelve beds, with a name on the door, and it is either mixed or women-only. Every bed has a label like 3B so the cleaners know which one we mean, and we do note whether it is a top or bottom bunk because people always ask.

When someone books, they are booking a bed, not a room. I need the arrival day and the departure day, how many nights, what we charged them a night, and where the booking came from -- about seventy percent is Hostelworld, the rest is our own site or people just turning up at the door. Prices swing with the season, sixteen to thirty-four euros a night, and if someone is staying a week or more we knock it down to a flat sixteen. Two weeks is the longest we will take, after that they need a proper rental. Most stays are short -- two nights, three nights, it averages out around two and a half. We take a ten euro deposit off everyone at the point of booking and note that down.

For the guests themselves it is just a name, an email, what country they are from and the year they were born, because we need to know if anyone is under eighteen. Nationality-wise, roughly four in ten are German, a quarter Australian, and the rest is a very long list of everywhere else.

Oh, and Elena does a walking tour on Tuesdays and a pub crawl on Fridays -- the walk is free, the crawl is twelve euros -- and she needs to know who has signed up for which one, so that wants to be in there somewhere too. Same person can do both, obviously.

We are small, mind. Maybe three thousand bookings a year between the two places.

I am the product owner at a European car hire outfit -- 340 branches, a fleet of about 22,000 and roughly 900,000 agreements a year. The current setup is two systems held together with a nightly file transfer, so we are re-modelling from scratch.

Branches need a name, a city, the airport code if it is an airport desk, and the opening and closing time, because after-hours returns are a whole separate mess.

We rent categories, not cars. A category has a code (ECON, COMP, INTER, PREM, SUV and so on), a description, a daily rate and a minimum driver age. Half the fleet is compact, a third intermediate, and the rest splits between economy, premium and SUV at roughly 8, 5 and 4 percent. The actual cars have a registration, a model year, an odometer reading and a home branch, and we sell them on once they hit 90,000 km, so nothing in the fleet is above that.

Customers we hold by name, date of birth, licence number and the country that issued it.

The agreement is the centre of the whole thing. It ties a customer to the booked category and to the specific car handed over, records the pickup branch and the return branch, when it was picked up, when it is due back, when it actually came back, how many days, the quoted total and the kilometres driven. Hires average just under four days and the distance driven is very long-tailed. We record the driver's age on the agreement itself, because the surcharge depends on it -- under 25 is a flat 12 a day. And we will not sign at all below the category minimum: most categories are 21, but premium and SUV are 25, and for those the driver has to be 25 or over. Nobody gets a car for more than 90 days.

There are two tariffs. The cheap one caps you at 1,500 km over the whole hire, the flexible one is unlimited, so there is a flag on the agreement and the cap only bites when it is set.

Extras -- child seats, sat nav, additional driver, winter tyres -- get added onto an agreement, several per agreement, and each extra has its own daily price.

Damage gets written up against the agreement with a severity, the time it was spotted and what the repair came to. Most of it is trivial; the average bill is about 340 but the shape is a long decay rather than a bell.

Target data model for a 28-ship premium cruise operator; we are consolidating three legacy reservation systems onto one warehouse.

Ships carry a name, gross tonnage, passenger and crew capacity and a launch year. Cabins belong to a ship, sit on a numbered deck, have a cabin number and a berth count -- that berth number is load-bearing, because a booking's guest count can never exceed the berths in the cabin it holds. Cabin categories group cabins by class (inside, oceanview, balcony, suite) and carry a base fare.

An itinerary is a reusable product: a name, a region and a night count, 2 to 21 nights, averaging around 7.4. Ports of call attach to an itinerary as a day-numbered sequence with scheduled arrival and departure times, and the same port shows up on many itineraries, so that is a proper association keyed on the itinerary and the port. Ports themselves have a name, a country and a UN/LOCODE.

A voyage -- marketing insists on calling them sailings, internally everything keys off voyage_id -- is one dated operation of an itinerary by a ship, with a departure date, a return date and a recorded occupancy rate. Note that occupancy is measured against double occupancy, so third and fourth berths push it above 1: expect roughly normal, mean 0.96, sd 0.04, and treat anything from 0 to 1.05 as valid rather than clamping at 1.

Bookings sit against a voyage and a cabin, with a lead guest, a booked-at timestamp, a guest count, the total fare, the deposit taken, the deposit percentage applied, a cancelled flag, the cancellation fee percentage and the number of days between booking and sailing. Guest count is 2 on about 62 percent of bookings, 3 on 16, 4 on 14 and a single traveller on 8. Total fare is log-normal. Lead time decays exponentially with a mean near 120 days. Every guest travelling on a booking is enumerated in an association table keyed on the booking and the guest; guests themselves have a name, a date of birth, a nationality and a running loyalty night total.

Deposit rules are firm: 15 percent when the booking is 90 or more days out, the full fare inside that. If a booking is cancelled within 60 days of sailing the forfeited share is between 50 and 100 percent.

Shore excursions belong to a port and have a name, a price, a capacity and a duration in hours; they are sold per booking with a guest count and a sale timestamp. Onboard spend posts against the booking as charge lines with an outlet, an amount and a posting time -- log-normal, and that is the monster table: about 90 million rows a year against 1.1 million bookings.

I have been running the walking and cycling trips for eleven years now off a laptop and a wall planner and it is finally too much to hold in my head.

So. We have about a dozen trips we sell. Each one has a name, a proper write-up for the website, how many days it runs -- three days at the shortest, a fortnight for the Dolomites one -- and a rough idea of how hard it is, which honestly is just my own judgement, easy, moderate or tough. Prices are per person and run from around six hundred up to two thousand four hundred. There is a ceiling on the group size for every trip and it is never above fourteen; below four we cancel, it does not pay to run.

Each time we actually go, that is a departure -- the start date, which trip it is, who is guiding it, how many places have gone, and whether it is confirmed or cancelled. We tend to fill nine or so, give or take three, sometimes as few as four, occasionally we are full. Marek guides most of them and I have two freelancers I bring in when it clashes; I need their name, what languages they speak and their day rate.

Then the people. Clients, walkers, guests -- whatever you want to call them, it is one list: name, email, phone and which country they are from. Mostly British, a good number of Dutch and Americans, a scattering of everyone else. When someone books, it is onto a departure, and I need how many of them are coming, what they have paid so far, what is still outstanding, and the date they booked. Roughly half book as a couple, a quarter come on their own, the rest are threes and fours. Groups of six or more get ten percent off and I want that recorded rather than just baked into the price.

Hotels I will keep in my own spreadsheet. That is a separate headache and I do not want it anywhere near this.

It is not a lot of data, by the way. Maybe a hundred and forty departures and twelve hundred bookings in a year.

Notes for the developer doing our booking system. We are a 96-pitch touring park in North Wales, open March to October, and we take somewhere around four thousand stays a season, so nothing enormous.

A pitch has our own code on it (A1 through to F16), a type -- hardstanding, grass or fully serviced -- a flag for whether it has an electric hookup, the maximum unit length it will take in metres, which is six to twelve depending on where it sits, and its nightly rate. Rates run from 22 to 41 pounds. Anything with electric is at least 28.

Campers we hold as one record each: name, email, the vehicle registration because we need it for the barrier, and their club membership number if they have one.

A stay is one camper on one pitch: arrival date, departure date, the number of nights, how many adults, how many children, how many dogs, and what the whole thing came to. Our licence caps any single stay at 28 nights. Two dogs per pitch, no more than that. Between one and six adults on a pitch. Stays average about 3.2 nights and the pattern is the usual count-like spread you would expect. The total charge is right-skewed -- a lot of long weekends and then a handful of three-week stays. Adults come out at two on about two-thirds of stays, one on 12 percent, three on 8 percent and four on the remainder.

Payments go against the stay -- the method, the amount and the date we took it -- and there can be more than one per stay because we take a deposit up front and the balance on arrival. Around 82 percent goes on card, 11 percent cash and the remainder bank transfer.

My brother and I have five places now -- two in Shoreditch, one in Peckham, the Islington room and the new one -- and the booking situation has completely got away from us. Each site needs a name, roughly where it is, a phone line and how many it seats. The smallest is about forty covers; the Islington room is the big one at a hundred and twenty.

The bookings themselves: who it is for, which site, when they are coming (the date and the time together, obviously, not two separate things), how many people, where the booking came in from -- about forty-five percent through the website widget now, a quarter on the phone, the rest walk-ins that we log after the fact -- and whether it is still live, cancelled, or they did not show. Roughly one in twenty just do not turn up, which is the thing that is actually costing us money, so I want it flagged plainly rather than buried in a status code.

Twos are the bread and butter, near enough half of everything. Then fours at a bit over a fifth, threes maybe fifteen percent, sixes eight and the rest are eights and up. We will not take anything over twenty on the system -- past that it is a private hire and my brother handles it on email. Eight and above we ask for a deposit, ten pounds a head, so at least eighty quid on the card before we hold it. And a party of ten or more can only go into a room that seats a hundred or more, which in practice means Islington.

For the people, we keep a name, a mobile, an email if they will give us one, and a notes field -- allergies, who the regulars are, and the two or three we would rather not have back.

We do not need the actual table layout in here. The floor plan lives on a whiteboard and the managers like it that way.

It adds up though. Something like one point four million covers a year across the group.

Ground handling data model for a two-terminal hub. Roughly 310,000 aircraft movements a year and a little over 4 million service-task rows, so partitioning and retention matter more than usual here.

Carriers sit in a small dimension: IATA code, name, home country. Movement volume by carrier is extremely skewed -- two based airlines dominate and there is a very long tail of once-a-week charters. A Zipf law with an exponent near 1.35 fits the carrier mix on turnarounds well.

Stands carry a code, the terminal they belong to, the maximum wingspan they can accept (24 m up to 65 m, spread more or less uniformly across the apron) and whether a jetbridge is fitted.

A turnaround is the unit of work: one carrier, one stand, an aircraft registration, a flight number, the scheduled off-block time, the actual on-block and off-block timestamps, the resulting ground time in minutes and the departure delay in minutes. Contractual minimum turn is 20 minutes, and anything beyond 240 gets reclassified as a parking event, so ground time lives inside that window; it is roughly normal, mean 47, sd 14. Delay minutes decay exponentially with a mean near 14. Remote stands -- the ones with no jetbridge -- need bussing in both directions, so we plan those at 35 minutes minimum.

Task types are catalogued with a name, a standard duration and the certification level needed to perform them. Ground crew have a name, a shift pattern and a certification level of 1, 2 or 3, and the mix across the workforce is about 40/35/25. A service task instance ties one turnaround, one task type and one crew member, with start and completion timestamps and the actual duration in minutes -- log-normal, and never below one minute.

Equipment (tugs, belt loaders, GPUs, de-icers) is tracked by asset tag with a type, an in-service flag and a purchase date, and gets assigned to individual tasks with an assigned and a released timestamp.

I look after pricing at a travel insurance MGA and we are rebuilding the policy admin database, so I am writing down what I think it actually needs to hold.

Products first: a name, whether it is single-trip or annual multi-trip, the longest trip it will cover, the medical expenses limit and a base premium. The limits sit between 2 million and 10 million depending on which product it is.

The customer -- we say policyholder on the certificate and customer everywhere else, same person -- gives us a name, a date of birth, a country of residence and an email. We store the age at inception separately from the date of birth because that is what the rating actually uses, and the book averages about 44 with a spread of 15 years or so.

A policy (the certificate, again the same thing) ties a product to a policyholder: the start and end date, the trip length in days, the destination region, the premium charged, how many travellers are on it, whether pre-existing conditions were declared, when it was sold, the age loading applied, and the name of the agent who sold it. Trip length averages around 11 days and behaves like a count. Nobody gets more than 60 days on a single trip, and for anyone 65 or over we will not write more than 45. Over-65s also carry an age loading of at least 50 percent. Premium itself is log-normal. Destination-wise it is 58 percent Europe, 17 percent worldwide excluding the US and Canada, 15 percent full worldwide and 10 percent domestic.

Claims come in against a policy: a type, the incident date, what is being claimed, what we eventually paid, a status and the settlement date. Medical is 41 percent of claims, cancellation 28, baggage 19 and the rest miscellaneous. Amounts claimed are log-normal with a very fat tail. Declined claims settle at zero, obviously -- nothing paid at all.

We are writing about 620,000 policies a year and seeing maybe 45,000 claims against them.

I'm the manufacturing analyst for a two-plant vehicle assembly operation and I've been asked to spec out where our line-monitoring dashboards should read from, because right now every number comes straight off the PLC historian and nobody can join anything to anything.

Each plant has a code that everybody uses in conversation -- BRM1, and the newer one down in Puebla -- plus the city it sits in. A plant runs two or three assembly lines. A line has a name and a takt time, which is the beat it's supposed to run to, in seconds. Along a line sit the stations, numbered in order from one; our longest line gets up to 42 of them, and every station has a short code stencilled on the floor next to it.

The thing that actually moves is a body-in-white, which by the end of the line is a vehicle. We identify it by VIN, and we know which model it's being built as and the date it was launched onto the line. Only three models are running at the moment: a bit under half the volume is the sedan, roughly forty percent is the SUV, and the remainder are pickups.

Every time a unit passes through a station we get a record -- when it entered, how long the cycle took, and which operator was manning that station. Operators belong to a plant, have a badge number, and work one of three shifts; days is the biggest at about forty percent of the roster, afternoons a bit over a third, nights the rest.

Cycle time is the number everybody stares at. The lines are set for 58 seconds and the actual spread is around six and a half seconds either side of that. If a cycle comes back longer than four minutes it isn't a slow cycle, it's a stoppage, and those get handled in a different system -- so nothing in here should be above 240 seconds, or negative for that matter. There's also a line-stop flag on the record. Pickups are genuinely slower to build, and the rule the plant floor uses is that on a pickup you don't raise the flag until the cycle passes 75 seconds.

On volume: we log somewhere around 40 million station events a year across the two plants, and three years of it has to stay queryable.

Schema for an electronics contract manufacturer's MES. Sizing first: roughly 40k parts under control, 6k work orders a year, about 3M panel rows and 9M defect rows in the retained history.

Parts are the core entity -- part number, description, a type discriminator (RAW, COMPONENT, PCBA, ASSEMBLY) and a unit cost. Unit cost is log-normal with a log-mean of 0.4 and a log-variance of 1.8: most parts are worth cents, a handful are $400 FPGAs. Parts nest into each other. A bill-of-materials line is a parent-part to child-part edge carrying the quantity per assembly and the reference designator, and the (parent, child) pair is the natural key for it. Depth is arbitrary -- a top-level assembly contains PCBAs, which contain components. Quantity per is at least 1 and never more than 500, and it is Zipf-like with an exponent around 1.6: overwhelmingly ones and twos with a long tail of decoupling caps placed two hundred to a board.

Parts are purchased, and the same part normally has two or three approved sources, so that's a second composite-keyed association, carrying the quoted lead time in days and a price per thousand. Lead time is exponentially distributed with a mean of 21 days, and we won't approve a source quoting past 180 days. Suppliers need a name and a country code.

Customers -- name and account code -- place work orders. A work order is for exactly one part, with an ordered quantity, a release date and a status. Costing rule we enforce at entry: if the part costs more than $50 each, the order must be released for at least 25 pieces, because setup doesn't amortise below that.

A work order is built across one or more production runs on a named SMT line; each line has a rated placement rate in components per hour. A run records its start time and the boards it built -- averaging 480, and never fewer than one. Every panel off a run gets a serial number and an AOI verdict: 94% pass, 5% fail, 1% get sent back for a rescan. Failing panels carry solder defects, each with a defect code and the component reference it was found at.

So we're a small brewery, six of us, and at the minute the whole thing lives in a shared spreadsheet that my head brewer keeps breaking. What we want is somewhere proper to put the brew records.

Right. We have recipes. Each one's got a name -- the pale ale is Harbour Light, the stout is Black Mole -- and a style, and a target strength, and we set a bitterness target as well although honestly nobody looks at that after the first couple of brews. Two out of every three batches we run are the pale ale, about a quarter is the stout, and the rest is whatever seasonal thing we've talked ourselves into that month.

Then every time we brew, that's a batch. Some of the lads call it a brew and Dave writes "lot" on the tank tags, it's all the same thing as far as I'm concerned. We want the date, how much we actually got into the tank, which tank it went into, and what it finished at strength-wise. We aim for 5.2 percent and we're normally within about a third of a percent of that either way. Nothing we make is under 3.5 or over 7.5 -- that's just not what we do. Oh, and the stout we only ever do as a half batch, six hundred litres at the absolute most, because the tank we ferment that one in is the little one.

Tanks have names, we name them after dogs, and a capacity in litres.

While it's fermenting someone goes round twice a day with the hydrometer and writes down the gravity and the temperature. Readings start around 1.050 when it's fresh and come down to about 1.010 when it's finished, and they're anywhere in between depending when you happen to look. We hold the fermentation between 18 and 22 degrees, and that's the one thing we are genuinely strict about.

We also note which maltster the grain came from against each brew, for traceability, in case there's ever a problem with a sack of malt.

It really isn't a lot of data. We do maybe 120 brews a year and we've got four years of history, so a few hundred batches and a few thousand hydrometer readings, that's your lot.

My grandfather started this dyehouse and we still run it much the same way, which is to say on paper. I'd like to get the shade records onto a computer before an auditor asks me for something I can't put my hands on.

What we do is dye cloth in lots. A lot is one drum-load: what fabric it was, what colour, the day it went in, and what it weighed. Lots run anything from forty kilos up to a couple of hundred, and it's fairly even right across that range -- depends entirely what the customer ordered. About half of everything through here is cotton jersey, a third is the poly-cotton blend, and the rest viscose.

The machines -- we call them drums, my father called them becks -- each have a name and a rated load. Ours go from fifty kilos up to three hundred.

Once a lot comes out, one of the girls takes a swatch over to the light box and reads it against the customer's standard. That gives you a colour difference number. Usually it lands around six tenths, give or take a quarter. Over one and the customer sends the whole thing back at our expense, so one is the line and never mind arguing about it. Whites are a different story -- on a white you can see everything, so we won't ship one above half. She puts her initials on the card and marks it pass or fail.

We do about eight hundred lots a year and we keep three years of cards in the cabinet, so this is not a big job for a computer.

We're a forty-person job shop -- CNC turning and milling, mostly aerospace subcontract with some oil and gas -- and we're finally replacing a 1990s ERP we outgrew a decade ago. I've sketched out what I think the data looks like; you'll know better than me whether it normalises properly.

A job is one customer order line: their drawing number, how many pieces, when it's due, what we quoted, and a priority code. For customers I need the name and the payment terms in days.
