Quotes are all over the map -- the typical one is around thirteen hundred dollars, but there's a long right tail and a handful of jobs a year run into five figures. Log-normal, or it looks it. We don't take a job under one piece, and anything over about five thousand pieces we hand off to a production shop, so quantities live between those two.

Each job carries a routing: a numbered list of operations in order, never more than twenty of them, each assigned to a machine, each with an estimated setup time and a per-piece run time. Setup averages about 45 minutes with maybe eighteen minutes of spread around that. Machines have a name, a type and an hourly rate -- roughly forty percent of the fleet is CNC mills, thirty percent CNC lathes, and the balance splits evenly between manual mills and surface grinders.

Machinists clock onto an operation and off it again, and when they clock off they declare good pieces and scrap. Scrap is usually one or two pieces on a ticket, sometimes zero, once in a while a proper disaster -- and it obviously can't be negative. For machinists I want a name and a skill level.

We also need what material went out to a job from the stores: material code, weight, cost. On the big titanium jobs the material is most of the price, so it can't be an afterthought.

One rule that really matters. When a job comes in flagged as a rush, we won't allocate more than half an hour of setup to any operation on it. If it needs more than that, it isn't a rush job, it's a project, and it gets scheduled like one.

Volume is modest by your standards: around 900,000 time tickets over the fifteen years we'd migrate, half a million operations, a couple hundred thousand jobs.

Time-series store for a vibration-based condition monitoring programme spanning fourteen plants. Volume drives every design decision here: about 11,000 wireless sensors reporting every ten minutes, which comes to roughly 90 million reading rows a month and 1.2 billion a year, held hot for eighteen months. Partition on the capture timestamp.

Assets are the monitored machines: asset tag, asset class (PUMP, FAN, GEARBOX, MOTOR, COMPRESSOR), installation date, rated power in kW. Each asset carries one or more sensors. A sensor has a type -- accelerometers and velocity transducers, mainly -- a sample rate in Hz, and a firmware version.

A reading is sensor, capture timestamp, RMS velocity in mm/s, peak g, and casing temperature. On healthy equipment RMS velocity is tightly normal: mean 2.1 mm/s, standard deviation 0.6. The transducers saturate at 45 mm/s and cannot report a negative, so that is the check on the column. Casing temperature is normal around 46 C with a sigma of 7, and the sensors are only rated from -20 to 120 C.

Alerts are raised against a sensor and record the raise timestamp, a severity, the RMS value that tripped them, and an acknowledgement flag. We precompute the elapsed hours since the previous alert on the same sensor, because reliability engineering wants MTBA straight out of the table rather than as a window function; that gap is exponentially distributed with a mean near 300 hours. Severity splits 72% warning, 24% alarm, 4% trip. Trigger RMS is non-negative by construction.

Per ISO 10816 the alarm threshold on our accelerometer channels is 4.5 mm/s, so any alert whose trigger RMS is above 4.5 on an accelerometer must carry severity ALARM, not warning.

Quality engineering wants out of the paper-and-Access situation we're in, and I've been told to explain how inspection actually works here so you can tell me what it needs to look like underneath.

We mould plastic components. Each one has an SKU, a name, and a nominal weight in grams. For each component quality writes an inspection plan; plans get revised over time, so a plan carries a revision label alongside the sample size it calls for and an AQL. The AQLs we're permitted to use run from 0.065 up to 6.5, and a sample size is at least one piece -- I've seen zero typed in and it caused a fight.

A plan lists the characteristics that get checked: a name, the nominal value, an upper and a lower tolerance, and the unit. Some characteristics are dimensional, some cosmetic, some functional. The cosmetic ones don't really have a nominal but the form insists on one anyway.

Production hands over lots. A lot is a product, the date it ran, how many pieces are in it, and which shift made it. Lot sizes are all over the place -- the median is around three thousand but it's badly skewed, some campaign lots are enormous.

An inspection ties a lot to the plan revision that was used, plus who inspected it, when, and the disposition. Nine times out of ten it's an accept; about six percent go to rework and three percent are rejected outright. Inspectors have a name and a certification level.

Within an inspection each characteristic gets measured several times, and every measurement is stored with its value and whether it came in within spec. The one everybody watches is the critical bore diameter -- twelve millimetre nominal, the process sits right on twelve with a sigma of about four hundredths of a millimetre, and the print tolerance is plus or minus four hundredths, so a measurement of that characteristic has to land between 11.96 and 12.04.

Separately from the measurements, inspectors log the defects they find. We keep a coded catalogue -- defect code, category, severity class -- and record how many of each turned up in an inspection. Typically a couple, call it two or three.

There's a sampling rule out of the customer quality manual that we have to honour: any lot over ten thousand pieces must be inspected under a plan calling for at least two hundred pieces.

For sizing: roughly 400,000 inspections and eight million individual measurements across the five years we'd load.

Small and tightly scoped: the calibration register for our metrology lab, run ISO 17025 style. About 900 gauges under control and maybe 2,000 calibration events a year, so five figures of rows in total. This is a correctness problem, not a volume one.

A gauge row is the asset number, the gauge type (MICROMETER, CALIPER, DIAL_INDICATOR, BORE_GAUGE, HEIGHT_GAUGE), its resolution in mm, and its recall interval in days. Intervals are set per gauge and are spread roughly uniformly between 90 and 365 days.

A calibration event references the gauge and the reference standard used against it, and records the date performed, the technician, the as-found error in mm, an outcome, and the next due date. As-found error is normal, centred on zero, standard deviation 0.004 mm. Anything outside plus or minus 0.020 mm and the gauge is condemned rather than adjusted, so that is the hard limit on the column -- except on micrometers, where we hold plus or minus 0.005 mm and scrap outside that.

Outcomes run 88% pass, 9% pass-after-adjustment, 3% fail.

Reference standards need a name, the certified value in mm, and the stated uncertainty. Ours are all certified to better than two microns, and an uncertainty is non-negative by definition.

I do the scheduling for the plant -- fourteen hundred people across three buildings -- and I do it in Excel, which is the entire reason I'm sitting here.

Here's the shape of it. I've got employees. For each one I need the name, when they started, what they earn an hour, and which department they sit in. Nobody is below the state minimum, which is seventeen twenty here, and I only mention it because the spreadsheet happily lets me type anything at all. Average is about twenty-four fifty an hour and most people are within four dollars of that either way.

Then there are the tickets people hold -- forklift, confined space, the two welding ones, food-safe handling. One person can have several of them and plenty of people hold the same one, and I need the date they certified because these things expire and I get audited on them.

Shifts come off patterns. A pattern has a name -- days, afters, nights, the weekend continental one -- a start time, and a length in hours.

Most of what I actually do is put a person on a pattern on a date, in a particular area of the floor. That's the bulk of it by a mile. I record what they actually worked and how much of that was overtime, because payroll takes those numbers off me on a Monday. A shift is nominally eight hours and in practice it's a bit over -- eight and a bit, with somewhere under an hour of variation on it. Nine days out of ten there's no overtime at all; when there is, it's usually an hour, occasionally a whole extra shift, so across everybody it works out to about an hour on average. Nobody is on the floor more than twelve hours in a day and nobody gets more than four hours of overtime -- both of those are straight out of the union agreement. The packing crew are capped at two hours because of the noise exposure rules, which is a separate thing entirely and catches me out constantly.

And absences: who, what day, why, and whether I signed it off. Just over half are sickness, about thirty percent is booked vacation, ten percent unpaid, and the odd bereavement.

We've got roughly two million shift rows going back to 2011, which is where Excel finally gave up on me.

This is for the melt shop and the caster, and I'll warn you up front that the vocabulary round here is a mess -- people say heat, melt and charge for what I think are two or three different things, and I won't be able to fully untangle that for you.

The unit of production is a heat. It comes out of a furnace; we've got the big electric arc furnace and a smaller induction unit we mostly keep for specials, and each furnace has a name, a type and a nominal tap capacity in tonnes. A heat records its heat number, the grade it was melted to, when it was tapped, how much came out, the tap temperature and the electrical energy it took. The arc furnace taps somewhere between a hundred and a hundred and sixty-five tonnes; the induction one is a completely different animal and I'd rather you didn't hard-code anything for it. Tap temperature is the number the melters live by -- 1635 is the aim and they hold it to about a dozen degrees. Nothing below 1550 or above 1700 is real data, it's a thermocouple fault. High-carbon grades have to go out hotter: if the grade's target carbon is above four tenths of a percent, we tap at 1650 minimum.

Grades have a code, a family -- roughly seventy percent of our tonnage is plain carbon, twenty percent HSLA, the rest alloy -- and a target carbon.

Into the furnace goes scrap and additions: shredded, busheling, pig iron, lime, ferro-alloys. Each material has a name, a class and a cost per tonne, and for a given heat we record how much of each went in. A heat obviously takes many materials and a material goes into many heats.

Out of the furnace the steel goes to a ladle. Ladles have a number and we track how many heats the lining has done, because they go about 120 heats before we reline. A ladle feeds a casting sequence on one of the casters, and a sequence records when it started and how many strands were running. Casters have a name and a machine type.

The sequence produces slabs. A slab belongs to a sequence and traces back to the heat it came from, and we keep its number, length, weight and a surface grade. Slabs run between eighteen and thirty tonnes, more or less evenly across that.

The lab pulls samples during the melt and gives us back carbon, sulphur and manganese. Carbon comes in around 0.18 with a couple of hundredths of scatter on it. Sulphur has to be under three hundredths of a percent or the heat gets downgraded.

Oh, and the PLC historian dumps tag readings against each furnace -- tag name, timestamp, value. That's tens of millions of rows a day and honestly nobody has decided yet what we're keeping, but it needs somewhere to live.

Mediation and rating store for a national mobile operator. Volume drives the design: roughly 40 million voice records a day, so the CDR table partitions on start timestamp and everything else stays a narrow dimension.

Subscriber is keyed on a surrogate integer, with MSISDN and IMSI as varchars, an activation date, a prepaid/postpaid boolean, and a mandatory rate plan reference. A plan row carries a short code, a name, the monthly recurring charge as DECIMAL and the per-minute voice tariff; the plan book runs 5.00 to 60.00 a month and nothing sits outside it. Fraud screening reads a rolling daily call-attempt counter denormalised onto the subscriber row -- a count process, lambda near 6.

A voice CDR references the calling subscriber and the serving cell and holds the dialled B-number as varchar, the start TIMESTAMP, duration_seconds as INTEGER and the charged amount as DECIMAL. The switch discards anything under a second and force-releases at 7200, hence CHECK duration_seconds between 1 and 7200. Holding time is memoryless: no characteristic length, flat hang-up hazard once a call is up, and an exponential with a mean near 110 seconds tracks the observed curve.

Messaging gets its own thinner table -- sending subscriber, destination number, submit timestamp, and a segment count that is 1 to 6 by construction.

Cells hang off sites; a site carries latitude and longitude as FLOAT plus a region code. Traffic per cell is brutally unequal, a few hundred cells taking most of it, and capacity planning models cell id as Zipf, exponent 1.4.

One rating rule: for a prepaid subscriber a call over 1800 seconds is charged at a flat out-of-bundle cap of 4.50 rather than per minute.

I run the provisioning side of a regional broadband outfit. We're in about four hundred thousand homes now across the west of the country, and the spreadsheets stopped coping roughly two years ago, so bear with me while I explain how the work actually flows.

Somebody signs up. Usually that's online, sometimes it's over the phone and we do want to know which, because the phone ones cancel less. We take a name, the address the service is going to, a contact number and an email. The address matters more than people outside think, because everything hangs off which exchange the property is wired back to, and there are a couple of hundred exchanges in our footprint. An exchange has a name, a code the engineers actually use on the ground, and whether it's been upgraded to fibre yet -- most have, not all. When an order is taken the system stamps the serving exchange onto it there and then, so nobody has to go and look it up again later.

Then the customer picks a package. There are four and we number them one to four in this order: Basic at 40 megabits, Family at 150, Pro at 500, and the gigabit one that we barely sell. Half the base is on Family, about a quarter on Basic, a fifth on Pro, and the rest is gigabit. Each package has its monthly price and a contract length, and those are only ever 12, 18 or 24 months.

An order turns into an installation job. The job has a date, a two-hour appointment window, one of our engineers on it, and an outcome -- completed, failed, customer not home, that sort of thing. Jobs get rebooked, so one customer can end up with three or four of them. Engineers work out of a depot and I want to know which depot somebody sits in, along with their name.

Two things bite us and I want the system to stop them. If the property is on an exchange that hasn't had the fibre upgrade, we cannot sell anything faster than 150 meg -- the order should just be refused. And nobody gets booked more than 45 days out; we write down how many days ahead each job was booked and that number must never go past 45, otherwise the order goes back to sales.

Last thing, and it's a sore point: installs take longer than we tell people. On paper it's a two hour slot. Real time on site averages nearer 145 minutes, and it's all over the place -- 40 minutes if there's a live socket already, most of a working day, eight hours say, when there's no duct into the property. A handful of very long jobs drag the average well above the typical one.

Physical asset register covering two colocation halls. Call it 3,000 devices total, so row volume is irrelevant and normalisation wins everywhere.

The location hierarchy comes first. A site holds a data centre and has a name; a site has one or more halls; a hall is laid out in labelled rows of racks. Each hall records the per-rack power cap we contracted for -- Hall A is 8 kW a rack, Hall B is 12, and no hall in the estate is outside that pair. A rack belongs to exactly one row, carries a label, is either 42U or 45U tall (CHECK rack_units between 42 and 45), has a design power envelope in kW as FLOAT, and records how many U are currently occupied. Occupancy is unremarkably flat across the estate, anywhere between 8 and 40 U with no preferred value, so treat it as uniform.

Devices mount into a rack at a start U position: servers, switches, PDUs, storage shelves. Each has an asset tag as varchar (a natural key, but we still carry a surrogate integer PK), a serial number, a model reference, a lifecycle status and a measured power draw in watts. Measured draw sits tightly around nameplate -- normal, mean 340 W, sigma 95.

A model is a dimension row: model name, form-factor height in U, nameplate power in watts, and a foreign key to a manufacturer, of which we hold the name and the support portal URL.

Devices are procured, and finance wants the trail. A purchase order has an order date, a supplier and a total value as DECIMAL; each PO has lines, and a line names the model, the quantity and the unit price. Every device points back at the line it arrived on. Warranty is per device -- start date, end date, support tier code.

Cabling: a device exposes ports, each with a port name, a speed in Gbps and a media type. Speeds are only ever 1, 10, 25, 40 or 100 Gbps and the estate is about 55 per cent 10G, 30 per cent 25G, 10 per cent 1G, 4 per cent 40G and 1 per cent 100G. A patch is a connection row with an A-end port, a B-end port and a cable label, both ends resolving to ports.

Positional integrity, since audit keeps failing on it. For an active device the start U is between 1 and 45; in a 42U rack the start U cannot exceed 42. A device whose lifecycle status is DECOMMISSIONED has no meaningful position, and we encode that as start_u = 0 rather than a null.

We're replacing a Jira-plus-Slack mess with something purpose-built for incident response, and I'd rather get the data model right before anyone writes screens. Scale: about 4,000 incidents a year, and something near 900,000 alert events feeding into them, so the alert side is where all the rows are.

Services own things. A service has a name, a tier -- we say tier 1 through tier 4, tier 1 being the customer-facing money paths -- and an owning team. Teams have a name and a Slack channel, and engineers belong to a team and have a phone number we page.

Alerts fire against a service. An alert carries a fired-at time, the rule name that produced it, a severity, and a flag for whether it auto-resolved; if it got promoted, it points at the incident it fed. Most never become incidents. Across everything we see, roughly 5 per cent come in at SEV1, 12 per cent SEV2, 38 per cent SEV3 and the remainder SEV4.

An incident has a title, a declared-at time, a resolved-at time, its own severity, the service it started on, and a flag for whether it was escalated. Several engineers get pulled into one incident and any engineer works plenty of incidents, so I need that pairing stored properly, with the role the person played on it -- incident commander, comms lead, subject matter expert. One row per person per incident, no duplicates.

On-call: each team runs a rotation of shifts, and a shift is a start and end timestamp plus the engineer holding the pager. Pages go out against a shift and reference the incident, with the time it was sent and how many seconds it took to be acknowledged. Acknowledgement time is a waiting time in the purest sense -- somebody is either at their laptop or they are asleep, most acks land in well under a minute and the tail is long. Mean is about 95 seconds. Nothing is allowed to sit unacknowledged past 900 seconds; the system re-pages at that point, so 900 is a hard ceiling on the field.

One escalation rule is non-negotiable: a SEV1 declared against a tier 1 service is always escalated, no judgement call. And the tier value itself is 1 to 4, nothing else.

Metering and rating store for a mid-size IaaS provider. The write path is the constraint: about 2.5 billion raw usage samples a month, pre-aggregated hourly before anything touches the billing tables, so plan on one wide fact table and narrow dimensions around it.

Accounts sit at the top -- company name, billing currency, signup date, payment status, plus a denormalised resource_count we read for quota checks. That count is savagely top-heavy across the customer base, a Zipf law with exponent 1.25 is what our capacity model uses. Under an account there are projects (name, region, soft-delete flag) and IAM users identified by email. A user can be granted access to several projects and a project has many users, with the role and the granted-on date recorded on the grant; exactly one grant row per user per project.

Resources are what get metered -- an instance, a bucket, a managed database. A resource belongs to a project, has a resource type, a creation timestamp, a termination timestamp once it is gone, and a SKU. SKUs carry a code, a unit (vcpu-hour, GiB-month, request), a unit price as DECIMAL and a service family. Tagging is free-form: tags are key/value, a resource carries many of them and the same key shows up across many resources, one row per resource per key.

The hourly rollup references the resource and the SKU and holds the hour bucket as a timestamp and a quantity as FLOAT. Quantity is never negative, ever. For a running instance the hourly vCPU quantity is close to normal, 0.72 with sigma 0.21, once idle hours are excluded. Rated line items reference a rollup and an invoice and carry the computed amount.

Invoices belong to an account and cover a monthly period with a start and end date, a subtotal, a tax amount and a total as DECIMAL, plus a status. Monthly invoice totals are heavily right-skewed -- a handful of whales and a very long left mass -- and a lognormal with log-mean 7.4 and log-variance 1.9 fits it well. Credits and adjustments are separate rows against an invoice with a reason code and a signed amount.

Two rating rules. An account whose payment status is DELINQUENT cannot have invoices go out, so invoice status is forced to HELD for those accounts. Tax is never negative, and for accounts billed in USD we do not levy it at all, so the tax amount there is exactly zero. Also, anything in the COMPUTE_RESERVED service family is a reserved-instance SKU and priced under 0.05 per unit by definition.

Analytics store for our edge request logs. It is three things, honestly, and one of them is enormous: at peak we ingest around 60 million requests an hour, call it 30 billion rows a month before any rollup, and the other two are lookups hanging off it.

A zone is the customer-facing unit -- a hostname somebody has onboarded. Against it we keep the account reference on our side, the hostname itself, the date it was onboarded, and whether caching is switched on. Traffic across zones is absurdly unequal: the single busiest zone is something like 8 per cent of everything, the second is roughly half of that, and it keeps decaying in a textbook power law rather than tapering off. When we model zone rank we use a Zipf exponent of 1.15.

The POPs are the other lookup: a three-letter airport-style code, a city, a country, and how many servers we have in it.

Every request row points at the zone it was for and the POP that served it, and records the timestamp down to the millisecond, the HTTP method, the URI path (which can be long), the response status, the bytes we sent, the cache result, and how many milliseconds the origin took on the occasions we had to go back to it. Cache result is one of HIT, MISS, EXPIRED or BYPASS, and the split is about 82 per cent hits, 11 per cent misses, 4 per cent expired and 3 per cent bypassed.

Origin fetch latency behaves like any queueing wait -- no typical value, a flat hazard, mean about 180 ms. Bytes sent is wildly skewed the other way: mostly small JSON and HTML, with a fat tail of video segments, and a lognormal with log-mean 9.1 and log-variance 2.4 matches what we measure.

Two rules came out of schema review. Response status is only ever between 100 and 599. And when the cache result is a HIT the origin latency is zero, because we never left the POP.

I'm trying to get a proper database behind our hosted phone product before we onboard any more resellers, because right now half of it lives in the billing system and half in the switch config and the two disagree.

The moving parts, roughly. A business customer -- we say tenant internally, sales insists on calling them accounts, it's the same thing -- has a company name, a billing contact and a status. Under a tenant you get extensions. An extension is somebody's desk line: an extension number, a display name, a voicemail PIN, and the device it's registered to. Devices are the desk phones and softphones, so a MAC address, a model and a firmware version. Plenty of extensions have no device yet, which the current setup can't even represent.

Numbers are separate from extensions and this is where everyone gets confused. We buy DIDs in blocks from carriers and point them at extensions. A DID has the E.164 number, the carrier we got it from, a monthly cost, and which extension it currently routes to. Carriers we barely track -- a name and our account number with them, that's the lot.

Then the calls. Every leg gets logged: the tenant, the from and to numbers, when it started, how long it rang before anyone picked up, the talk time, and how it ended -- answered, busy, no answer, failed. We're doing something like a million and a half legs a month across all tenants now. Talk time is the classic shape where most calls are short, there's no typical length, and a few go on forever; the average sits around three and a half minutes. Ring time before answer behaves the same way, averaging about nine seconds. There's a MOS score too, which the vendor hands us on a 1 to 5 scale, and in practice we sit just above 4 with not much spread either side.

Concurrency is capped per tenant and it comes off the package they're on. Starter gets 10 simultaneous calls, Business gets 50, Enterprise is unmetered which we store as 999. And a leg that wasn't answered has zero talk time, obviously -- that one keeps getting violated by the switch and it drives our reporting mad.

There's an IVR thing as well that a few of the bigger tenants use, menus and options and so on, but nobody has agreed what we're storing for it so leave it out for now.

We're a small outfit -- fourteen shops around the region, we sell airtime and handsets for two of the big networks. My son set us up a spreadsheet years back and it has become a disaster, so we'd like something proper built.

What we genuinely need to know is what stock is where. A handset is a physical thing with that long IMEI number printed on the box, a make, a model, what we paid for it and what we're asking for it, and it sits in one particular shop. There'll be three or four hundred handsets across the shops at any one time. There are SIM cards too, thousands of them, but we buy those in bags of fifty and frankly we just count them -- the accountant only wants the long ICCID number written on the docket when one actually goes out with a customer, so that's the one place it needs to live.

Every shop has a name, the high street it's on, and a manager. What I'd love is to glance at a shop and see what it's holding and what it shifted last week.

Selling works like this. Somebody comes in, buys a handset, maybe a SIM with it, maybe just a SIM. We take their name and their mobile number, and we note who served them. The sale itself has the date, what they actually paid, and whether it was cash or card -- it's about sixty forty card to cash these days, a bit more card if anything. Handsets go out at a markup and it's the cheap Androids that move; average selling price is somewhere around 210 pounds, though we've had the odd thousand-pound flagship go out the door, and those few big ones pull the average up above what a typical sale looks like.

The refurbished ones are a headache. They come back to us, we test them, some go out again cheaper. So a handset needs to say whether it's new or refurbished. Nothing at all leaves below 40 pounds, that's the floor we agreed, and a refurbished one we never ask more than 400 for however nice it is.

Staff, last thing -- about thirty of us including the part-timers. I don't think we need much beyond a name, which shop they're at, and whether they're part-time, because the rota is somebody else's problem.

This is for the fault side of a regional transmission network -- microwave links, fibre spans, and the power and environmental kit at each site. About 1,800 sites, and we take in something like two hundred thousand alarms a month, so it isn't big data, it's messy data.

Sites are the anchor. Each has a site code, a name, a grid reference, and a criticality band from 1 to 5 where 1 is the worst thing to lose; most sites end up band 3 or 4, only a few are band 1 or 2, and a similar few are band 5. Sites sit in regions and a region has an area manager. Equipment is installed at a site, each piece with a serial, a type, a vendor, a commissioning date and a software version. Links join two sites, an A-end and a B-end, and carry a capacity in Mbps and a media type, microwave or fibre.

Alarms come off equipment, and because the correlation engine needs it fast, each alarm is also stamped with its site directly rather than being resolved through the equipment every time. An alarm has a raise time, a clear time once it clears, the minutes it took to clear, a probable cause code, a severity from the vendor MIB, flags for flapping, for suppressed and for whether we ticketed it. Behind the codes there are alarm definitions -- the code itself, a human-readable description, a default severity, and whether the alarm is suppressible at all. On a normal month about 60 per cent of what arrives is warnings, 25 per cent minor, 11 per cent major and 4 per cent critical. The site record also carries a daily alarm count that the trending dashboard reads; it sits around 3.7 and behaves like a count of independent events in a fixed window.

Self-clearing alarms clear on their own schedule with no characteristic duration -- the ones still up after an hour are no more likely to clear in the next minute than the fresh ones -- and the mean time from raise to clear is 22 minutes.

When something is real we open a fault ticket: an opened time, a closed time, a fault class, the field team it went to, a resolution note, and the hours it took to restore. Several alarms usually roll onto one ticket. Field teams have a name, a base depot and a headcount. Time to restore averages 4.5 hours with a standard deviation of about 2.1 and is roughly symmetric around that. Nothing is allowed to sit open beyond 30 days -- 720 hours -- because the KPI system force-closes it.

If a truck rolls we log a site visit against the ticket: which team went, when they arrived, when they left, and which parts they consumed and how many of each. Parts come from a stores catalogue keyed on the part number, with a description and a unit cost; a visit can burn several part numbers and a part number turns up on many visits, but only one line per part number per visit.

Planned work is tracked apart from all this: maintenance windows have a start and end, the site, an owner and an approval state, and alarms raised inside a window are meant to be suppressed. Which leads to the one rule I keep having to explain: if the alarm's definition says it isn't suppressible, then it cannot come back marked suppressed, window or no window. The other one is escalation -- a critical alarm at a band 1 site is always ticketed.

I have ended up running IT support here almost by accident. We're a 320-person architecture practice and there is no IT department beyond me and two contractors who come in on Tuesdays. At the moment, when somebody's laptop dies they walk over and tell me and I write it on a pad. That is the entire system.

What I want is somewhere to log the thing that came in. Who reported it, when, what it's about -- printers, the network, the CAD licences, email, hardware, and "other", which is most of it if I'm honest -- and how urgent it is. We get somewhere between forty and sixty of these a week, so a few thousand a year, we are not talking about a mountain of records.

For each one I need to know who is dealing with it and whether it's still open. Things get handed between the three of us fairly often and I'd like that history rather than just the current name, because at the moment nobody can tell me who had it last Thursday. And I want to be able to answer how long things took, because the partners ask and I never have a number. My gut says most get sorted the same day but a handful drag on for weeks -- the licence renewals especially, those are hostage to the vendor. If I had to put an average on it I'd say around eleven hours of elapsed time, which sounds far too high until you remember it's the licence ones pulling it up; the typical one is much quicker than that.

People: everyone is already in the staff list for payroll, so I only need their name, which studio they sit in, and whether they're a partner. That last one matters, because anything a partner raises gets treated as high priority and there's no arguing about it.

On urgency: roughly one in twenty is what I'd call an emergency, about a quarter are high, and the rest splits fairly evenly between normal and low.

Equipment is the other half of the story. Maybe half these tickets are about one specific machine and I would love to link them up, but the asset list lives in a different spreadsheet that facilities own and I am not taking that on as well -- so at most I want the asset tag written down against the ticket and they can keep the rest.

One thing I want the system to shout about: nothing should be sitting open past a fortnight. Call it 336 hours.

Right, so I look after the collection side of things for the borough -- bins, basically. There's about ninety-two thousand properties on our patch and every one of them sits on a round, which is what we call the route a lorry does on a given day of the week. Some of the lads say runs instead of rounds, same thing. We hold the address and the postcode for each property and which round it's on, and a note of what sort of property it is, because the mix is mostly houses but there's a good chunk of flats and they behave completely differently. The rounds are split across two depots, Kingsmead and the little one out at Fenn Lane, and each round has a name that nobody outside the depot understands, things like NE3 Tuesday. A crew is assigned to a round -- that's a driver and either one or two loaders, so two or three bodies, never more than that because there isn't room in the cab -- and each crew has a name on the rota, usually the driver's.

Every property has its bins, and this is where it gets fiddly, because a house might have four of them. The black one is general waste, the blue is your dry recycling, then there's the green garden waste bin which people pay a subscription for, and food caddies. If I look at every bin we've got out there, roughly four in ten are black, another four in ten blue, about one in seven is a green garden one and the little bit that's left is caddies. They come in different sizes too -- the caddies are only twenty-three litres and at the other end we've got the big communal bins on the flats which are eleven hundred. We record when each bin was delivered to the property, because people do ring up asking.

The lorries weigh each lift now, which is new and honestly a bit of a headache. An average bin comes in around eleven and a half kilos, give or take four either way. There's a hard limit -- the lifting gear won't take anything past ninety kilos, full stop -- and with the food caddies in particular, if one comes in over about twelve kilos then somebody's put the wrong thing in it and the crew are told to leave it and tag it. Every lift gets logged against the bin and against the round, with the time it happened, and there's a yes-or-no on whether it actually got emptied, because sometimes the bin's blocked in or contaminated and we go away again.

Then there's the missed bin reports. Residents ring up or use the form on the website, and we log it against the property with the time it came in and a reason -- blocked access, crew error, resident put it out late, that sort of thing -- and the time we closed it off. It's steady, that: any given round will pick up about six of these in a week, week in week out. Now the important bit is assisted collections. If somebody's registered as assisted -- elderly, disabled, whatever the reason -- the crew have to go into the garden, fetch the bin and put it back where they found it. And if we miss one of those we're supposed to be back within twenty-four hours. Everybody else it's three working days, and between you and me we don't always hit that either.

All in we do something like nine million lifts a year, which is a lot of rows to keep.

This is the library management system for a county service -- twelve branches plus a mobile, and the mobile behaves like a branch as far as the data goes, so it gets a flag rather than a table of its own. Members are attached to a home branch and to a membership category, and the category is what drives the rules: how many items you can have out, and for how long. Allowances run from six items on a junior card up to thirty for a school or institutional borrower. Roughly speaking our membership is 62% adult, 22% junior, 13% concession and 3% institutional. On the member themselves we hold the usual -- name, date of birth, email, and the date they joined.

We distinguish the title from the physical copy, and that matters, because a popular title might have forty copies spread across branches, each with its own barcode, the date we bought it and a condition grade. A title has its text, an ISBN and a year of publication. Titles have authors, and a fair number have several -- editors, translators, illustrators -- so that is a proper many-to-many, with the contribution role recorded on the link itself.

Loans hang off a copy and a member: when it went out, when it is due, when it came back, and how many times it has been renewed. Renewals average a bit under one per loan. Juniors are capped at two renewals; adults get up to five. Reservations are placed against the title rather than a specific copy, with a pickup branch and a status, and there is a 75p charge to reserve which is waived for junior cards -- those come through at zero. Overdues raise a fine against the loan, with the date it was raised and the date it was paid if it has been: median is about three pounds with a long right tail up to the twenty-pound replacement charge, and nothing above that.

One thing worth flagging for sizing. Borrowing is wildly top-heavy. If you rank titles by lifetime loans it is a clean power law with an exponent somewhere around 1.6 -- a few hundred titles carry an enormous share of circulation and the tail barely moves. We are at about 310,000 members and 4.2 million loan records going back to 2009.

Case management for a national courts service. I am scoping the reporting replica, so I care about shape and cardinality rather than UI.

The root entity is the case file: court, case reference, case type, procedural track, filed date, disposal date and a derived duration in days. A court has a name and a tier, and holds courtrooms with a seating capacity -- six in a district judge's room up to about 120 in the big crown courtrooms. Judicial officers are a separate entity with a name, an office title and an appointment date, and they are listed onto hearings, not onto cases.

Parties are their own entity, with a name and a kind flag for person versus organisation, because the same party recurs across cases. So case-to-party is many-to-many with the role -- claimant, defendant, appellant, intervener -- carried on the association and a composite key on case and party. Legal representation sits on top of that: a firm, identified by name and SRA number, represents a given party in a given case, so that association keys on case, party and representative, with the retainer date as payload.

Hearings: case, courtroom, officer, hearing type, listed timestamp, scheduled minutes, actual minutes, outcome code. Listing slots run from a fifteen-minute directions appointment to a full 480-minute day, and small-claims-track hearings are never listed longer than an hour. Actual duration is roughly normal, mean 62 minutes, sd 25. Hearings per case is Poisson with lambda about 2.4. Disposal time is lognormal on log-days with mu 5.2 and sigma-squared 0.9. Case type splits 46% civil, 24% family, 22% criminal, 8% tribunal.

Also on the file: documents, with a type, a filed timestamp and a page count that is at least one; orders made by a named officer, with an order type, a date made and a sealed flag; and fee payments carrying a fee code, an amount, a paid timestamp and a remission flag. There is no issue fee in the criminal jurisdiction, so criminal fee rows come through at zero.

Volume: 2.1 million case files live plus archive, roughly 14 million hearing rows, and documents are the big table at north of 60 million.

Driver licensing registry -- a rebuild of the core record. I will be honest up front that the medical side is where the requirements are still soft, so treat that part as indicative.

A driver record keys on the driver number and carries surname, forenames, date of birth, sex and current postcode. A driver may hold more than one licence record over time -- provisional, full, exchanged foreign -- each with an issue date, an expiry date and a status code. Entitlement categories are reference data: code, description, minimum age. A licence carries a set of those categories with valid-from, valid-to and an optional restriction code, and that is a composite key on licence and category rather than a repeating group on the licence. Minimum ages across the reference table run from 16 to 24.

Applications are the transactional side: driver, application type, received and decided timestamps, decision code, the applicant's age at the point of application, and a fee. Fees are effectively three-valued -- 34, 43 and 62 pounds -- splitting about 55 / 31 / 14. A first provisional car application cannot be taken from anyone under seventeen. Every application from someone seventy or over has to be referred for medical review; medical declarations hang off the application with a condition code, a declaration date and that referral flag.

Theory tests attach to an application: test centre, timestamp, score out of fifty, pass flag. Scores are near-normal, mean 41.3, sd 7.8.

Endorsements attach to a licence -- offence code, offence date, points, expiry date. Points come out 3 in about 72% of cases, 6 in 19%, 9 in 5% and 11 in the remainder, and the statutory range is 3 to 11. Disqualifications sit on the driver rather than on the licence, because a ban survives the licence being surrendered: start date, length in months (Poisson-ish, mean about 8.5) and a reason code.

Motorist volumes: 52 million driver records, 9 million applications a year, endorsements north of 30 million. We also hold tachograph card data but that is out of scope for this piece.

Planning. OK so the thing we are trying to get off a spreadsheet is the development management caseload -- applications, or submissions, or cases. People here call them all three and mean the same thing.

Somebody applies, usually through an agent rather than in person, and honestly the agent is the one we end up emailing, so we want their name on the applicant record along with whether they are acting. The application lands against a site, and the site is a physical thing with an address, a ward and an area. Most of them are tiny -- a back garden, a shopfront -- but every so often there is a fifteen-hectare allocation, so the size distribution is horribly skewed, tiny median and a very long tail. On the application itself there is a reference code, a type (householder, minor, major, listed building consent, that sort of list), the date it came in, the target date, and eventually a decision and a decision date. Most things get granted -- call it four in five -- around one in eight refused and the rest withdrawn before we get to them.

Each one has a case officer. They sit in teams and they each carry a caseload in the mid-thirties, plus or minus about nine, and obviously that cannot go negative.

Consultation is the bit that generates the volume. Neighbours, the parish, statutory consultees like the Environment Agency -- each response has a type of respondent, whether they object or support or are neutral, and a date. A typical application picks up three or four responses, though a controversial one picks up hundreds.

Determination clock: eight weeks for the ordinary stuff, thirteen for a major. So a major is allowed ninety-one days and everything else fifty-six, and that is what we get measured on, so we hold the days it actually took.

Conditions get attached when we grant -- there is the text of the condition and a type. And appeals, if the applicant does not like the answer: date lodged, appeal type, outcome, date decided.

Oh, and the conservation area thing. If a site is in one then it cannot be signed off by an officer, it has to go to committee, so we record who it was decided by. That is a flag on the site rather than on the application.

We are looking at something like 4,000 applications a year and about fifteen years of history to migrate, so a few hundred thousand rows once you count consultation responses.

Food safety team, district council. We keep a register of every food business in the district -- about 2,700 of them -- and we are the ones who publish the hygiene ratings, so the data ends up public and it needs to be right.

A premises has a trading name and an address, a business type, and a risk category we assign, A through E. The types come out roughly a third restaurants and cafes, a quarter retailers, getting on for a fifth takeaways, an eighth pubs, and then small numbers of schools and care settings and a handful of manufacturers. The operator is held separately from the premises, partly because one company can run six chip shops and partly because operators change while the premises stays put -- we hold the operator name, whether it is a company or a sole trader, and the company number where there is one. We also keep the date the premises registered with us.

Inspections: which premises, which officer, the date of the visit, and then the three scores that make up the rating -- hygiene, which is out of 25, structure, and confidence in management, which runs 0 to 30 and is honestly all over the place, more or less flat across the whole range. Those three combine into the 0 to 5 rating that goes on the sticker in the window. Our distribution is about 62% fives, 19% fours, 11% threes, 5% twos, 2% ones and the odd zero.

Each inspection also sets the interval until the next one, in months. Category A premises get revisited at six months or less. And anything that comes out with a one or a zero, we are back inside three months whatever the category says.

Where things are bad enough we take enforcement action off the back of the inspection -- the type of action, the date it was issued and the date they complied. We manage maybe 1,600 visits a year and enforcement is a couple of hundred of those.

Officers carry a qualification code, which matters because only some of them can sign off a prohibition.

Register of electors, national scale. Four entities in the core and I want them right, because everything downstream joins through them.

Polling district is the geographic spine: district code, ward, parliamentary constituency, and the polling station it maps to. Households sit in a district and key on UPRN -- address line, postcode, the number of registered electors at the property, and the date the canvass form came back. Occupancy is Poisson-ish with lambda 1.9, legitimately zero for voids, and I would cap it at 30 for the HMOs. The lag in days between the canvass form going out and a response arriving is close to exponential with a rate of about 0.07 per day, so a fortnight on average.

Electors hang off the household: elector number, surname, forenames, date of birth, age in years, nationality code, franchise code, registration date, absent vote type and the open-register opt-out flag. Franchise splits roughly 93% G, 3% E, 2% K and 2% L. Absent voting is 79% none, 19% postal, 2% proxy. There is also a status on the elector, full or attainer. Minimum registration age is 16 and I would bound the top at 115; attainers are exactly 16 or 17 by definition, so that is a conditional bound rather than a global one.

Canvass contacts are the audit trail -- household, channel, timestamp, responded flag. Where a property comes back with zero occupants we stop posting to it and send a personal visit instead.

Sizing: 46 million elector rows, 25 million households recanvassed annually, and contacts run three to four times that.

I have been doing housing options here for nine years, so I will just tell you how it actually works rather than what the policy says, and you can make of it what you like.

Someone comes in, or more often rings, and we take their details. Might be a single lad sofa-surfing at his mate's, might be a family of six in a two-bed. Whatever the situation, we treat it as one household with one lead person -- that is whose name and phone number goes on it -- and we note how they are housed at the moment, whether that is private rented, staying with family, temporary accommodation, or we have accepted them as homeless. And the size of the household, and how many bedrooms we reckon they need. The average family on our list is a bit over two people. Bedroom need, if you look across the whole list, is nearly half of them needing a one-bed, around a third on two, one in six on three, and a handful needing four. We do not advertise anything bigger than a four-bed, so four is the ceiling both on what they can ask for and on what we can offer.

Then they go on the list. They get a band -- that is the priority thing, A down to D -- and the date they registered, and a points total, and a flag for whether they are still active, because people find something themselves and do not think to tell us. The points are the bit nobody understands, including me some days. Most people are sitting somewhere around the two hundred mark, but there are people up in the thousands because of medical awards and time spent waiting, and it cannot go below zero, obviously. And the one hard rule I can give you for certain: if we have accepted a household as homeless, they go into band A. That is statutory, there is no discretion in it.

When something comes up we make an offer. That sits against their entry on the list -- the address of the place, how many bedrooms it has, the date we offered it, and then the outcome. Roughly six in ten accept, coming on for three in ten turn it down, and the rest just never get back to us at all, which is its own kind of answer. If they refuse, we are supposed to record why, though whether that always happens is another matter.

We have got about nineteen hundred households on the list at any one time and we only let around two hundred and forty places a year, which is the whole tragedy of the thing in one sentence. There is usually a support worker involved on the more complicated cases but that is all in a different system that I do not touch.

I am a trustee and I also end up running the fundraising database because nobody else will, so bear with me, this may wander.

There are two halves to what we do. Money comes in from the public, and money goes out again as grants to small community groups. They are quite different animals and the system we have smushes them together very badly at the moment.

The giving side first. We have got somewhere north of four hundred thousand people on the supporter file -- donors, givers, supporters, I use all three words and they are all the same people. For each one we hold the name, the address and postcode, an email where we have got one, the date of their first gift, whether they have signed a Gift Aid declaration, and how they have asked to be contacted, which we have to respect now. Then every gift is a row of its own: who gave it, which appeal it came in on, how much, when, how they paid, whether it is a standing order or a one-off, and the Gift Aid we can claim on it. If somebody has signed a declaration then there is Gift Aid on the gift, always -- it is twenty-five pence in the pound and it is a quarter of our income, so if that figure is sitting empty on a declared donor then something has gone wrong.

Gift sizes. The typical one is about eighteen pounds, but the shape of it is that long-tailed thing where the average is much higher than the middle because of a handful of enormous ones. The biggest single gift we ever had was two hundred and fifty thousand, from an estate, and the website will not take anything under a pound. Payment mix is about four in ten by direct debit, a third on cards, one in nine cash -- that is the collection tins -- a small amount still by cheque, bless them, and the rest through payroll giving. Our regulars give roughly every three months, but that average hides an awful lot of variation: loads of very short gaps and then a long straggly tail of people who give once a year at Christmas and that is that.

Appeals -- campaigns, whichever word you prefer -- have a name, a channel, a start and end date, and a target.

Now the grants side. We run three programmes, each with an annual budget and a maximum award. Groups apply to a programme: how much they are asking for, when they applied, then a panel score out of a hundred which averages out in the low sixties, and a decision, and what they actually got in the end. No single grant goes above fifteen thousand. We hold the group itself separately because they come back to us year after year -- name, charity number, region, and their annual income. That last one matters, because we only fund small organisations: anything turning over more than a quarter of a million we turn down and point elsewhere.

There are volunteers as well but they are on a spreadsheet in the office and I would leave them out of this for now.

Small rescue centre, two of us on the admin side. I have built bits of this in Access before so I roughly know what I want, I am just not sure where some of it ought to live.

An animal comes in -- intake, admission, whatever you want to call it -- and we record the name we give it, what it is, breed if we can tell, sex, a rough age because a lot of them are strays and nobody knows, weight, the date it came in and the reason. Species mix over a year is a bit over half cats, a third dogs, a small number of rabbits, and then the odd guinea pig or bird which I would just lump in together. Weight is the awkward one: the typical animal through the door is six or seven kilos, but you have got a two-kilo kitten and a forty-kilo lurcher in the same column, so it is very skewed. Ages we cap at twenty-two, which was a cat, and nothing sensible goes below zero.

Length of stay -- we hold it as a number of days in care -- is the thing the trustees always ask about. Half of them are gone inside a month, but a handful of the older dogs are with us the best part of a year, so it is that decay shape, mean somewhere around thirty days. There is also an outcome on the animal: adopted, returned to owner, transferred on, died.

Adopters we hold separately -- name, postcode, phone, whether the home check passed, and whether there are children in the house. That last one is there for a reason. Some animals are flagged as not suitable for a home with children, and if an animal carries that flag we will not place it with an adopter who has kids. Full stop, no exceptions, and I would like that enforced rather than left to whoever is on the desk.

The adoption itself links the animal and the adopter with a date, the donation they paid, and a flag for if the animal came back to us. The donation is forty-five pounds for a cat, and between a hundred and twenty and a hundred and eighty for a dog depending on age, and occasionally nothing at all when it is an old animal going to a long-standing supporter, so zero up to a hundred and eighty overall.

We take in maybe eight hundred animals a year and we have got about six years of records, so this is not a big database, it just needs to be a correct one. We use foster carers for the under-eights too but they are a different conversation.

Design note for the settlement store we are replacing. The unit of account is the supply point, keyed on its MPAN, and each one carries an address with postcode, a profile class and a GSP group because settlement needs both, plus the date it was energised. A supply point normally has exactly one meter fitted at a time, identified by serial number, with an install date and a firmware version, and we care which of three generations it is -- SMETS2 covers about 72 per cent of the estate, SMETS1 another 21, and the residual 7 per cent are still legacy mechanical units. Legacy mechanical meters cannot report at interval level, so any half-hourly row we hold against one is flagged ESTIMATED rather than actual.

Interval data is the volume driver: per meter, per half hour, the import kWh, an export figure for the sites with PV, and a quality flag. At 2.1 million metered supply points that is a bit over 100 million rows a day. Consumption per interval is log-normal with log-mean -1.0 and log-variance 0.8, and is never negative. We also sample supply voltage off the smart meters -- a timestamp and a volts reading -- which sits normally around 239.5 V with a standard deviation of 4.1; anything outside the statutory 216.2 to 253.0 V envelope is a compliance event.

Contracts bind a supply point to a tariff for a date range and record the payment method. A tariff has a code, a type, a standing charge and day and night unit rates in pence, effective from a date; on the ECONOMY_7 type the night rate must land between 7.5 and 12.0p. Billing periods roll consumption up per contract with the period dates, the total kWh, the amount due and an estimated flag. Period totals average 705 kWh with a standard deviation near 240, and a period totalling more than 6,000 kWh must be settled on actual reads, never estimated.

Right, so what we're after is something to replace the spreadsheets the billing team have been nursing since forever.

Everything hangs off the account. An account has a reference we quote on letters, the account holder's name, wherever they want the post sent, when they came on to us, and how they pay -- direct debit, card, or the ones who still send cheques. Most people here say customer, some of the older staff say account holder, it's the same thing, don't build two of them.

Then there's the property itself, which is not the same as the account, because landlords hold accounts for places they don't live in. For each property we hold the address, what kind of place it is -- roughly a third are terraces, a bit over a quarter semis, about 22 per cent flats and the rest detached -- how many people live there, which averages out at about 2.4 and nobody has ever put down fewer than one or more than a dozen, and crucially whether it's on a meter or not. Metered ones have a meter fitted, and for that we want the serial, the date it went in and the size of the pipe in millimetres. I suppose in theory a big place could have two meters but I've honestly never seen it.

The readings themselves are nothing much: which meter, the date, the number off the dial, and where the reading came from -- our own reader, the customer phoning it in, or the estimating routine.

Bills are the thing people ring up about. A bill belongs to an account and to a property, covers a period with a start and an end and a number of days on it, states the volume used in cubic metres, what's owed, and whether it's open, paid or in dispute. Metered properties get a bill every quarter and there is never less than 84 days of usage on one and never more than 98. Unmetered properties are charged off the rateable value instead, so there is no volume figure on those bills at all -- it sits at zero. A typical quarter's usage on a metered place is about 27 cubic metres, give or take 11, and volumes are obviously never negative. Most bills come out around 130 pounds but the tail goes a long way up -- we have estates with swimming pools on them.

Payments come in against a bill with the date, the amount and how it arrived. Part payments are completely normal so one bill can have several against it.

Oh, and there's a hardship discount scheme -- I don't know the rules well enough to tell you how it works, someone in revenue would have to explain that bit.

Volume-wise we bill around 1.6 million properties, so it's several million bills a year and rather more payments than that.

Notes from the asset-data workshop -- what the new network model has to hold.

We're organised by district. A district has a name, a region code and a rough population served (that number only ever appears in board packs, so don't over-think it).

The physical asset is the main, which we track as segments. A segment sits in a district, is fed at one of the pressure tiers -- low, medium and intermediate, each with a name and a nominal pressure in bar -- and has a material, a diameter in millimetres, a length in metres, the year it was laid and a condition grade from 1 to 5. Grades run roughly 12 per cent at 1, 31 at 2, 34 at 3, 17 at 4 and 6 at 5. The replacement mains we lay are all PE, and those are always between 63 and 180 mm; the old cast iron and ductile stuff can be far wider. Segment lengths are log-normally spread, log-mean about 4.4 with log-variance 0.9. Nothing in the ground predates 1850 and obviously nothing is laid later than 2026.

Pressure is stepped down at the governor stations -- some of the field teams call them regulator stations, it's the same asset. Each belongs to a district and has a reference, an inlet pressure in bar, an outlet in millibar and a commissioning date. Outlet sits around 75 millibar with a standard deviation of about 8.

Service connections branch off a segment to a premises, with a premises reference, a connection type and a connection date. There are roughly 1.1 million of them on our patch.

Leak reports are the operational side: which segment, when it came in, how we heard about it, a severity and the gas-in-air percentage the operative measured. Around 400,000 a year. About six per cent are the immediate-risk A1 kind, another 19 per cent are A2 and all the rest are B. An A1 has to be attended within the hour -- that's regulated, not an internal target.

A repair job comes off a report and records which crew went, when it started and finished, the response time in minutes and what it cost. Response averages about 50 minutes with the usual long tail behind it.

Crews -- the older lads say gangs -- have a name, a depot and a headcount, and each crew holds a set of qualifications. A qualification has a code, a description and a renewal interval in months; no certificate we recognise runs longer than 60 months. We need the certified date and the expiry date against each crew-and-qualification pairing, because that pairing is exactly what the auditors ask to see.

I run the O and M side for a solar portfolio and honestly the reporting is held together with string, so bear with me.

We've got about 140 plants. People here use plant, site and farm interchangeably, don't read anything into which one you hear. For each one we want a name, roughly where it is, how big it is, when it switched on, and the reference of its grid connection. They run from about 5 megawatts up to 50 and they're spread pretty evenly across that range -- no clustering at either end, we've got as many little ones as big ones.

Inside a site the thing that matters is the inverters. Who made it, what it's rated at, when it went in, and whether it's behaving. Ratings go from a hundred kilowatts right up to four megawatts depending on the vintage. At any one time about 93 in a hundred are running normally, five in a hundred are running derated for one reason or another, and the odd couple per cent are properly offline.

Every inverter reports in every five minutes -- what it made, the light reading, and the panel temperature. That is the bulk of the data by a mile; across the portfolio it came to something like 60 million rows last month alone. The light readings are the ones the analysts argue about: on a good summer noon we're north of 900, and averaged over daylight it works out somewhere around 340 with a huge amount of scatter, easily 200 either side. Whatever else it is, it can't be negative and we have never recorded above 1200. Generation obviously can't go negative either. Panel temperatures have hit minus fifteen in a cold snap and gone over seventy in a heatwave -- call it minus twenty to eighty-five and you'll cover everything we've ever seen.

When something trips we raise a fault against the inverter: when it came in, the code, when it cleared, and how long the thing was out for. Most clear inside an hour or two, a few drag on for days, and the average works out around three and a half hours. Anything on an inverter rated over 2 megawatts we have committed contractually to have back inside 48 hours, no excuses.

The bigger jobs go out to the maintenance firm we're contracted to rather than our own techs. We just hold their name and a phone number, and we note against the fault which firm dealt with it.

Small internal schema for the wind fleet -- 82 turbines, around 2,000 work orders a year, maybe 300 component swaps, so nothing here needs partitioning or archival.

Turbines are the root asset: surrogate integer key plus the asset tag the techs actually quote, the model, hub height in metres (the fleet spans 60 to 120), rated output in kW and a commissioning date. Three models only -- 45 per cent are the 3600 kW machine, 40 per cent the 2300, and the remaining 15 per cent are the old 850 kW units.

Work orders hang off a turbine with open and close timestamps, a work type of SCHEDULED, CORRECTIVE or INSPECTION in roughly a 55/38/7 split, labour hours, parts cost and an integer priority from 1 to 4 weighted 8/22/45/25 with 1 the most urgent. Labour hours are log-normal, log-mean 1.6 and log-variance 0.7; anything below 0.25 or above 400 is a keying error and should fail the check constraint. Scheduled work never carries a priority better than 3, so on those rows priority is always 3 or 4.

Where a part is actually swapped out we record it against the work order -- the component name, its serial, the date, and the running hours the part had on it when it came out. Those hours cluster normally, mean about 41,000 with a standard deviation near 9,000.

Handing over the data model brief for the new CPO platform. I'm a product owner, not a DBA, so treat the shapes as intent rather than gospel.

We are one operator among several and we need the others in the model too, because of roaming: an operator has a name and a country code. Roaming works as a pairing -- for any home operator and host operator combination we hold the date it took effect and the commission the host takes, which is capped at 25 per cent and obviously can't be negative. A given pair appears exactly once.

Sites belong to an operator and carry a name, a latitude and longitude, a postcode, an opening date and a running count of sessions in the month. That count is wildly skewed -- a handful of sites do enormous volume and there is a very long tail of sites doing one or two a week. It's a proper power law with an exponent around 1.5.

Each site has charge points, which are the physical EVSEs: a reference, a maximum power anywhere from 3.7 kW up to 350, a connector type (CCS just over half, Type 2 about 36 per cent, CHAdeMO 9, Tesla the remainder), a commissioning date and a status.

On the customer side, drivers register with an email, a registration date and a home postcode. A driver can have several vehicles -- make, model, usable battery size and the maximum DC rate the car will accept -- and several RFID cards, each with a UID, an issue date and an active flag. Batteries average about 64 kWh with a standard deviation of 18.

Sessions are the fact table: which charge point, which card, which vehicle, which tariff plan, start and end, energy delivered, peak power, duration in minutes and what we billed. Tariff plans belong to an operator and carry a per-kWh price, a session fee and an idle fee per minute. Energy delivered is log-normal, log-mean 2.8 and log-variance 0.6, and durations are exponential with a mean near 45 minutes. On the rapid units -- 50 kW and above -- a session essentially always lands between 5 and 100 kWh. And we never draw more than the car will take: if the vehicle's DC limit is under 50 kW then peak power on that session stays at or below 50.

Faults are raised against a charge point with a category, a raise and a resolve time and the hours it was down. Drivers get a monthly invoice covering a period, with the total and the number of sessions on it -- and if they charged nothing that month they still get a zero invoice.

Scale: about 1.4 million sessions a month across roughly 38,000 connectors, and the session table is already past 40 million rows.

We're a small housing association and we've inherited a heat network that we don't really have any systems for.

There are four blocks on the scheme, just under 900 flats in total, all fed from the one energy centre behind the shops. That's a couple of gas boilers and a CHP engine, but for our purposes it's just a name and the year the thing was commissioned. The scheme has a name and it sits in one town. I gather other associations run several schemes each, so whatever you build shouldn't assume there is only ever the one.

For each flat we need to know which scheme it's on, its flat number, which block it's in, the floor area and the tenure. About 62 per cent are social rent, 29 per cent leasehold, and the rest are privately rented out by leaseholders who moved away. The flats average around 58 square metres and most are within fifteen either way -- the smallest is a 22 square metre studio and the biggest is a 140 metre maisonette.

In every flat there's a heat interface unit. The contractors call it a HIU, the residents call it the box in the cupboard, and the old paperwork calls it a substation, which confuses everybody. We need the model, when it was fitted and when it was last serviced. The metering firm reads them for us -- I don't think we need to hold anything about them, they just send us a file every month.

Charging is monthly and per flat: how much heat they used, the standing charge, the usage charge and the total. Usage can't be negative, and if it comes through as zero -- empty flats between lets, mostly -- then the usage charge has to be zero too, though the standing charge still applies. A typical month is somewhere near 270 units of heat but the winter ones are far bigger than that, it's very skewed. And the council tenants' standing charge is capped by the management agreement: it cannot go above twelve pounds in a month, whatever we end up doing with the leaseholders.

domain: Wholesale Energy Trading and Grid Balancing
nl_description:
Schema for the balancing and wholesale book, replacing three Access databases and a great deal of Excel.

Markets are the outer dimension: a code, a name, the settlement granularity in minutes and a currency. Counterparties carry a legal name, an LEI, a credit limit and an onboarding date, and admission to a market is held per counterparty per market with the admission date and the collateral posted against it -- exactly one row per pairing, no duplicates.

Balancing units (BMUs, or just units in most of the desk's vocabulary) belong to a counterparty and have a reference, a fuel type, a maximum export in MW and a minimum stable level which is never negative. Fuel mix across the register is wind 31 per cent, CCGT 24, solar 15, battery 14, hydro and biomass 6 each, nuclear 4.

Settlement periods belong to a market, are numbered 1 to 48 within the day, and hold a start timestamp, the cash-out system price and the net imbalance volume. System price averages about 78 with a standard deviation near 41; net imbalance is centred on zero with a standard deviation around 240 MW. Note that people will say half-hour when they mean settlement period.

Bid-offers are submitted per unit per period with a direction, a volume in MWh, a price per MWh and a submission time. On the OFFER direction the price is allowed to run from minus 100 up to a cap of 4,000 per MWh; bids are not bounded that way. An acceptance references a bid-offer and records when it was accepted, the accepted volume and the resulting cashflow -- and since a bid is a request to turn down, the cashflow on an accepted BID is never positive to us.

Bilateral trades sit against a market and a counterparty with a trade timestamp, a delivery start, a volume, a price and a side. Trade volumes are log-normal, log-mean 3.0 and log-variance 1.1. Counterparties on a credit line below a million are hard-limited to 500 MWh per trade.

Demand forecasts are issued against a settlement period, several times over, with an issue timestamp, the forecast MW and whichever model version produced it. The versioning is currently a free-text mess and I would leave it that way for now.

Volumes: 17,520 periods a year, a few hundred thousand bid-offer rows a month, around 2 million acceptances on the book.

Scoping note for the outage reporting rebuild. Written by me, an analyst, so treat the modelling as indicative and shout if I've got a cardinality wrong.

The network side we only need shallowly. Substations get a name, an operating voltage, a count of how many feeders come off them, and a region; voltages on our patch run from 6.6 kV up to 132. Feeders -- half the control room says circuits, it's the same object -- belong to a substation and have a reference, a count of customers connected and a flag for whether they are overhead or underground. Customers per feeder averages about 420.

An outage is raised against a feeder: start, restoration time, a cause, whether it was planned, how many customers it hit and the duration in minutes. Causes break down roughly as weather 31 per cent, equipment failure 27, third-party damage 18, vegetation 12, animals 7 and unknown 5. Restoration averages around 80 minutes -- most are quick but there's a fat tail of multi-day ones after storms. We don't log anything shorter than three minutes, and the customers-affected count is never negative.

Calls come in against an outage: when it came, the number they rang from, the channel (phone is still 58 per cent, web 27, app 13 and the rest social) and the postcode they gave us. About 600,000 calls a year against roughly 190,000 outages.

Dispatches are per outage -- a crew reference, when they were sent, when they arrived and the travel time. Travel averages 34 minutes with a standard deviation of about 15. We don't hold a crew register in this system; the reference is just whatever resource management gave us.

Compensation is the bit the regulator cares about. A payment sits against an outage with the account reference, the amount, when it was paid and a reason code. Anything over twelve hours triggers at least 75 pounds a household under the guaranteed standards. Planned shutdowns we notify in advance and no compensation is due on those, so where a payment does get raised against a planned job the amount comes through as zero.

I run the retrofit scheme for the borough and at the moment it lives in two spreadsheets and my head, which is why I'm here.

The way it works is somebody gets referred to us -- usually by the advice centre, sometimes they just ring up. We take their name, the address and postcode, whether they own the place or rent it and off whom, what they earn in a year, and the EPC band off the register. Eligibility is income-based: we can only take referrals from households under 31 thousand a year, that's the funder's line not ours. Most of the people we see are somewhere around twenty-two thousand, with a tail running up towards the ceiling. We note the referral date too, because the funding is annual and we have to report against it.

Then we fit things. People here say measure, upgrade or just job depending who's talking -- it's all the same thing. Roughly a third of what we do is loft insulation, a quarter or so cavity wall, then heat pumps at about 17 per cent, solar panels 13, and the expensive external wall stuff makes up the rest. For each one we record what it was, when it went in, what it cost us, how much of that was grant, who fitted it, and the guarantee in years -- most come with one, usually twenty-five years on the insulation, but I wouldn't swear the field is always filled in. Costs are all over the place: the typical job is around three thousand but a heat pump with a new cylinder is ten times that. Heat pump grants top out at seven and a half thousand and can't be negative -- that's a hard funder rule. And the very worst homes, the band G ones, get a minimum of five thousand towards the work whatever we end up fitting.

We ring people six months afterwards. That gives us a date, a satisfaction score out of five, what they reckon they've saved as a percentage, and whatever else they said. Scores are good -- about 42 per cent give us a five, 36 a four, 14 a three, and only a handful come in at one or two. The saving figure is self-reported so it's anywhere between nothing and, well, it can't sensibly be more than a hundred per cent.

Numbers are small: about 380 homes in three years, so a few hundred measures and a similar number of follow-up calls. Nothing that needs a big machine.

We don't hold anything about the installers as such beyond the name -- they're all on the framework and procurement manages that list, not us.

Right, I'll try and explain it the way it works rather than the way you'd want it written down.

We're 360 hectares up on the wolds, sixty-two fields, and every field has a name because that's how everyone talks about them -- Long Meadow, Chapel Piece, Stone Close. Average field is a shade under six hectares, the smallest is barely one and the biggest is twenty-two. Soil matters more than anything else: about half of it is heavy clay and the rest is sand over chalk, and they behave like two different farms.

Each year a field gets one crop drilled into it, and I want the drilling date and the harvest date sat against that. Out of every ten fields in a year, five would be wheat, two oilseed rape, two barley and one beans, and now and again one sits fallow.
