Everything comes over the weighbridge so I know the tonnes off each field to a decimal place, and I work in tonnes a hectare when I'm comparing years -- wheat here averages about eight point six, we've had six in a bad year and just under eleven in a cracking one.

Then there's what we put on. Fertiliser, sprays, seed, all of it goes onto one field for that year's crop, on a date, at a rate per hectare, and it costs what it costs. I buy off two or three merchants and I want to see who sold me what and what I actually paid, because the invoice and the quote are never the same number.

Grain doesn't go straight off the farm. There are four sheds, each one holds so many tonnes, and I need to know what's sitting in which shed. Then it goes out on lorries -- twenty-nine tonne loads, near enough, three hundred loads a year -- and every load has a ticket with the moisture on it. The mill knocks money off over fifteen percent so nothing should be leaving here above that, and they pay us a bit extra when a wheat load comes in under fourteen, so those tickets want flagging as premium. It's not a big pile of data, a few thousand rows a year at the very most.

Last thing. The agronomist walks the fields every fortnight through the spring and writes half a page of notes each time, and those notes need to hang off the visit so I can find them again.

Spec for the herd system that replaces the Access database that finally gave up. 620-cow Holstein-Friesian block-calving unit.

The cow is the anchor entity: surrogate integer PK plus her official ear tag as a unique 14-character natural key, with breed, birth date and a herd status flag. Her dam is usually in the herd as well, so that is a nullable self-referencing FK. One cow has many lactations, and a lactation carries its sequence number, the calving date and the dry-off date. Services hang off the cow and point at a sire from the bought-in bull catalogue, which we hold with its predicted transmitting ability for milk. Service outcome is held, returned or aborted -- about 55 percent hold to first service, 35 percent return and the rest abort.

The volume driver is the parlour. Two rotaries, 60 and 50 stalls, three milkings a day, so roughly 680,000 cow-milking rows a year and we retain seven years. Each of those rows is a timestamped yield in litres plus the conductivity reading off the meter, with FKs to both the cow and the parlour. Per-cow daily yield averages 31.5 litres across the three milkings with a standard deviation near 7, which per session is a mean of 10.5 and an sd of 2.6. Anything the meter reports below zero or above 30 litres for one session is a sensor fault, so 0 to 30 is the hard domain on that column.

Tanker collections are a separate daily row: volume, butterfat, protein, bactoscan and the price per litre we were paid. Butterfat runs a 4.05 percent mean with sd 0.22. The contract floors milk price at 0.28 a litre and it has never been above 0.52.

Somatic cell counts come back monthly per cow in thousands per ml and are heavily right skewed -- lognormal, log-mean about 4.4, log-variance 0.55. Two rules to enforce. Any cow with an SCC reading over 400 has her mastitis follow-up flag set. And a health event can carry a milk withdrawal period in days, so while a cow has a withdrawal against her the milking rows are not saleable, which is a flag on the session row.

Feeding is five diets and a cow is on exactly one at a time, so a dated cow-to-ration assignment with start and end dates. The ration itself is dry matter kilos and a cost per head per day.

I do the reporting for a broiler business and I'm rebuilding the whole thing off spreadsheets, so bear with me on the details.

There are 14 grow-out farms with 96 houses between them. The farms belong to growers who are contracted to us -- some growers have more than one farm -- and we pay each grower a rate per bird per week they hold it. The rate is set per grower but it also depends on the house, because the newer tunnel-ventilated ones earn more than the old naturally-ventilated sheds, so I need the ventilation type on the house along with its number on the farm.

The thing everyone actually cares about is the batch. I call it a flock, the field guys call it a crop, the old reports say batch -- it is one and the same. A flock lives in one house, starts on a placement date with a head count of day-old chicks, and finishes when the last bird is caught. Typical placement is 28,000 birds, give or take a thousand. Chicks come from one of four hatcheries and we want to know which. Breed is nearly all Ross 308 with about a tenth Cobb.

Somebody walks each house every day and writes down the day number (day 1 through to about day 42), how many birds died that day, the average bird weight off the sample scales, the house temperature and how much water went through the meter. Daily mortality on a healthy flock is low, about 22 birds out of the 28,000, and since it is a straight count a Poisson at lambda 22 is what I have been using and it fits. Temperature is meant to sit between 30 and 34 in the first week and be down between 19 and 23 from day 35 onwards. That daily sheet is the big table -- 96 houses, 42 days, eight or nine crops a year, five years of history, so a couple of million rows.

Feed arrives by lorry into the bins outside the house. Each delivery is a tonnage of one feed type -- starter, grower or finisher -- at a price per tonne.

At the end the birds go to one of two processing plants and a kill sheet comes back: the date, how many birds were delivered, the total dead weight, how many were rejected and the reject percentage that gets worked out from it. Reject percentage is meant to stay under one percent. Average finished bird is 2.45 kilos live with a standard deviation of about 0.2.

Vet visits produce a medication record against the flock with the product and its withdrawal period. Any medicine with a withdrawal period of seven days or more means the kill sheet is held for review before we invoice.

Right, so. Eighteen hectares under vine on the south slope and a winery in the old barn, and the whole lot lives in my notebook plus a spreadsheet my daughter set up that nobody else understands.

The vineyard is in blocks. Parcels, plots, whatever you want to call them -- I say block, my father said parcel, it's the same thing. Each one is planted to a single variety on a single rootstock in a particular year, and I know its size, its row spacing and how many vines are in it. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are most of it, roughly a third each, then Bacchus about a fifth and a bit of Pinot Meunier we're still not sure about.

Picking runs over about three weeks in October. A picking is one block on one day: we weigh the bins as they come in so it's kilos, a bin holds about four hundred kilos and a picking is anywhere between five and thirty bins. Someone takes a sugar reading and the acid at the same time, and I write down whether the fruit looked clean or whether there was rot in it. Sugar comes in anywhere from fifteen to twenty-four brix, and anything over twenty is too ripe for the sparkling so I mark that fruit for still wine there and then. The pickers are a gang from an agency and I do need to know which of them worked which picking and for how many hours, because they're paid by the hour and there are always arguments about it.

Then the fruit goes into a tank or a barrel and becomes a lot. This is the bit that's hardest to explain. A lot might be one block's fruit, or it might be three or four pickings blended together, and one picking can end up split across two lots -- so it isn't one to one in either direction, and I write down what share of the blend each picking was. Every lot sits in a vessel and I know what each vessel is and what it holds, they run from a thousand litres up to eight thousand. Lots move about -- racked off, blended, bottled -- and I write the movements down with the volume each time. Each lot is red or white, which matters below.

Ferments get logged twice a day, temperature and density. They sit in the low twenties mostly, twenty-two ish, swinging a few degrees either side, and if a red goes over thirty I have to do something about it quickly. Sulphur additions get written down too with the milligrams a litre, because the legal ceiling on total sulphur is two hundred.

Bottling happens in runs. A run is one lot going into one product, the product being the label and the vintage -- the 2024 Classic Cuvee, that sort of thing -- and we get so many bottles out of it and a few get broken. Then it sells: which wine, how many bottles, what it came to. More than half the orders are people at the cellar door taking a case or two, restaurants are maybe a quarter and the rest is the two merchants. Most orders are tiny and a merchant order can be several hundred bottles, so the sizes are very lopsided. We're small -- forty thousand bottles a year, a few thousand orders -- so it isn't a big database, but the traceability has to be right, because if there's a problem I have to get from a bottle back to the block.

There's also a bloke who comes and takes samples off the lots for the lab over in Kent. I suppose his results have to sit somewhere but I don't know what we'd keep besides the date and the number.

Data platform for a 12-hectare glasshouse tomato nursery. Small schema, very large data, and the whole design question is the telemetry.

The site is divided into 48 compartments, each with its own floor area in square metres, a glass type (single, diffuse or hortiglass) and the identifier of the climate computer that controls it. Everything else keys off the compartment on a surrogate integer.

A compartment carries one crop at a time and we open a fresh cycle at each planting, holding the cultivar as a short code, the planting date, the date the crop is finally cleared, the plant density we went in at and the cumulative marketable yield when it comes out. Density is set anywhere between 2.4 and 3.1 plants per square metre and in practice it is spread flat across that band. A full eleven-month cycle lands around 68 kilos per square metre with a standard deviation of about 5.

Telemetry is the problem child. Nine sensors per compartment logging every minute is roughly 227 million rows a year and we hold three years, so it wants monthly partitioning on the timestamp. A row is the compartment, the timestamp, which sensor type produced it, the float value, and a daylight boolean the climate computer hands us for free. The mix is nowhere near even: air temperature is 30 percent of rows, relative humidity 22, CO2 18, PAR 12, slab moisture 10, and the remaining 8 percent is everything else. Because the value column is a bare float shared across sensor types, the valid band has to be enforced per type -- air temperature must sit between 18 and 26 degrees during daylight and between 16 and 19 at night, and a CO2 reading is only credible between 420 and 1100 ppm.

Picking is recorded against the crop cycle: the date, the graded class, the weight in kilos and a truss count. By weight it comes out around 62 percent class 1, 30 percent class 2 and 8 percent waste.

It's a trout farm, spring-fed. Twelve ponds and four raceways -- I call the whole lot ponds when I'm talking, but the raceways are concrete and the ponds are earth and that difference matters for the paperwork, so whatever you build wants to know which is which and what each one is called.

What I actually need is to stop losing track of the fish. Stock arrives as fry, mostly from the hatchery down the road but not always, goes into one pond as a batch with a count and a date, and comes out fifteen or sixteen months later at a pound and a half or so.

While they're in there, three things get written on the board by the pond and they may as well all go on the same daily line. First, what's died -- mostly it's a handful a day, it climbs when the water's warm and drops right off in winter, and if a heron finds us it's a bad week. Second, feed: I count in sacks, a sack is twenty-five kilos, and a big pond gets through a couple of sacks a day in summer and hardly anything in the cold, so anywhere between nothing and two. Third, the water -- temperature and oxygen, taken at the same time. The spring comes up around twelve and the top ponds can touch eighteen in a heatwave, and above eighteen they stop eating so I have to cut them right back to half a sack. Oxygen mustn't go below six or you're in real trouble.

Once a month I net out thirty fish off a pond, weigh them, put them back, and the average goes on that same day's line.

Sales are to two smokehouses and to people at the gate, and there's a chap who takes the small ones for restocking fishing lakes. It's not a lot -- maybe two hundred sales a year, and a few thousand records in the whole thing once you count the daily lines. I just want a list of what went out of which batch, how many kilos, who had it and what they paid.

The vet has been here once in eight years so I'm not fussed about that side of it.

Replacement traceability and performance store for a chilled ready-meals site. Three lines, about 1.1 million retail units a week, 340 live SKUs, and five years of retention.

Upstream first. Approved suppliers, each with an audit score out of 100 and an approval status. Ingredients, each with an allergen code, a unit of measure, a shelf life in days and a storage class -- ambient, chilled or frozen. Goods in writes one receipt per supplier per ingredient per delivery, carrying the supplier lot code, the quantity in kilos, the probe temperature on arrival and an accepted flag. Arrival temperature runs a 3.2 C mean with an sd of 1.1. Two hard rejection rules are enforced right there at goods in: a chilled ingredient probing above 5 C is rejected, and anything from a supplier whose audit score is under 70 is rejected regardless of temperature.

Product side: an SKU with its code, name, retail price and target pack weight. A product has versioned recipes, each effective from a date, and a recipe is a set of ingredients with a kilo quantity per batch. That association is the genuine many-to-many in the model, so it takes a composite key on recipe plus ingredient rather than a surrogate. We also hold weekly unit volume per SKU, and it is savagely skewed -- a Zipf with an exponent around 1.25 fits the rank curve better than anything else we have tried.

Production: a run is one recipe on one line over a shift window, with the units produced and the giveaway percentage. Traceability is the association between a run and the specific receipts consumed in it, with the kilos drawn from each, and that is the table a recall query walks. QC checks are per run, typed, each with a measured value and a pass flag; the chill-temperature check type is only valid between 0 and 5 C. About 40 percent of checks are metal detection, 25 percent chill temperature, 20 percent seal integrity and 15 percent organoleptic.

Checkweigher sampling is the row-count driver: one pack weight sample every 90 seconds per line, which is tens of millions of rows over the retention window. On a nominal 400 gram pack the samples come out at 402 grams mean with an sd of 6, and no individual pack may be under 385 grams.

Downstream: despatches against a run to a named customer with a case count and a timestamp, and customer complaints against a product with a category and the units affected. Complaint categories split roughly 45 percent foreign body, 30 percent quality, 15 percent packaging and 10 percent labelling.

We run four markets a week across the county. Tuesday in the market square, Thursday on the leisure centre car park, Saturday is the big one, and there's a Sunday one at the garden centre that's new and we'll see if it survives the winter. Each of those runs on its own day at its own venue, and every time one happens it's a separate market day with its own date, because that's what everything else hangs off.

The people who sell are members of the co-op. I call them stallholders, the committee minutes call them traders, the lottery grant paperwork insists on 'vendor' -- all the same people. About 140 on the books though only sixty-odd turn out in a given week. Each one pays an annual membership, and then a pitch fee on the day. Fees go by frontage: a three-metre pitch is eighteen pounds and a six-metre is thirty, and most take the three, maybe a third want the six. First two markets for a new trader are free, that's the taster deal, so the booking sheet carries a count of how many markets that trader has done and if it's one or two there's no fee.

Every market day I need who booked in, how much frontage they took, whether they wanted power for a hot food unit, whether they actually turned up, and what they took. The takings are voluntary but most of them tell us because it goes in the funding report, and it is wildly uneven. Your average grower does two or three hundred quid on a Saturday, the man with the paella pan can do two thousand on a good day, and there's a candle woman who barely clears forty. Two or three stalls account for most of the money on the site.

Some of them use our card readers under the till-share scheme, and every one of those transactions comes through to us with its amount and we pass the money on less our commission. That's what makes this bigger than you'd think -- with the years of individual card transactions we're at roughly half a million rows.

Produce type matters because of the funding: we have to report what proportion of stalls are growers and meat versus prepared food versus crafts. It's about half growers, a third prepared food, and the rest crafts and the occasional charity stall.

Two more things. If a trader no-shows twice in a season they lose their booking priority, so we keep a running count of no-shows against them and a flag for whether they've still got priority. And there are volunteers who put the barriers out -- I suppose we ought to have them on a list against the market day with their hours, since we're meant to report volunteer time.

I'm doing the data side for a machinery hire business. Six depots, about 480 machines on fleet, and we go back to 2016, so it's just under 400,000 hire lines and roughly 1.6 million engine-hour readings pulled off the telematics. Nothing enormous, but well past what the spreadsheet it currently lives in can cope with.

A machine sits at one depot -- each depot has a name and the county it's in -- and it has an asset number, a type, a make and model, the year it was built and its engine hours, which tick up. Nothing on fleet is older than 2006; that's policy, we trade them out before that. Each machine also carries a list day rate. Just under half the fleet is tractors, a fifth telehandlers, trailers about 15 percent, mowers a tenth and the rest is odds and ends -- toppers, rollers, a couple of chippers.

Customers, which some people here call accounts and the invoices call customer, are either contract or cash, and we hold a credit limit against them. A hire -- the yard calls it a job, the rate card calls it a rental, same record -- is one machine out to one customer with the date it went, the date we expected it back, the date it actually came back, the hours it did while it was out, the discount applied, what we charged, and how far we delivered it. Contract accounts come off list at a flat 15 percent and that gets written onto the agreement as the discount. We won't deliver further than 120 km. Average delivery is about 34 km with a fair spread either side of it, call it 18. Hours on a hire average 50 but the shape is a decay curve -- masses of one and two day jobs, then a long thin tail of six-week silage jobs.

A tractor never goes out under 180 a day whatever anyone has typed on the rate card, because below that we're subsidising the customer.

Servicing: every machine has a history of services and breakdowns against it, with the date, what kind of service it was, the engine hours when it happened, whether it was a breakdown rather than a scheduled one, and the cost. Most of those invoices are a couple of hundred pounds but there's a fat tail -- the odd four-thousand-pound gearbox -- so it's a lognormal shape, log-mean around 5.5 and a log-variance about 1.

Insurance claims exist but leave them out for now, and there's an operator involved on some hires where we supply the driver, which I haven't thought through yet.

We're rebuilding the order history for an agricultural inputs distributor -- seed, fertiliser, crop protection -- trading out of 22 branches across the country. The reason we're doing it at all is size: about 31 million order lines since 2004, growing by roughly 1.8 million a year, and the current warehouse takes eleven minutes to answer 'what did this grower buy last spring'.

The line is the grain of the thing. One line is one product to one account on a date, with a tonnage, the price per tonne we actually charged, and the delivery week they asked for -- weeks are numbered one to fifty-two and that is how the entire logistics side talks. I'll be honest, there is no proper order header in the source system, just lines that happen to share a date and an account, and I've never been sure whether we should invent one.

Products carry a code, a category, the pack size in kilos, a list price per tonne, and for the fertilisers a nitrogen percentage, which runs from nothing at all up to 46 percent for straight urea. By line count, fertiliser is about 42 percent, seed 30, crop protection 20, and the last 8 percent is everything else -- lime, netting, twine.

Accounts (the reps say growers, finance says customer, it's the same entity) belong to a home branch, which has a name and a region, and each account has a status and the hectares they farm. The average is about 180 hectares, the median nearer 120, and a handful of estates are over five thousand, so it's a long right tail -- lognormal, roughly 4.8 on the log scale with a variance around 0.9.

Line sizes have a similar shape: median about three and a half tonnes, with everything from a single 25-kilo bag up to a 600-tonne blanket fertiliser order, so log-mean around 1.25 and log-variance about 1.1.

Two commercial rules need baking in rather than living in someone's head. Fertiliser never goes out below 190 a tonne, that's a hard floor and sales can't override it. And any line of 24 tonnes or more earns the bulk discount, six percent, which we want written on the line itself.

Right, so we're a two-branch estate agency -- my father started it in 2018 and I took over the sales side of it last year. Nothing fancy. At any one time we have somewhere around a hundred and eighty houses on our books, and across the whole eight years we have sold maybe two and a half thousand, so we are really not drowning in data here; the problem is more that the same house exists in four different notebooks.

For every house we take on I want the street address and the postcode held apart from each other, because the postcode is how we do our local price comparisons. Then what sort of house it is -- roughly a third of what we handle is semi-detached, a quarter terraced, about a fifth detached and the rest are flats. Bedrooms obviously; we have never listed anything smaller than a one-bed and the biggest we ever had was six. The asking price, the date the instruction came in, and the EPC band, which sellers always forget to send us.

Asking prices sit around two hundred and eighty-five thousand as a typical figure, but there is a long tail upwards -- we did a farmhouse at 1.4 million in 2023 and that one number ruins every average I try to work out. We have never taken on anything below sixty thousand, that is a floor we hold to.

Viewings are the bit that goes wrong most. A viewing has to say which house it was for, which of our negotiators took it, the applicant's name and a phone number, the date and time, and whatever feedback came back afterwards. I also want a marker for whether it was a second viewing, because those are the ones that actually convert. For the negotiators themselves we only need their name, which branch they sit in, their mobile, and the date they started with us -- we pay a length-of-service bonus and I am forever digging that out of old contracts.

Offers come in against a house. We write down the applicant's name, the amount, the day it was made, whether they have anything of their own to sell (chain-free buyers, we love those) and where the offer got to in the end. On average it takes about thirty-four days from us putting a house up to the first offer landing, although some go the same afternoon and some sit for half a year.

Oh, and the one rule Dad never broke: if a house has been with us more than seventy days and nothing has happened, the asking price gets cut. So I need to know how long each one has been on and whether we have already reduced it once.

We are a lettings and management outfit, nine and a bit thousand properties under management across the north west, and the honest truth is our current system was built for about four hundred. There are getting on for two million rent transactions sitting in it now and it takes forty seconds to open a statement.

Start with the clients, by which I mean the landlords -- half the office says landlord and half says client and they are the same person. We hold their name, a correspondence address, a mobile, an email, their tax reference for the non-resident ones, and the date they came to us. Some of them own one flat and one of them owns two hundred and eleven.

Then the properties themselves, each one belonging to a landlord: the address, the number of bedrooms, whether it is furnished, the EPC rating, and whether it is licensed as an HMO because the council are very keen on that at the moment.

A tenancy is the agreement that sits on a property. Start and end dates, the monthly rent, the deposit, what kind of agreement it is, and the date the deposit was protected. Nearly all of ours are standard assured shortholds -- about six in a hundred are company lets and there is a small slice, call it eight per cent, that are licences for the HMO rooms. The rent averages around eleven hundred and fifty a month and most of the book is within a couple of hundred either side of that. On a normal assured shorthold the deposit is capped at five weeks' rent, which in practice means we never hold more than about fifteen hundred pounds; company lets are not capped at all so those can be anything. It used to be six weeks before the rules changed, so you will see older numbers in the data that look wrong and are not.

Everybody named on the agreement gets recorded separately -- name, date of birth, mobile, email, and whether we have completed their right to rent check. They are each attached to the one tenancy they signed.

Rent payments are per tenancy. Date received, amount, how they paid, and how many days late it was. Anything more than a fortnight late and a notice goes out, and we need to know for each payment whether that notice was actually sent, because a tribunal will ask.

Repairs get logged against the property rather than the tenancy, which I know is annoying, but that is how the maintenance lads work. Date reported, what is wrong, how urgent, the contractor's name and what it ended up costing. A tenancy generates about two and a half repair jobs in a year on average -- some years none at all, and then a boiler goes and you get five in a fortnight.

Lease admin platform, commercial landlord group. Four hundred buildings, eleven thousand demised units, 8,500 live leases; the service charge apportionment table is the fat one at roughly 3.5 million rows after fifteen years of quarterly runs.

Buildings hang off a holding entity, one entity to many buildings, and carry name, address, year of practical completion, total lettable area in sqm. Each building subdivides into demised units: unit reference, net internal area, floor level, planning use class. Tenant covenants are held apart from leases because the same covenant re-lets -- legal name, company number, covenant strength grade, guarantor name where there is one.

A lease is one unit to one covenant: term commencement, term in whole years, contractual annual rent, review pattern, a tenant break flag, repairing obligation. Term is an integer 1 to 25, nothing longer exists on this book, and it clusters on the round numbers -- 34 per cent at five years, 29 at ten, 18 at fifteen, 12 at three, the last 7 at twenty-five. Rent is log-normal, log-mean 11.6, log-variance 1.1. Standing rule from our solicitors: where the unit's use class is B8, storage and distribution, the lease always carries a break clause.

Reviews are child rows on the lease -- review date, passing rent before, reviewed rent after, uplift percentage, whether it went to third party determination. Uplifts average 8.5 per cent, standard deviation near 4.

Apportionments are per lease: charge year, certified quarter, apportioned percentage, demanded amount. The percentage is bounded 0 to 100 and a run whose per-building total exceeds 100 gets rejected.

I look after reporting for a main contractor -- civils and fit-out, turnover about ninety million, twenty-odd live jobs at any time. We book roughly six hundred thousand timesheet lines a year and there are four years of them in the current system, so it is a couple of million rows plus everything hanging off it. I have been asked to write down what we actually track before the new system gets specified.

Clients first. Name, what sector they are in -- public bodies, private developers, utilities -- and which of our account managers owns the relationship. A job belongs to one client: job name, the site address, the contract value, when we started on site, the practical completion date, what stage it is at, and the retention percentage. Retention is normally five per cent, but where the client is a public body the standard form gives us three, and nobody remembers that until the final account. Contract values are all over the place -- the middle of the range is around 3.2 million but we have done a 40 million spine road and a 90 thousand pound shopfront in the same year, so it is very much a long-tailed thing.

Subcontractors are a shared list, not per job -- company name, trade, whether their CSCS checks are verified, and when their insurance runs out. The same firm turns up on lots of our jobs and a job has thirty or forty of them, so the appointment itself is the thing we need to hold: which firm on which job, the value of their package and when they were appointed. That pairing is unique, we never appoint the same firm to a job twice.

A job is broken into work packages -- package name, planned start and finish, and a percent complete figure the site manager updates on a Friday. It only ever runs from 0 to 100 although you would not believe how often somebody types 110.

Operatives belong to a subcontractor: name and trade card number. They book time against a work package -- the date, and hours worked. A normal day is about 8.6 hours with a spread of an hour and a half either way, and we do not allow anybody to book more than twelve hours on one date.

Then the commercial side. Variations against a job: what changed, when it was submitted, what it was valued at, and where it got to. Monthly valuations, also per job: the valuation number, period end, gross amount and the retention held. Material deliveries come in against a package -- supplier, date, tonnage and the ticket reference off the weighbridge.

Safety is the one the board actually reads. Incidents are logged against a job with a date, a severity grade of 1 to 4, whether it is RIDDOR reportable and how many days were lost. About sixty-eight per cent are grade 1 near misses, twenty-one per cent grade 2, nine per cent grade 3 and the last two per cent grade 4. Anything graded 3 or worse is reportable, full stop.

So my patch is hard FM across about nine hundred buildings -- schools, a couple of leisure centres, offices, the lot. The reason I am even in this meeting is the meter data. Every bit of plant with a meter on it reports every fifteen minutes and that is something like sixty million readings a year, and the spreadsheet approach died about three years ago. A reading is just the meter, the timestamp and the consumption in kilowatt hours. Typically it is around forty units on a fifteen minute read, give or take fifteen, but the leisure centres in January are a different animal entirely.

Sites: name, which region they fall in, and floor area. Region matters because the regional managers all want their own numbers.

Every site has kit on it -- assets, plant, whatever you want to call it. Air handling units, lifts, boilers, chillers. We hold what type it is, the year it went in, and how critical it is, which is a flag the client sets. Critical kit is the stuff where the building stops if it stops.

Then the jobs. Some of the team say job, the helpdesk say ticket, the contract says work order, they are the same thing and I would like to stop arguing about it. A job is raised against a piece of kit. We need when it came in, what the caller said, how urgent it is, when it was closed, how long the response took, the labour hours booked and what it cost. Urgency is banded one to four. Nearly everything comes in as a three -- call it sixty-three per cent -- with seventeen per cent fours, sixteen per cent twos and only about four in a hundred coming in as ones. A priority one has to be attended and cleared within four hours under the contract, and if the response goes past four we are paying a deduction, so on those the response time is never above four. And anything raised against critical kit comes in as a one automatically -- the helpdesk has no say in it.

The interesting thing, and the reason the client keeps asking for a report we cannot produce, is that the callouts are not spread out at all. A tiny number of assets -- the old AHUs at the two big sites, mainly -- soak up most of the jobs we raise in a year, and the overwhelming majority of the kit on the register never generates a single one. It is a very long tail and every average I quote them is meaningless because of it.

Jobs go to contractors. We just need the firm's name and their trade -- they are a short list and I do not want to build a whole procurement module.

Last thing, planned maintenance. Each bit of kit has a service schedule: how often it is due, in months, and when it was last done.

There are five of us. Two directors, two Part 2s and Jean who does everything else, and we have been going since 2011, so call it four hundred jobs all in and a few thousand drawings in the archive. It is not a lot of information. It is just in nine hundred folders on a NAS and Jean is retiring.

The unit of work is -- well, we call it a job, the invoices call it a commission and the directors say project, and it is one thing. Whatever it is called, we want the client's name, the title we gave the scheme, the town the site is in, how far up the RIBA stages it got, whether the fee was fixed or a percentage or time-charged, what fee we agreed, and the date the enquiry first came in.

Fees are wildly uneven. Most of what we do is a domestic extension worth a few thousand -- nine grand is about the middle of it -- but every couple of years one lands that is worth six figures and then the year looks nothing like the year before. On the fixed-fee ones we have a floor of two and a half thousand; below that it is not worth opening a file, and that has been the rule since about 2016. There is no such floor on the time-charged work, we will do a two-hour appraisal for a builder if we like him.

Most jobs die at stage 3. That is just the reality of planning work -- you get consent and the client goes off to a contractor who does the technical package. If I had to put numbers on it, about a tenth of the jobs stop at stage 1, one in seven at stage 2, a good third and a bit at stage 3, a bit over a fifth at stage 4 and the remaining sixth run through to stage 5.

Drawings hang off the job. Number, title, revision letter, the date it was issued and the scale it was drawn at. That is the bit that actually causes arguments -- somebody issues revision C to the contractor and the structural engineer is still working off B.

And time. Who, what day, how many hours, against which job. A full day usually comes out at six or seven chargeable hours once you take out the phone calls -- six and a half is about right, and it varies by a couple of hours either side. Nothing over twelve, if someone books fourteen hours they have fat-fingered it.

We also used to write down which planning officer was handling each application, and honestly it was the single most useful thing we ever recorded, but it lived in an individual's head and I do not know what to do with that.

Cost management database, QS practice. Only a few thousand cost plans, but the bill of quantities lines underneath them come to roughly two million rows, and those are what need modelling properly instead of living in workbooks.

Client organisations at the top: name, procurement route. A cost plan belongs to one of them -- project reference, version number (we reissue four or five times over a scheme's life), base date, gross internal area in sqm, total estimate. Plans decompose into elements keyed on NRM code, with element name, elemental cost and the cost per square metre derived from it. Elemental rates land near 2,150 per sqm, standard deviation about 640, across all sectors. Under each element sit the bill items: description, measured quantity, unit of measurement, rate applied, extended amount. Item amounts are log-normal, log-mean 7.6, log-variance 2.1 -- thousands of trivial items and a handful carrying the bill.

Two reference libraries, neither of them keyed to a plan: resource rates, on resource code plus type, unit rate and an effective-from date; and the TPI, a dated index value per month that we rebase to.

Tenders come in against a plan -- contractor name, submission date, tender sum, compliance flag. Interim certificates likewise: certificate number, valuation date, work done to date, retention, and retention is never negative. Risk allowances are per plan too -- description, a band of LOW, MEDIUM or HIGH, and the allowance as a percentage. Allowances run anywhere from 1 to 12 per cent and are flat across that interval, no clustering; on anything banded HIGH we will not sign off below 7.5.

One check I want in the data rather than in somebody's head: over 15,000 sqm of gross internal area, economies of scale mean no element should exceed 2,500 per square metre. If one does, it is mis-measured or the area is wrong, and that has embarrassed us twice.

Six self-storage sites, and I have been asked to sketch the model before we talk to developers. Scale is genuinely small -- about 2,700 units across the six and a little under 9,000 agreements since the first site opened in 2014.

A facility has a name, the town it is in, how many units it holds and the date it opened. Units belong to a facility and each one has a reference like B-114, a size, the floor level (ground is 0, we go up to 2 at Warrington), whether it is climate controlled, and the current list price per month. We only sell five sizes, deliberately, because it keeps the site plan simple: 25, 50, 75, 100 and 200 square feet. The 50s are the workhorse at about a third of the estate, the 25s a bit over a fifth, the 75s not quite a fifth, the 100s about a sixth, and the 200s the remaining eight per cent. List prices average near 96 pounds a month with a spread of maybe 38 either way -- a climate-controlled ground floor 200 and a second floor 25 are not the same product at all. Which is the reason for our one hard pricing rule: a ground floor unit that is climate controlled never goes out below 120 a month, whatever a walk-in offers us.

Customers are just name, email, phone and the date they first signed up. An agreement links one customer to one unit -- start date, end date if they have gone, the monthly rate they actually pay (not always the list price), whether they are on autopay, and how much insurance cover they took. Cover starts at a thousand and we cap it at twenty-five thousand, above which the insurer wants a survey.

The number I care about most is how long people stay. Average is around nine months, but the shape is a decay curve -- most are out inside a month or two after a house move, and then there is a hard core in the same unit since 2015. So put the tenure in months on the agreement.

Portfolio is fourteen purpose-built student blocks, just over eleven thousand beds, and the operational data volume is dominated by one thing: door access. Every swipe on every door is logged and across the estate that is somewhere around forty million events a year. Everything else is small by comparison.

A residence has a name, a city, the university we have the nominations agreement with, and its bed count. Inside a residence there are flats -- flat number, floor, and how many bedrooms the flat contains -- and inside a flat, the bedrooms themselves. Each bedroom has a room reference, the band it is sold in, whether it is ensuite, and the weekly rent. Bands are Classic, Premium and Studio: about 52 per cent Classic, 31 Premium and 17 Studio. Weekly rents average around 189 pounds with a standard deviation of roughly 42. Studios are the exception to everything -- we never sell a studio below 240 a week, they are the margin.

Residents -- students, tenants, whatever the sales team is calling them this week -- have a name, the university they actually attend (which is not always our nominations partner), their year of course, and whether they are an international student.

A booking puts one resident in one bedroom for an academic year. It carries the academic year, the contract length in weeks, the weekly rate agreed, a flag for whether a guarantor is required and whether the deposit has been paid. Contracts are either 44 weeks or 51 weeks and nothing else, which makes the arithmetic easy. International students always need a UK guarantor -- that comes from the finance policy, not from us, and there are no exceptions to it.

Rent goes out in instalments against a booking: due date, amount due, amount received, and whether it landed late. Nothing negative in the received column, even for the refunds, we handle those separately and badly.

Access events are per resident per residence -- when, which door, and whether entry was granted. Denied swipes matter, that is usually somebody who has not paid or a lanyard that has gone walkabout.

Incidents get raised against a residence, and against a resident where we know who it was: when it was reported, what category, and whether it is resolved. A block generates about four or five of them a month on average, more in freshers' week, obviously.

This is the valuation stack, and I will be honest that half of it is well defined and half of it is whatever the last contractor left behind.

The well-defined half. We hold a property record per UPRN -- postcode, the address as a single text blob because we never managed to parse it, property type, floor area, build year and tenure. Sales come off the registry against a UPRN: sale date, price, and a new-build flag. That is 29 million addresses in the record table and the automated model runs over all of them monthly, so the estimate table is the one that hurts -- it is tens of millions of rows a run, each with the run date, the model version, a point estimate and a lower and upper bound. Median sale price on the index is a bit over 228,000, so log-mean 12.33, and the log-variance is about 0.42.

Surveyors: name, RICS number, grade, region. A valuation is one surveyor against one property -- instructed date, inspection date, the basis of valuation, the market value reported, and a confidence score which is a fraction between 0 and 1, sitting around 0.78 with a standard deviation of about 0.11. A typical inspection also turns up one or two defects worth writing up, so the count of them belongs on the valuation itself, and the defect rows carry a category, a severity grade and an estimated remedial cost. Grade 3 is our top severity and it is defined by cost -- anything we grade a 3 is going to be more than five thousand pounds to put right, that is what makes it a 3.

Now the messy half. Comparables -- the surveyors say comps, the report template says comparable evidence, the schema calls them something else again. A valuation cites several other properties as evidence and the same property gets cited across many valuations, so it is genuinely both ways round, and the pair carries the percentage adjustment applied and the weight the surveyor gave it.

Instructions come from lenders -- a lender being a name and a panel tier. The instruction sits against a valuation with the time it came in, the SLA in hours and the product type. Tier 1 lenders are contractually on 48 hours, every time; the rest vary and I would have to look it up. We also keep a monthly regional index series -- region, month, index value -- which is what we revalue the book against. There is an EPC feed landing on the same box that nobody has opened since 2023 and I am ignoring it here. Floor areas are supposed to be square metres, incidentally, and a chunk of the older rows are clearly square feet, and we have never cleaned it.

domain: Amateur Football League Fixtures and Results
nl_description:
Backing store for a regional amateur football league, eleven divisions, currently being lifted off a pile of Access files.

TEAM is keyed on an integer team_id and holds the club name, the year the club was founded, the division it plays in, and a reference to its home ground. Grounds are their own entity -- two or three clubs share a pitch -- and a ground carries a name and a licensed capacity. Nothing in the league is licensed below 250.

MATCH is the interesting one. It points at the season it belongs to (a season is just a label like 2024-25 plus its opening and closing dates), at the ground it was played on, and at TEAM twice: home_team_id and away_team_id, both foreign keys into the same table, which is the bit every ORM tutorial skips. Kick-off is a TIMESTAMP. home_goals and away_goals are non-negative integers, and goals for one side in one match are Poisson with lambda 1.4. Attendance is lognormal in log space, mean 6.1, variance 0.8. Grounds licensed under 2,000 are all-seated and we cap the recorded gate there at 1,800.

Every goal also gets its own row, against the player who scored it and the minute it went in, so minute is an INTEGER in 1..120 to allow for extra time. A player belongs to one team; we store the name, the position, and the age at registration -- normal, mean 26.5, sd 5.1. Positions run roughly 10 per cent goalkeeper, 32 per cent defender, 34 per cent midfielder, 24 per cent forward.

Volumes: 900 teams, 14K players, 400K matches back to 1994, about 2.6M goal rows.

domain: Gym Chain Membership and Group Classes
nl_description:
I run operations for a gym chain -- forty-one sites, two more opening before Christmas. It is all spreadsheets and it is falling over, so bear with me while I explain how the thing actually works.

People join. They pick one of our packages -- Off-Peak, Standard, Premium, and a Student one -- and each package has a monthly price and says whether it is one gym only or all of them. Premium is 54.99 a month and Standard is 34.99. The Student one is never more than 25, that is a rule marketing gave us and I have stopped arguing. Every member is tied to a home gym even though the Premium lot can walk into any site. For a member we need the name, the email, the date of birth and the date they signed up. A site is just a name and a town.

Memberships are not forever and that is what the spreadsheets cannot cope with. Someone joins in March on Standard, upgrades to Premium in May, freezes in July because they are away, cancels in November. We need all of that as history -- when it started, when it ended if it has, what state it is in, and which package it was on -- not just where they stand today.

Classes are messier. We run spin, yoga, HIIT, boxing, aquafit and a couple of others; each of those is a kind of class with a bit of blurb and a normal length, spin is 45 minutes and yoga is an hour. Then a real class happens: six o'clock on a Tuesday at the Leeds site, spin, one named instructor taking it, and a limit on how many bodies fit in the room. Those limits average around 24 and vary either side by about 7, and they are never above 40, because that is our biggest studio. Spin is the exception -- it is limited by bikes and nobody has more than 24 of those.

Members book onto a class, and the same person obviously cannot book the same class twice. Afterwards we mark them turned up or no-show; no-shows are about one in six and they are killing us.

Instructors are freelance. Each has an hourly rate somewhere between 22 and 45 depending on what they hold, spread fairly evenly across that, and each is only signed off to teach certain kinds of class -- the yoga people cannot take boxing. Each one is based at a site but covers others.

Then there is ordinary gym use, nothing to do with classes: the turnstile logs who came in, which site, and when. That is the monster -- about 250,000 a month across the chain and we keep two years of it.

Payments are monthly direct debit. Amount, the date, and whether it went through -- roughly 4 per cent bounce. Around 60,000 people are paying us right now.

I am the data lead at a race-timing outfit -- we do chip timing for road races, about 1,100 events a year across Europe. Here is roughly how I think about the model.

An event is the thing on the calendar: a name, a date, a host city. Inside one event there can be several races -- a marathon, a half, a 10K, sometimes a kids' fun run. Each race has its own distance in kilometres (42.2, 21.1, 10, 5), its own start time and its own entry fee. Fees run from 25 to 95 euros depending on the distance and are spread pretty evenly across that.

A runner is a person and we keep them across events: name, date of birth, gender, and the club they run for if they run for one. A club has a name and a country. Club sizes are wildly top-heavy -- a handful of big city clubs supply an enormous share of the entries and there is a very long tail of clubs with two members each. That matters a lot when we generate test data.

An entry is one runner in one race. It has a bib number, which is between 1 and 99999, the age group we assign, and once they have run, the gun time and the chip time in seconds plus a finish status. About 94 per cent finish, 4 per cent are DNF, and 2 per cent never start. If someone does not finish we store a chip time of zero rather than a null -- a decision made in 2011 that we are stuck with. Marathon finishers average about four and a quarter hours with a spread of roughly 45 minutes either side. Nobody has ever run a marathon under 2h02, so any chip time below 7,320 seconds on the 42.2 is a mat error and we reject it. Half marathons and anything shorter have a four-hour cut-off, so for a race of 21.1 km or less we will not accept a chip time above 14,400 seconds.

The volume comes from splits. A race has timing points -- start mat, 5K, 10K, halfway and so on -- each with a name and the distance along the course where it sits. Every runner crossing every mat is a row holding the elapsed seconds, which is never negative. Six or seven mats per runner gives us north of 20 million split rows a year and about 90 million sitting in the warehouse, on top of 3.4 million entries.

domain: Cycling Club GPS Ride and Segment Tracking
nl_description:
Schema notes for the club's ride-logging platform. We ingest GPS activities off head units and phones; 'activity' and 'ride' mean the same thing in every conversation you will have here, and the code says ride.

A rider has a display name, a sign-up timestamp, a body weight in kg and an FTP in watts. FTP is normal, mean 238, sd 46. Weights below 40 or above 140 are rejected on ingest. A rider owns bikes; a bike has a type and a frame weight, and about 62 per cent of them are road, 20 per cent gravel, 10 per cent mountain, 8 per cent TT.

Clubs are separate and the relationship is genuinely many-to-many: a rider can be in several clubs, a club has many riders, and the association itself carries a role and the date they joined, so it is a junction keyed on (club_id, rider_id). A club has a name, a founding year and a region.

Routes have a name, a distance and a total elevation gain. A route is cut into segments, each with a name, a length in metres and an average gradient percent, which we clamp to the range -15 to 30 because sign errors happen constantly.

A ride references its rider, the bike used, and a route where we can match one -- often we cannot. It carries a start timestamp, distance, moving time and average power. Ride distance is lognormal, log-mean 3.5, log-variance 0.6. Inside a ride there is one row per segment crossed, holding the elapsed time and the average power for that effort. Effort counts per segment are viciously Zipfian with an exponent around 1.3 -- the town-sign sprint has millions of them, the farm track has four. Two sanity rules live there: a segment shorter than 1,000 m has never legitimately taken more than 300 seconds, and on anything averaging 8 per cent or steeper the effort's average power comes in at 200 W or more, because you cannot soft-pedal up it.

Raw telemetry is the volume driver -- one trackpoint per second per ride with latitude, longitude, heart rate and power. Heart rate is normal, mean 138, sd 18. We are taking about 40 million trackpoints a week.

Last piece is the club calendar. A club schedules a group ride on a route at a time, with a pace group (A, B or C -- what those actually mean is a perennial argument), and riders sign up, again many-to-many, with a status on the signup.

Right, so this is for the leisure centre pool. The council wants it computerised and I have been told to write down how the booking works, which I have never done before, so it might be a bit all over the place.

We have got six lanes. Depending on the hour the pool is either general swimming, or lane swimming, or it is a lesson, or the aqua-aerobics lot have it. Whatever it is, it is a slot on a particular day at a particular time with a price on it, and we write down how many people we will let in the water for that one. Never more than thirty in total, and for lessons it is a lot tighter, eight, because that is what the teacher can watch. We also note how many lanes that slot is using, and obviously that cannot be more than six or fewer than one. Prices run from the 2.30 concession up to about eight quid for the aqua class, all sorts in between.

The lessons have a teacher. I do not need much about them beyond who they are and what level they are qualified to, but we do have to be able to say which teacher took which lesson, because parents ask.

Then the people. We call them swimmers, the till system calls them customers, and the council's letter calls them users -- it is all the same person. Name, a phone number, whether they live in the borough, and what sort of concession they get. Roughly half pay full whack, about a quarter are pensioners, and the rest is students and children, rather more students than children. Pensioners are 2.30 no matter which slot it is; that is fixed by the council and it never changes.

A booking is one of them against one of the slots. When they booked it, how much they actually paid, and how many are coming, because it is usually just the one person but every so often a family turns up on one booking, four or five of them. Very lopsided, that.

It is not a big operation. Maybe nine hundred people on the list, a couple of thousand bookings in a month, and the whole thing currently lives in a ring binder and a Google Sheet that Denise looks after.

Product analytics at an esports tournament platform. I will describe the model the way I understand it and the engineers can correct my types afterwards.

We support several game titles. A title has a publisher and a number of players per side, and that number drives a surprising amount of downstream logic. Each title has its own set of maps, and a map is really just a name hanging off a title.

Players have accounts: a handle, a country, when they signed up, and an MMR that the matchmaker maintains. MMR is normally distributed, centred on 1500, standard deviation around 320.

Teams -- the community says orgs, or squads, same thing -- have a name, a short tag, a region and a founding date. The regional split is roughly APAC 34 per cent, EU 30, NA 22, SA 9, MEA 5. A team's roster is many-to-many against accounts, because an account moves between teams over time, and each roster row says what role they play, when they joined, and whether they are a starter or a sub. Tournament participation works the same way: a tournament has many teams and a team enters many tournaments, and that association is where the seed and the final placement live.

A tournament belongs to a title and has a prize pool, a start date, a format and an entry fee, which is zero for most of the open ones.

A match sits inside a tournament and is between two teams -- and yes, both of those point at the same team table, which caused us a lot of grief in the first version. A match has a scheduled time, a best-of number between 1 and 7, and a winning team. Within a match, each game records which map it was on, its number in the series, how long it lasted and who won it. Game duration is lognormal, log-mean 7.3, log-variance 0.35. Anything with a prize pool of a million or more is never a single game -- best-of-three at absolute minimum.

Per game per player we keep kills, deaths, assists and damage. Kills average about 7.5 per player per game and behave like a Poisson count. None of kills or deaths ever goes negative, which sounds obvious until you see what the ingest does with a crashed server.

We sample the stream viewer count every ten seconds while a match is live; concurrent viewers are lognormal, log-mean 9.1, log-variance 1.4. And there is a payouts table -- which tournament, which team, how much, and the date it went out. In a million-dollar event no single cheque is under 500 dollars.

Volume: roughly 90 million player-game stat rows a season, and the viewership samples are the same order of magnitude.

Handicap and scoring store for a members' golf club running WHS.

A course has a name, a par and a hole count -- we own an 18 and a 9. Each course carries several tee sets, one per colour, and the tee set is what holds the numbers that matter: course rating, slope rating, and total yardage. Slope is 55 to 155 by definition and is essentially uniform across that band in our data.

A member has a name, a join date, a gender, a current handicap index and the WHS category, an integer 1 to 5, derived from that index. Anyone at 5.4 or better is category 1. Indexes across the membership are normal, mean 16.2, sd 7.4, and the rules do not permit an index below -10 or above 54.

A round references the member and the tee set played. It stores the date, the gross score, the adjusted gross, the computed score differential, and the round type -- about 78 per cent of rounds are social and 22 per cent competition. Gross scores are normal, mean 91, sd 11. Off the forward tees, meaning any tee set under 5,200 total yards, an adjusted gross above 120 is not credible, so the stored adjusted gross is capped at 120 there.

Below a round sits one row per hole: hole number 1 to 18, strokes, and putts. Putts per hole are Poisson, lambda 1.9.

Handicap revisions are their own history table -- member, effective date, the new index and the reason it changed -- because auditors ask.

About 2,300 members, 340K rounds since 2009, just over 5 million hole rows.

We are a small sports academy, after school and weekends, and I have been asked to explain what we need to keep track of. I am not technical so this will be in my own words.

The kids are the main thing. We call them players, or athletes if we are being posh, and there are about two hundred and forty of them on the books across roughly ninety families. For each one we need the first and last name, when they were born because everything here is age-banded, which sport they do, and any medical bits -- inhalers, allergies, that sort of thing, written out longhand because it never fits in a box. Football is the big one, getting on for half of them. Netball and athletics are about a fifth each and the rugby lot are whatever is left.

Every child has a grown-up attached. Mum, dad, gran, sometimes a foster carer -- we just need who they are, a mobile, an email, and what they are to the child, because if a kid goes over on an ankle we are not ringing round guessing. One grown-up often has two or three kids with us.

The kids are grouped into squads -- Under-9 girls' netball, that kind of thing -- and a squad has one coach running it, a name, its age band and the sport. We never put more than twenty in a squad, and under six is not worth running so we do not. If it is one of the volunteer dads taking the squad rather than a paid coach we keep it to a dozen at most, because they are not insured for more than that. For coaches we need the name, whether they are volunteer or paid, and the expiry on their background check -- that one is not optional, the county asks for it every year.

A squad trains on a schedule. Each training session is a date, a start time, the place, and how long it runs -- normally an hour and a half, though about a third of them are just the hour. For every session we tick each child off as there, not there, or late. Most turn up, somewhere around four in five, a bit over one in ten just does not appear, and there is always a handful arriving late.

The money side is simple. We bill the families monthly: an amount, the month it is for, and whether it has been paid. It is anywhere from thirty to sixty pounds depending on how many sessions the child is down for, and obviously never a negative number.

Oh -- there is a physio who comes in on Thursdays, but she does her own paperwork and none of it comes near us.

I am a personal trainer, one-man band, and I want to get off paper.

Twenty-eight people on the books at the moment. For each one I want the name, a mobile number, what they are actually after -- weight loss, strength, marathon prep, whatever they told me in the consult -- when they started with me, how many sessions they have got left in the tank, and what I charge them an hour. The rate is not the same for everybody: if they have bought a block of ten up front it is forty an hour, otherwise it is fifty, and I need the system to know which of those they are on. Sessions left cannot go below zero; that is the whole point of tracking it.

Then the sessions themselves. Date and time, how long, where -- their house, the park, or the unit I rent on Fridays -- and whether it actually happened. Most do, call it seven in eight; about one in twelve gets cancelled and the odd one is a straight no-show, maybe one in twenty-five. And what I charged for it, because a cancellation inside 24 hours still gets billed and I want to see that in black and white. An hour is the standard, a fair few do forty-five minutes, and I do a handful of half-hour top-ups -- call it six in ten, three in ten, one in ten. Nothing under half an hour and nothing over ninety minutes.

Last bit is the measurements. Every four to six weeks I weigh them, do the calipers and take a resting heart rate. My lot average around seventy-eight and a half kilos with a fair spread, twelve or thirteen kilos either way, and body fat sits around twenty-five per cent give or take six and a half. I will not write down a body fat reading under 4 per cent, that is the calipers lying to me.

Two thousand sessions in the diary since I started, so it is small -- I just want it searchable.

Notes for whoever builds the new system at the climbing centre. I am the duty manager and I know just enough SQL to be dangerous, so treat the shapes as suggestions and the rules as gospel.

The walls have things on them. We call them routes, the boulderers call them problems, and the setters write 'lines' on the whiteboard -- it is one concept and I genuinely do not care what you name it. Each one lives on a named wall, has a grade, a hold colour so people can find it, the date it went up, and the date it came down if it has come down yet. Some are boulder problems, some are lead, a few are top-rope only: about seven in ten boulder, two in ten lead, the rest top-rope. We write down who set it -- they are all staff and their details already sit in the rota system, so a name in a field is enough on our side.

Climbers register once. Display name, the date they registered, when their waiver runs out, and what they are to us: a member, a day-pass punter, or a student rate. Roughly 58 per cent members, 34 per cent day pass, 8 per cent student.

Logging is the interesting part. A climber logs an ascent of a route: when they logged it, how many goes it took, and the style. Attempt counts are savagely long-tailed -- most things go first or second try, but there is always somebody forty attempts into a project -- Zipf-ish with an exponent around 1.8. It is at least one attempt by definition, and if the style is recorded as a flash then it is exactly one attempt, because that is what the word means.

Separately, the door scanner logs visits: the time in, the time out, and the minutes between. Session length averages about ninety-five minutes but the tail is long -- students park themselves in here all afternoon -- so it is exponential rather than anything symmetric. Nothing shorter than five minutes counts as a visit, and anything over ten hours is the scanner having missed the exit.

We are busy: around 11,000 registered climbers, 300,000-odd visits logged, and about 1.4 million ascent rows, because the app nags people to log.

Data model for the EDC back end of a phase III oncology programme; I am specifying it, not asking whether we need it. One row per protocol at the top, with its code, title, phase and therapeutic area, and every activated site hangs off exactly one protocol -- ninety-odd sites across fourteen countries, each with a country, an activation date and a single principal investigator who, in this system, never appears at more than one site. Arms belong to the protocol rather than to a shared lookup, because the dose text is protocol-specific; there are two per protocol, treatment and control, randomised 2:1, so allocation lands at 0.667 treatment / 0.333 control and the arm row carries that weight. Roughly 42,000 subjects, each pinned to one site and one arm, carrying consent date, age at consent (INTEGER, protocol window 18 to 89), sex, baseline ECOG performance status on the usual 0-4 integer scale, baseline weight in kg -- normal, mean 71.4, sd 14.8 -- and the number of days from consent to first dose, which is exponential with rate about 0.11. Visits are child rows on the subject: cycle number 1 through 12, protocol nominal day, actual date, completion status. A visit may collect specimens (blood, biopsy, urine) with a collection timestamp and a draw volume in mL bounded at 0.5 and 30.0. Specimens fan out to assay results -- analyte code, numeric value, unit, lab flag -- and each result names the central laboratory that produced it, since we use three of them and audit needs the lab's accreditation on file. Result values are log-normal, log mean 1.1 and log variance 0.8. That table is the volume driver: about 4.6 million rows. Safety data attaches to the subject, not the visit. Adverse events carry a MedDRA preferred term, a CTCAE grade 1-5, onset and resolution dates, a seriousness boolean and an outcome; observed grade mix is 46 / 31 / 15 / 6 / 2 percent from grade 1 upward. Grade 5 means death, so grade = 5 forces outcome 'FATAL'. Separately, a grade 3 or worse event in a subject who was 75 or older at consent sets the geriatric dose-review flag. Concomitant medications are also per subject: drug name as free text, indication, start and stop. Protocol deviations are recorded against the visit where they happened, with a category, a narrative and a report date; a deviation on a visit whose completion status came back 'MISSED' always takes category 'VISIT_NOT_DONE'.

Core LIMS tables for a clinical-grade short-read sequencing lab. Projects come in under a project code, a PI and a consent type, with the date the project opened; biosamples belong to a project and record tissue, receipt timestamp, DNA concentration in ng/uL (log-normal, log mean 3.1, log variance 0.6) and a RIN between 1.0 and 10.0 that in practice sits at 8.1 with sd 0.9. One biosample yields one or more libraries -- prep kit, target insert size in bp, index barcode, prep date. Runs are keyed to an instrument (model, serial number, install date, maximum read length) and carry the run folder, start timestamp, chemistry and cycle count. A run has eight lanes numbered 1-8, each with a cluster density and a Q30 fraction, and libraries are pooled across lanes many-to-many, so the pool membership row is keyed by lane plus library together and carries the intended fraction of the pool. On S4 chemistry we hold lanes to a Q30 of at least 0.85, capped at 1.0. Per-library alignment metrics are stored against the library and the run that produced them: mean coverage (normal, 38.5 with sd 6.0), duplicate rate, mapped read pairs, callable fraction, and a QC status that is set to 'FAIL' whenever the duplicate rate exceeds 0.30. Variant calls are the large table -- about 60 million rows -- each naming its library and the gene it falls in, plus chromosome, position, ref and alt allele, genotype, depth (never negative), allele fraction in [0, 1] which clusters near 0.48 with sd 0.09 for heterozygous calls, a QUAL score and a filter status. Calls per gene are savagely uneven -- Zipf-like with exponent about 1.35, because the long genes dominate -- so genes are their own table with HGNC symbol, chromosome and transcript length. FFPE material is noisy, so a call from an FFPE-prep library is only reported when its allele fraction is 0.10 or more, and anything under depth 10 gets filter status 'LOW_DEPTH'.

Spec for the regional air-quality archive we are rebuilding off the old flat files. A monitoring station has a code, a site classification, lat/long, elevation and a commissioning date; across the 214 stations the classification mix is about 42 percent urban traffic, 33 percent urban background, 18 percent rural background and 7 percent industrial. Each station hosts one or more analysers, and an analyser measures exactly one pollutant, so the analyser row carries its station, its pollutant, model, serial number, a non-negative detection limit and a top of scale. Pollutants are a small reference table: code, reporting unit, the statutory limit value, and the averaging period in hours, which is never below 1 or above 24. The fact table is hourly observations against the analyser -- timestamp, concentration, a QC flag, the co-located ambient temperature and a validated boolean. Concentrations are strongly right-skewed and log-normal, log mean 2.9 with log variance 0.55; ambient temperature is normal, 14.2 C with sd 8.6. A row may only be marked validated if its concentration lies between the 0.5 detection limit and the 985.0 top of scale -- raw rows outside that band stay in the archive but never get the validated tick. Analysers get span-gas calibrations: timestamp, span gas concentration, percent drift (kept within plus or minus 10, and normally distributed around zero with sd 1.4) and a pass boolean, where drift beyond 5 percent is a fail by definition. Finally, exceedance alerts point at the offending observation and carry a severity, a raise timestamp and whether the authority was told; where the observed concentration is above 150, notification is mandatory. Volume: 38 million observation rows today, plus about 4.5 million a year.

Notes toward the schema for the state seismic network's analysis database. Stations are identified by network code plus station code, with lat/long, elevation and a vault type -- posthole, tunnel, surface vault, we have not standardised that vocabulary yet. Channels hang off the station: channel code, sample rate in Hz, sensor type, gain, azimuth in degrees and dip. Sample rates across the network are roughly 20 Hz for 18 percent of channels, 40 Hz for 24 percent, 100 Hz for 51 percent and 200 Hz for the remaining 7 percent, and strong-motion channels are never run below 100 Hz. Events carry an origin time, hypocentre lat/long, depth from 0 to 700 km (and depth is essentially exponentially distributed with a mean near 12 km, so rate about 0.083), an event type, a single-letter location quality and the location RMS residual in seconds. Phase picks are the volume -- past 240 million rows -- each tying an event to a channel with a phase label, an arrival time, a timing uncertainty in seconds that is log-normal with log mean -2.3 and log variance 0.4, a polarity, and the initials of whoever made the pick. Magnitudes are separate rows per event so ML, Mw and mb can coexist: type, value between -2.0 and 9.5, contributing station count, uncertainty, and a preferred flag. Gutenberg-Richter means magnitude is exponentially distributed with rate about 2.3. An estimate built from fewer than three stations is never preferred, and a local magnitude ML is never preferred for an event deeper than 300 km. Waveform segments record the channel, the event they were cut for, start time, duration in seconds, sample count and the archive path. We also keep a log of channel outages -- when the channel went dark, when it came back and why, though the why is free text and nobody fills it in consistently.

I look after the herbarium here and honestly the current arrangement is a card index plus three spreadsheets that disagree with each other, so we would like something proper. What we hold is sheets -- pressed, dried plants glued to card -- a bit under nine thousand of them, which is small by herbarium standards but it is a hundred and forty years of work. Every sheet gets an accession number when it comes in, and we write down when it was collected, what state the sheet is in (good, fair, poor -- roughly six in ten are good, three in ten fair, and the rest we would rather nobody handled), how tall the pressed specimen is on the card, and whether it is a type. A type is the actual sheet the original published description was based on, which makes it irreplaceable. Heights are mostly around thirty or thirty-one centimetres because that is the size of the card; the smallest scraps are two centimetres of moss and the tallest thing we have folded onto a sheet is about a hundred and twenty. Then there is the name, which has to be its own thing, because names change and plenty of sheets share a name -- family, genus, species, who published it, and the common name if it has one. Three families account for a third of the whole collection and then there is an enormous tail of families we hold one or two sheets of. And where it came from: a place name, the region, the country, the latitude and longitude if the label bothered to say, and the altitude. Most of our collecting is lowland, a couple of the Andean sheets are up over four thousand metres and there is one from a salt flat twenty metres below sea level. Collectors are the awkward part. A sheet often has more than one person on the label -- a lead collector and whoever was with them -- so you cannot just put one name on the sheet. We need to be able to say which people collected which sheet and what each of them was doing, and for each collector we keep their institution and roughly when they were active. Something else: when a botanist collects a plant they usually press several duplicates to send to other herbaria, and we note how many went out. It is usually one or two, sometimes five or six. Last thing, and it matters for insurance -- we lend sheets to other institutions. A loan record says which sheet, who borrowed it, when it went, when it is due back, when it actually came back, and what state it was in when it did. Loans are written for a number of days, normally about a hundred and eighty, never longer than two years, and the shortest we would bother with is a month. And a type never physically leaves the building. If somebody wants a type we send photographs, and the loan record gets ticked as photographs only.

We are the research office, and the reporting we owe the funders is currently three people with spreadsheets, so here is what we think we need. Start with people: every researcher sits in one department, and we hold their ORCID, career stage, appointment date and their h-index, which we refresh from Scopus -- it is a stored number, not something we compute. Departments roll up into faculties and carry a headcount. Grants are the centre of it. A grant is awarded by one funding agency (we keep the agency's country, its type -- national council, charity, industry, EU -- and its overhead rate) and has one lead researcher, a title, an awarded amount, start and end dates, a duration in months and a status. Durations run between 6 and 60 months in practice. Awards are wildly spread: median around 220 thousand, from small travel awards up to programme grants in the tens of millions, so log-normal with a log mean near 12.3. The complication is that a grant has several investigators, not just the lead, each with a role and an FTE fraction between 0.05 and 1.0, so that has to be its own thing keyed on the grant and the person together. Anything awarded over 2 million needs council sign-off, and for a charity funder that threshold drops to half a million. Then publications -- about 340,000 records and 900,000 authorship links, which is why authorship also has to be keyed on the paper and the person, with the author position and whether they were corresponding. A paper sits in one journal (name, ISSN, publisher, impact factor, open-access flag) and carries a DOI, a publication date, an article type -- we lump journal articles, conference papers and preprints in the same place -- and a citation count. Impact factor is never negative and is log-normally spread. Citation counts are never negative and about as skewed as data gets: Zipf-ish with exponent around 1.6, a handful of papers with thousands of citations and most of them under five. Article processing charges are recorded on the paper, and if the journal is not open access that charge should be zero. Papers acknowledge grants, and a paper can acknowledge several while a grant gets acknowledged by many, so that link is keyed on both as well. Progress reporting: each grant has milestone reports with a due date, a submitted date, an outcome and a reviewer score on a 1-5 scale -- mostly 4s at about 44 percent, then 24 percent 5s, 22 percent 3s, 7 percent 2s and 3 percent 1s. Spend is posted against the grant with a category, an amount and a posting date; equipment purchases just come through as one of those categories, we do not track assets separately.

This is for the reserve's collaring work, and I should say up front that I am a field ecologist, not a database person. We put transmitters on animals and we need to stop losing the data in spreadsheets. So, the animals first.
