Each one we handle gets a field name -- usually something the team makes up, Notch, Big Mama, that sort of thing -- and we record the species, the sex, roughly how old we think it is, what it weighed when we had it down, and the date of that first capture. Weights: the cows come in around forty kilos and the bulls more like fifty-five, so call it high forties on average with maybe ten kilos of spread either way. The smallest we have ever collared was a yearling at twelve kilos and the biggest bull went ninety-five. We also need to know whether the animal is still alive as far as we know, because that changes what we do with its collar. Now the collars. People here say collars, tags, transmitters, units -- it is all the same object. Each one has a serial on the housing and a type, and the record needs to say which animal it went on, the day it was fitted, the day it came off, and who did the fitting, usually one of the rangers and sometimes the vet -- just the name is fine, we are not building a staff directory. The collar is programmed to take a position every so many hours, four times a day mostly, and the battery lasts the better part of a year if we are lucky, less in the wet season, so we note how many days we got out of it. When a collar comes off there is a reason recorded, and one rule is absolute: if we have confirmed the animal dead, that collar record closes as recovered off the carcass, no other reason is allowed. Then the positions themselves, which is the big pile -- we are at just under three hundred animals across eleven seasons and a few hundred thousand fixes. Each fix is a time, a latitude and longitude, how many satellites the unit saw, how good it reckons the position is in metres, and the battery voltage at the time. Most fixes see seven or eight satellites, and if it saw fewer than four we mark the fix as dodgy so the analysts drop it. One more thing: we only work in the one reserve, so every position should fall between 24.5 and 21.8 degrees south -- anything outside that is a glitch, not an animal.

Materials lab, mechanical testing group. Right now every test goes into a workbook per project and nobody can answer 'show me all the quench-and-tempered material that failed elongation'. Here is roughly what we hold. Stock arrives as batches -- supplier, heat number, receipt date, mass in kg -- and each batch is one alloy grade, where the grade record is just the code, the alloy family and the nominal density. Batches get heat treated: a process name, a soak temperature, a soak time in minutes and a quench medium. For the study work we deliberately sweep soak temperature uniformly between 820 and 960 C, and the furnaces themselves will not go outside 500 to 1200. Specimens are machined out of a batch and tagged with the treatment they went through; each one has a specimen code, a geometry, a gauge diameter between 3 and 25 mm, a gauge length, the machining date, and a stamped condition code -- as-received, annealed, or quench-and-tempered. That stamped code matters because the acceptance bands differ: as-received material should yield between 250 and 380 MPa, quench-and-tempered between 400 and 620. Across everything we have tested, yield comes out around 345 MPa with sd 22, UTS around 512 with sd 30, and elongation 24.5 percent with sd 4.1, and elongation is physically between 0 and 60. A tensile test names the specimen and the frame it ran on, plus the timestamp, the strain rate, yield, UTS, elongation, the operator's initials and a result status -- anything under 8 percent elongation goes to status 'REVIEW' automatically. The frames are their own record (name, load cell capacity in kN, manufacturer, last calibration date), and the small frames under 100 kN can only be driven quasi-statically, so a test on one of those runs at 0.001 per second or slower. Hardness is separate because we take several indents per specimen: method, indent number, load in kgf and the value, which sits around 178 with sd 12 and can physically be anywhere from 20 to 950. Broken tensile specimens sometimes get a fractography write-up against the test -- fracture mode, an image path on the share, and free-text observations. Scale is modest: about 4,200 specimens and 11,000 indents.

Survey ops here. The thing I want modelled is the frame archive -- people call them frames, exposures or images and it is all one object, so pick a word and stick to it. We tile the sky into fields; a field has a name, a tile number, its centre in RA and Dec, the galactic latitude, and a running count of how many times it has been visited, which averages about a dozen a season. Every frame belongs to one field and one filter. There are five filters, u g r i z, and each carries its own central wavelength and a photometric zero point, so they are worth their own record rather than a bare code on the frame. On the frame itself we log the start time, the exposure length, airmass, seeing, sky background and the limiting magnitude we reached, plus a quality flag. Nearly all frames are 30 seconds -- call it 55 percent -- with 30 percent at 90 and the rest the long 300 second ones. Airmass is between 1.0 and 2.5 by scheduling. Seeing typically comes in around 1.15 arcseconds and it is skewed, because a bad night is far worse than a good night is good, so log-normal rather than Gaussian -- log mean about 0.14, log variance about 0.10. Sky background is all over the place depending on the moon and I would not put a number on it. If seeing is worse than 2.5 or airmass over 2.0, the frame gets flagged 'BAD'. Then the detections, which are the volume: 210,000 frames and about 4 million source rows. Each detection points at the frame it came out of and has its own RA and Dec, a magnitude and a magnitude error, an extended-source flag, and a bitmask of processing flags whose meaning honestly lives in the pipeline code rather than anywhere documented. Magnitudes pile up near the survey limit, mean about 21.4 with sd 1.6, and nothing outside 12 to 24.5 is real. Detections off a frame flagged BAD are not published, and we carry that as a flag on the detection rather than working it out at query time. The observers also keep a night log in a wiki, which is not part of this.

I run the shift schedule and the logbook for the beamline, so I have been asked to describe what we actually need to keep -- which is not the physics, the physics people have their own systems, but the record of the running. A run is what we call a stretch where the beam was on and we were recording. People say run, fill, spill, sometimes 'the file' when they mean the run, and they all end up meaning the run as far as we are concerned. We number them, and we are at about eighteen hundred and fifty since the beamline came back up. For each one we write down when it started and when it stopped, what energy the beam was at, what target was in, how much charge went through the target by the end of it, who the shift leader was -- just the name, we are not making a staff system out of this -- whether the run was any good, and then a free-text comment, which is where the actual story lives. Energy is mostly 12 GeV, that is nearly half our runs, then a good chunk at 10.6, some at 6.4 and a handful of low-energy ones at 2.2. Nothing above 13 and nothing below half a GeV has ever been taken here. Charge is very lumpy -- most runs get a few tens of microcoulombs but the aborted ones get almost nothing, so the spread is enormously skewed, log-normal if you want a name for it. If a run got less than one microcoulomb it is junk, full stop. Then there are the detector subsystems -- the drift chambers, the calorimeter, the Cherenkov and so on -- and each of those has a name, the group responsible for it and its nominal high voltage. The part I think is the hard part: for every run, every subsystem has a status. Whether it was actually in the readout, how many dead channels it had that night, what voltage it was really set at, and a note. So it is one entry per run and subsystem together. Dead channels are usually two or three, occasionally a lot more, and no subsystem here has more than two hundred channels. Voltages run from zero up to about three thousand. If a subsystem was not in the readout at all we just put zero dead channels for it rather than leaving it blank. And a run is only ever called good if every subsystem was in the readout -- if the calorimeter was out, the best that run gets is suspect. Roughly seven in ten runs come out good, about two in ten suspect and one in ten junk.
